World.title: Twelve students receive Refrigeration and Air Conditioning scholarships as Belize marks World Ozone Day
World.content:
Twelve students receive Refrigeration and Air Conditioning scholarships as Belize marks World Ozone Day

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Department of the Environment (DOE), through the National Ozone Unit, awarded 12 scholarships under the Refrigeration and Air Conditioning (RAC) Scholarship Programme.

The recipients are enrolled in RAC programmes at ITVETs in Belize City, Orange Walk, and Stann Creek, and will receive support for the 2026–2027 academic year, including tuition, a toolbox of servicing tools, and personal protective equipment.

Three of the twelve recipients are female trainees, marking a step toward greater participation of women in the RAC sector.

The ceremony coincided with World Ozone Day, observed annually on September 16. This year’s theme, “Global Action for a Cooler Planet,” marks ten years of sustainable cooling efforts under the Kigali Amendment.

The DOE said the scholarships reflect Belize’s ongoing transition toward lower-global-warming-potential refrigerants and more efficient cooling technologies, which requires a pipeline of skilled technicians.

Through the programme, the DOE said it is investing in the next generation of RAC professionals to help promote safe, efficient, and environmentally responsible cooling practices going forward.

The twelve scholarship recipients are Zadiel Dias, Patrick Zetina, Samuel Alamilla, Brandon Ysaguirre, Gerardo Magana, Milcar Ku, Rilma Urbina, Edwardo Coc, Cierra Teck, Jahleel Flowers, Erwin Colon, and Dorda Castillo.

World.title: Garbage dumped at Yo Chen Village entrance cleaned up, Department of Environment steps up surveillance
World.content:
Garbage dumped at Yo Chen Village entrance cleaned up, Department of Environment steps up surveillance

By Zoila Palma: The Department of the Environment (DOE) has cleaned up a garbage site at the entrance of Yo Chen Village following a media report regarding the issue.

The DOE said it investigated the matter promptly and worked with the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing (MIDH) to address the concern.

The area has since been cleaned and placed under surveillance to help prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.

The DOE is reminding the public that under the Pollution Regulations, it is an offence to place or permit refuse to be placed on any land without written permission from the department.

The DOE is encouraging community members to remain vigilant and report instances of illegal dumping at this or any other location.

World.title: Belize @45 History Tour brings dialogue on Independence to Orange Walk Town
World.content:
Belize @45 History Tour brings dialogue on Independence to Orange Walk Town

By Zoila Palma: The Belize @45 Magical History Tour made its way through Orange Walk Town on September 15, continuing a series of events aimed at encouraging dialogue and reflection on the country’s history.

The tour is led by the Institute for Social & Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) in partnership with historian Dr. Assad Shoman, and focuses on Belize’s path to independence, the experiences that have shaped its national story, and ongoing conversations around decolonization.

During the day, the tour engaged students from New Hope High School, Muffles College High School, and Orange Walk Technical High School in discussions on Belize’s history, national identity, and the range of experiences that continue to shape the country. Students were given the opportunity to ask questions and share their perspectives on how the past connects to present-day Belize.

That evening, the tour held a public forum at the Banquitas House of Culture, bringing together community leaders and residents of Orange Walk Town. The forum allowed attendees to discuss the country’s shared history and consider how a deeper understanding of the past could inform Belize’s future direction.

ISCR-NICH thanked the students, educators, community leaders, and residents who took part in the day’s events, noting their questions and input as central to the tour’s goals.

The Magical History Tour is made possible through the National Celebrations Commission and the National Institute of Culture and History, along with partners including the University of Belize.

World.title: International News: Trump names Haiti security expert Austin Holmes as Ambassador nominee
World.content:
International News: Trump names Haiti security expert Austin Holmes as Ambassador nominee

By Zoila Palma: U.S. President Donald Trump has nominated Florida businessman Austin Holmes to serve as the next U.S. ambassador to Haiti, as the Caribbean nation continues to grapple with a severe political and security crisis.

Holmes’ nomination was submitted to the U.S. Senate on Monday, September 14, and he must receive Senate confirmation before taking up the diplomatic post.

Holmes has longstanding ties to Haiti through humanitarian and security work and has previously lived in the country with his family.

Earlier this year, he testified before a Senate appropriations subcommittee during a hearing examining U.S. security and foreign assistance priorities in Haiti.

During his testimony, Holmes said he has participated in security operations in Haiti, including kidnapping recoveries and emergency extractions. He cited the 2023 recovery of American humanitarian worker Jeff Frazier, who was kidnapped by gangs while participating in a food distribution mission and held captive for 43 days. Holmes said his team “successfully recovered” Frazier.

Holmes said his approach to operations in Haiti is based on local knowledge and long-term engagement. “Deep cultural fluency, long-term presence and operational leadership rooted in local context” have driven the results achieved by his teams, he said, adding that many of his personnel are Haitian and Haitian American with local experience, language skills and relationships.

World.title: Police intercept pickup carrying suspected uncustomed goods in Orange Walk
World.content:
Police intercept pickup carrying suspected uncustomed goods in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police intercepted a pickup truck near the Blue Creek Dam in Orange Walk earlier this month and reportedly discovered several boxes and sacks of food products suspected to be uncustomed goods.

According to police information, personnel from the North HIT conducted a staging operation in the area between approximately 5:30 p.m. and 8:40 p.m. on Friday, September 4.

During the operation, officers intercepted a white Dodge Ram being driven by a 25 year old man from San Felipe Village.

A search of the vehicle reportedly led to the discovery of six boxes of oxtail, five sacks of cabbage and 15 sacks of onions.

The driver and the goods were subsequently escorted to the Orange Walk Customs Department.

Police say the matter was handed over to a Customs officer for further action.

No information was provided on the estimated value of the goods or whether any charges have been filed.

World.title: Police chase ends with reckless driving charge in Orange Walk
World.content:
Police chase ends with reckless driving charge in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 24 year old Orange Walk man has been charged with reckless driving following an early morning police pursuit.

According to police information, officers were conducting mobile patrol on San Narciso Street at around 1:20 a.m. on September 15 when their attention was drawn to a black motorcycle with a defective rear light.

Police say the rider was signalled to stop but allegedly drove off and began swerving from side to side along the street.

Officers reportedly followed the motorcycle for approximately five minutes before managing to intercept the rider.

Police say the man told officers he had not been trying to escape.

A search was conducted and nothing incriminating was found. Checks on the motorcycle documents also reportedly showed that the licence and insurance were up to date.

The rider was then informed that he was being detained for reckless driving and was escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station.

Police identified him as Nathan J. Navarrete, 24, a labourer of Santa Familia Street, Orange Walk.

He was later formally arrested and charged with reckless driving.

World.title: Jamaica, US finalise operating procedures related to TCNs
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith confirmed that the United States and Jamaica have finalised operating procedures related to the memorandum of understanding for TCNs that was signed earlier this year..

JAMAICA could soon receive its first batch of third-country nationals (TCNs) from the United States (US) as Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith confirmed that both governments have finalised operating procedures related to the memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was signed earlier this year.

Jamaica now joins 30 countries, including several members of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), which have similar arrangements with the US Government amid its ongoing crackdown on illegal immigration.

“After internal consultations and thoughtful negotiations, both governments have now finalised operating procedures related to the MOU in order to settle the guard rails and parameters underpinning the agreement. The arrangements were also finalised, taking into account Jamaica’s capacity constraints and our belief in the principles of safe, orderly, and lawful migration,” said Johnson Smith, speaking at a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House on Wednesday.

The agreement, Johnson Smith clarified, will see 25 TCNs entering the country biweekly. While here, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) will provide basic services, like health care and counselling, to help with their transition.

The minister reiterated that under no circumstance will more than 25 TCNs be present in the island.

“We have also not agreed to receive 10,000 individuals. We have negotiated guard rails to address capacity constraints, and have, therefore, agreed to a maximum of 25 individuals per two-week period, which the IOM will, of course, be on a continuous basis making arrangements for their return.

“Furthermore, this arrangement will be suspended if 10 TCNs apply to remain in Jamaica through asylum procedures or other humanitarian applications. This, again, is specifically negotiated by Jamaica,” said Johnson Smith.

She further explained that TCNs were not deportees but the nationals of other countries who entered the US unlawfully and are being returned to their home countries through the IOM’s Assisted Voluntary Return Programme.

Johnson Smith added that while she is aware that some countries have opted to accept TCNs with criminal records, Jamaica will only facilitate those with no previous convictions.

“The Government reiterates its commitment to working with the IOM and the Government of the United States of America to ensure that all arrangements for the next stage of TCN implementation are appropriately governed and implemented in accordance with both our domestic laws and international law,” she said.

Additionally, while acknowledging Minister of National Security Dr Horace Chang’s previous commitment to release the agreement, Johnson Smith explained that the MOU’s bilateral status prevents it from being made public.

“As indicated, this is not a unilateral arrangement; it is a bilateral arrangement, and one in which they [the United States] have not generally released their agreements, and they have not agreed to release this one,” she said.

“I give you every assurance as well that we have all shared all the relevant and material matters, provisions, in relation to the matter. So there’s nothing being hidden per se, but as you would note, even under the ATI [Access to Information Act], bilateral agreements, security agreements, arrangements that are sensitive to relations between countries and otherwise are treated differently from other agreements,” explained Johnson Smith.

Despite not being able to give an official start date for when the first TCNs are expected to arrive, Johnson Smith affirmed that Jamaicans will be regularly updated as conversations advance.

World.title: Family services shake-up
World.content:
The Ministry of Education has severed ties with the heads of two of its primary family services agencies — the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) and the National Parenting Support Commission (NPSC) — reportedly to undertake a major shift in their operations, the Jamaica Observer has learnt.

As part of that shake-up, chief executive officer of the CPFSA Laurette Adams-Thomas, who took the helm of the agency in October 2023, will demit office next month.

In a brief response to the Observer, Adams-Thomas said her contract expires on October 1, 2026 and she was “officially notified on July 23, 2026” that it would “not be renewed”.

The CPFSA is an executive agency which was formed from the merger of the Child Development Agency (CDA) and the Office of Children’s Registry (OCR). Adams-Thomas, an educator and social worker, took over its leadership following an eight-year stint as general manager of the largest infirmary in the Caribbean — Jamaica’s Golden Age Home — where she had oversight responsibly for protection and welfare services for more than 450 indigent people from the parishes of Kingston and St Andrew. Prior to assuming that position, she was interim executive director/registrar at the OCR, where her focus was centred on ensuring that an effective system was maintained to facilitate the confidential receipt, assessment, and referral of reports of known or suspected cases of child abuse.

She holds a master’s degree in business administration, bachelor of science in human resource management, and a number of certifications in leadership, corporate governance and strategic planning.

In the meantime, the Observer was reliably informed on Monday that NPSC CEO Kaysia Kerr “is no longer with” the entity. Efforts to get an official response from Kerr were unsuccessful. A pre-recorded message on her personal mobile phone directed all callers with queries related to the commission to contact the education ministry or the commission itself.

A source with knowledge of the development said the ministry had decided to disengage with Kerr due to a breakdown in relations.

She took the helm of the commission in 2017, succeeding Dr Patrece Charles. In an interview with the

Observer at the time, Kerr said she hoped to craft and design programmes for parents and children of all 13 categories of disabilities, move the organisation out of eastern Jamaica to serve other parishes, take some of the programmes internationally, and get the unit to a stage where it generates income.

The former NPSC head has a solid background in education and has completed studies in business and professional management at Nova Southeastern University, along with a first degree in special education and a master’s in administration and supervision from Western Carolina University.

The commission coordinates a wide range of services for parents and also delivers programmes that build parenting skills and promote parental involvement in education.

The Government of Jamaica mandated the establishment of the NPSC in response to the 2004 task force report on the status of education in Jamaica.

The NPSC began operating in January 2013.

World.title: Global aviation squeeze
World.content:
Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose says Jamaica needs more airline seats to meet strong demand as carriers face aircraft shortages and higher fuel costs amid the impact of the war in the Middle East.

Addressing the media during the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) forum in Ocho Rios on Tuesday, Rose said Jamaica’s immediate challenge is not a lack of demand, but having enough airline seats to bring visitors to the island.

“The immediate thing that we do need is more seats into the destination. The good news is, and I really want this to land, the good news is the airlines know this. The airlines are preparing because they don’t want to leave business on the table. The airlines know that the demand is there. The airlines are preparing to put in additional flights,” he said.

His comments come as Jamaica’s tourism industry continues its recovery following last year’s Hurricane Melissa, with hotel capacity gradually returning and airlines looking to adjust their schedules accordingly.

Rose said the global aviation industry is itself under pressure, making it difficult for airlines to simply add capacity whenever demand rises. He pointed to higher fuel costs linked to developments in the Middle East, as well as problems affecting aircraft engines, servicing and maintenance.

“As you all know, there are global pressures now on the aviation space. What’s happening out there in the Middle East has really impacted oil prices, which impacts fuel prices. In the best of days, the margins are exceedingly thin for airlines. You’re going to add this increase in jet fuel, it puts additional pressure on the industry,” he explained.

“Along with that, there is a shortage of aircraft because of issues to do with the engines, which I won’t really bore you all with. There are some service and maintenance things that are going on, which means a lot of aircraft have been pulled out of service,” he added.

The result, he said, is that Jamaica cannot depend on unlimited airline capacity, even as demand remains strong

“Airlines across the world don’t have infinite aircraft. That means that seats are not infinite. When the seats are full, the seats are full. Because of the demand that we have been generating for Jamaica, the vast majority of the flights into Jamaica are full,” he added.

Still, Rose said the outlook for airlift is positive, with airlines preparing to increase service as more hotel rooms become available.

He said airlines are also preparing to return to the flight schedules that existed before Hurricane Melissa, although they first have to resolve their own aircraft availability issues and factor in Jamaica’s accommodation capacity.

World.title: Sugar Cain promises powerful music, deep message
World.content:
Members of the cast of Sugar Cain, Father Ho Lung and Friends’ upcoming stage production, rehearse the songs for the show, last Wednesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

A sober message of moral commitment complemented by powerful music is in store for audiences at Father Ho Lung and Friends’ upcoming stage production Sugar Cain.

“It’s a show that I think everybody will be able to relate to, even if you are not Jamaican,” music director for the group Jody Anne Johnson told the Jamaica Observer last Wednesday, just before the start of rehearsals for the production scheduled to run over two weekends — October 3-4 and October 10-11 at the National Arena in St Andrew.

“There are a lot of emotions that we go through every single day that will be explored, and the music is powerful… in kind of fuelling those emotions and setting the stage for the whole story to unfold,” added Johnson, who described the music as a “kind of melting pot of different genres”.

“We have traditional Jamaican music; there’s mento, there’s reggae — a lot of nice Jamaican reggae. We also have a little bit of hip hop; there are ballads; a little bit of music from the 60s, 70s; and then it comes up to dancehall as well,” Johnson explained, adding that the show contains 20 songs.

The script and all 20 tracks were written by Ho Lung in keeping with the tradition of his stage productions over the years, but Johnson, who took over from Wynton Williams as music director in 2019 after joining the group in 2003, wouldn’t be drawn when asked whether Sugar Cain tops all the previous productions.

“You remember them for different things. I remember Moses for all the tech — all of the interesting lights and special effects. And the Messiah is remembered because it is the story of our Lord and Saviour when He was crucified and risen. So each story has a special kind of brand that it leaves on our audience. So, I wouldn’t want to compare,” she told the Observer.

“I believe, though, that the music in Sugar Cane is a little bit more current, because of the addition of the hip hop, and we have some dancehall and stuff like that. But I think it’s going to be a powerful story… and all the stories that Father Ho Lung has done are powerful,” Johnson added.

She reinforced Director Hugh Douse’s observation, shared in an earlier interview with the Observer, that the ego often associated with artistic personalities is conspicuously absent among the cast, whose members have instead embraced a spirit of humility and collective purpose.

“The persons in this group are very easy to work with. We’ve been doing this for a long time, so we kind of have an idea of how things are to go, exactly what is to be done. So a lot of those initial growing pains where you have different ideas and people getting at each other, it doesn’t really happen,” Johnson said.

World.title: KINGSTON BOOKSHOP’S $1-B EXPANSION
World.content:
Kingston Bookshop’s new distribution centre on Lyndhurst Road in St Andrew.

Kingston Bookshop has pumped approximately $1 billion into a new distribution centre on Lyndhurst Road in St Andrew as its wholesale business takes a larger share of sales.

The company told the Jamaica Observer that business-to-business (B2B) sales now account for approximately 25 per cent of revenue, up from just under 20 per cent about four years ago as it widens the range of products supplied to schools, bookstores, pharmacies, offices, and other businesses across Jamaica.

That growth had begun to stretch an operation that was still being run from three separate warehouse properties on King Street in downtown Kingston.

The new Lyndhurst Road facility, which became operational in May 2025, brings warehousing, purchasing, and business-to-business sales together in one location and gives Kingston Bookshop significantly more room to handle stock.

Director of Strategy and Innovation Shauna Fuller Clarke said the company had reached the point where its old warehouse arrangement no longer matched the scale of the wholesale business.

“As that side of the business grew, so did our warehousing and operational requirements. At one point we were operating from three separate warehouse locations, so the decision to develop the Lyndhurst Road facility was a strategic one,” Fuller Clarke told the Business Observer.

“It allowed us to consolidate our warehousing, B2B sales, and purchasing operations in one location, creating a more efficient operation and, importantly, enabling us to provide better service to our customers.”

The approximately 42,000-square-foot facility includes a 39,000-square-foot warehouse and another 3,000 square feet for the company’s B2B sales and purchasing teams.

Kingston Bookshop previously operated with about 34,000 square feet of warehouse space across 72, 74, and 80 King Street.

The gain at Lyndhurst Road, however, is larger than the difference in floor space suggests.

Fuller Clarke said the height of the building and the racking system allow the company to make far greater use of vertical storage, taking usable capacity to the equivalent of approximately 50,000 square feet.

“The investment was, therefore, about much more than simply adding square footage. It was about creating the infrastructure to operate more efficiently, improve inventory management, and better support our retail and B2B customers,” she said.

The expansion comes more than three decades after Kingston Bookshop first moved into wholesale distribution. The company said that business began with stationery in the 1990s and later expanded into textbooks, general books, games, and technology products. It has recently added sports gear and equipment, particularly for schools.

That widening product range has helped Kingston Bookshop deepen its relationship with existing wholesale customers rather than relying only on traditional book sales.

“As our customers seek to diversify their own product offerings, we have been able to respond by supplying more of what they need rather than limiting our B2B operation to traditional books and stationery,” Fuller Clarke said.

The company now supplies customers in all parishes through its own delivery fleet.

New plan for former warehouses

The move to Lyndhurst Road is also changing how Kingston Bookshop uses its downtown real estate.

The company has already vacated 72 King Street, which was leased, while an expansion of its retail footprint at the 74 King Street head office is under active consideration.

That leaves the other warehouse property, at 80 King Street — one of its busiest retail stores — as the likely candidate for a mix of Kingston Bookshop operations and commercial rental space similar to what the company has adopted in Portmore, St Catherine, with the Script Cafe. The location is particularly significant given its position along one of downtown Kingston’s main retail corridors, where a large volume of shopping activity is concentrated.

“One option under active consideration is expanding our retail footprint at 74 King Street, while another property may incorporate a mix of Kingston Bookshop operations and commercial rental space, similar to the mixed-use approach we have successfully adopted at our 31 East Plaza location in Portmore,” she said.

The possible expansion downtown comes after Kingston Bookshop closed its Boulevard location earlier this year, but Fuller Clarke said that decision should not be read as a pullback from physical retail.

She told the Business Observer that stores remain Kingston Bookshop’s largest sales channel, even as wholesale contributes more and online purchasing continues to grow.

“The two decisions should not be viewed as Kingston Bookshop moving away from physical retail. They reflect our ongoing assessment of how and where we deploy our resources across the business,” she said.

“Our physical stores remain our largest sales channel, while B2B now represents approximately 25 per cent of sales and continues to grow. We are also steadily seeing increased purchasing through our e-commerce platform.”

Kingston Bookshop is continuing to invest across those three areas, but Fuller Clarke said expansion will be driven by where the company sees a commercial case rather than simply adding more locations.

“Our focus is not expansion simply for the sake of adding locations. We are looking at how we can strengthen the business across our retail, B2B, and digital channels while improving the customer experience and the efficiency of our operations,” she said.

That investment is being made at a time when one of Kingston Bookshop’s most important retail periods has produced little growth.

Fuller Clarke disclosed that revenue from the company’s stores during the 2026 back-to-school period was broadly similar to 2025 and, after accounting for inflation, the company considers sales relatively flat year on year.

The company continues to see strong demand for early childhood and primary-level material, including supplementary resources for Primary Exit Profile preparation, but purchasing at the secondary level has become more selective.

Parents have access to the Government’s textbook rental programme, second-hand books, online resources, and are increasingly deciding which items must be bought immediately and which can wait.

“Given the cost of preparing children for school, particularly for households with more than one child, parents are understandably making very deliberate choices about what they purchase,” Fuller Clarke said.

According to the company, workbooks and other books considered essential tend to be purchased first, while stationery and other supplies are sometimes bought later.

The company is also reporting a rise in parents choosing to pay for purchases in instalments.

“We have also seen more parents taking advantage of our lay-away programme, which allows them to make a deposit and pay towards their purchases over time,” Fuller Clarke said. “That provides families with another way of managing the cost of back-to-school preparation without having to meet the entire expense at once.”

The investment at Lyndhurst Road also leaves Kingston Bookshop with additional capacity that could eventually support more business outside Jamaica as well.

The company has previously supplied special orders to customers in smaller Caribbean islands, although Jamaica remains its main wholesale market.

Fuller Clarke reasoned that while the new facility puts Kingston Bookshop in a better position to pursue opportunities elsewhere in the region, the cost of distribution will determine how aggressively it moves.

“The cost of moving stock across the Caribbean can be significant, so both demand and logistics are important considerations in determining where and how we expand. We, therefore, see the Caribbean as an area of opportunity, but one where expansion has to be driven by sustainable demand and commercially viable distribution arrangements,” she said.

World.title: Visual Vibe to take screens off-grid with solar partnership
World.content:
A Visual Vibe outdoor screen at Mandela Park in Half-Way-Tree, St Andrew.

Digital advertising company Visual Vibe Limited is moving to take its entire network of outdoor screens off the national grid as it seeks to halve energy costs and eliminate outage-related downtime.

Following a recent partnership with Florida-based renewables firm Rush Hour Engineering, the Kintyre Holdings (JA) Limited subsidiary is getting ready to install solar power across its network of outdoor advertising screens.

Kintyre Holdings founder, chairman, and CEO, Tyrone Wilson, who also heads Visual Vibe, said the plan is to have every screen in the network — existing and new — powered by solar energy.

Visual Vibe currently operates 14 outdoor digital signs, for which energy costs now averages about $24 million annually, but the company will be adding another 15 screens shortly, which Wilson said could push annual electricity costs to as much as $60 million as the network expands.

The solar roll-out is, however, expected to reduce those costs by at least 50 per cent, bringing yearly energy expenditure to about $30 million.

“Electricity cost has long been one of the digital advertising business’s largest single monthly expenses, and with the war pushing up gas prices, we don’t see that easing anytime soon. So we had no other choice than to tap into solar,” Wilson told the Jamaica Observer.

“If we can cut our electricity bill by about 50 to 60 per cent, that would lift Visual Vibe’s profits enough so that we can keep funding growth from our own cash flow instead of seeking outside investment,” he further said to the Business Observer.

Stressing the need to have more efficient systems, Wilson said the new partnership also allows Visual Vibe to offer greater reliability to its clients during periods of disruption.

“Reliability is the currency of advertising. When a brand invests in our network, their campaign must be on screen every single time — and rising energy costs and grid outages have been a real challenge for our entire industry, and so this partnership with Rush Hour Engineering aims to solve those issues permanently “ Wilson said.

“By taking our screens off-grid, we are eliminating downtime completely while protecting our advertisers’ investment, as we also build the kind of resilient, sustainable media infrastructure that Jamaica deserves. It is a multimillion-dollar commitment to our clients and to the environment,” he added.

The solar programme forms a part of broader upgrades and expansion of Visual Vibe’s network and coincides with the company’s latest quest to deploy its newest high-resolution screens to flagship sites and premium locations along some of the city’s busiest corridor.

Phase one of the solar installation is scheduled to begin this week in the new Kingston area before being rolled out across the wider network.

Visual Vibe was acquired by Kintyre (trading then as iCreate) about three years ago for more than $500 million. Since then, the company has continued to expand its digital advertising operations, which now account for a substantial portion of group revenue.

In addition to its outdoor signs, Visual Vibe operates more than 50 indoor screens. Through a multichannel model combining outdoor billboards, indoor screens, and mobile formats, the company seeks to give advertisers multiple ways of reaching their target audiences.

Rush Hour Engineering President and CEO Edwin Xiao, commenting on the partnership, said the project demonstrates the potential for renewable energy to transform commercial infrastructure.

“We are proud to partner with Visual Vibe on a project of this scale,” Xiao said.

“Powering Jamaica’s largest digital advertising network entirely with solar energy demonstrates what renewable technology can do for the country’s commercial infrastructure. This partnership sets a new standard for how media assets are powered across the region.”

Rush Hour Engineering is a provider of engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) services for residential and commercial projects. In addition to solar systems, its capabilities include electric vehicle chargers; LED lighting; and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) design.

The Florida-based company, as a Tesla-certified partner, also provides energy-efficiency and renewable-energy solutions aimed at reducing electricity costs and carbon emissions.

As Kintyre doubles down on opportunities arising from the shift towards renewable energy, the Jamaica Stock Exchange-listed holding company earlier this year announced, through a separate partnership with Rush Hour Engineering, plans to strategically enter the EV market as it also positions to capitalise on developments in the transport sector.

“Renewable energy is the future, and we’re investing in it. It has been on our radar for a very long time, but we are now actively tapping into its potential,” Wilson said.

World.title: Raheem Sterling pleads guilty to dangerous driving after Lamborghini crash
World.content:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - AUGUST 02: Raheem Sterling #17 of Chelsea FC looks on during the pre-season friendly match Borussia Dortmund at Soldier Field on August 2, 2023 in Chicago, Illinois. Justin Casterline/Getty Images/AFPJustin Casterline / GETTY IMAGES NORTH AMERICA / Getty Images via AFP

LONDON, United Kingdom (AFP) — Footballer Raheem Sterling pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving after he crashed his Lamborghini on a motorway in May.

The 31-year-old also admitted possession of six nitrous oxide canisters for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen for analysis when he appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court, about 50 miles southwest of London.

Sterling, who attended court wearing a black suit jacket, black trousers, black shoes and a dark top, was arrested after crashing on the M3 on the morning of May 28.

Police said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.

READ: Raheem Sterling arrested for suspected drug-driving

The winger won 82 England caps, the last of which came at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

Sterling made his senior debut at Liverpool before joining Manchester City in 2015, winning four Premier League titles and other silverware at the Etihad.

He left for Chelsea in 2022 but subsequently fell out of favour and spent the 2024/25 season on loan at Arsenal.

Sterling joined Feyenoord on a short-term deal in February, playing eight times in the Eredivisie.

World.title: JAMAICA gets Disney boost
World.content:
Disney Cruine Line’s Disney Destiny will make its inaugural call on Jamaica next month.

OCHO RIOS, St Ann — Jamaica’s tourism industry is set to receive a big boost on October 13 when one of Disney Cruise Line’s top modern vessels, Disney Destiny, makes its inaugural call at Falmouth’s historic cruise port bringing just under 2,800 passengers to the island.

The announcement was made by Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) Deputy Director of Tourism for the Americas Philip Rose during Monday’s opening of the Jamaica Product Exchange (JAPEX) at Moon Palace Jamaica in Ocho Rios.

The arrival of Disney Destiny adds to the growing roster of Disney Cruise Line vessels calling on Jamaica, alongside ships operated by Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Princess Cruises, and Virgin Voyages.

From January to July this year, according to data shared by Rose, Jamaica recorded 234 cruise calls and 736,372 passengers. Montego Bay, Falmouth and Ocho Rios accounted for most visits, while four ships also called at Port Antonio and Kingston.

Rose pointed out that the cruise industry remains an important partner, particularly in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa — which hit sections of Jamaica last October — and reminded that it could provide a pathway to attracting visitors for longer stays.

“It’s often said you can come down, get a little taste of Jamaica on the cruise ship, then we can convert them, or they go back home and say that was too much of a teaser, and they come back,” he said.

The JTB official said cruise visitors are encouraged to venture beyond established resort centres, particularly towards Kingston and Port Antonio, to experience a wider range of the Jamaican product.

Reacting to news of Disney Destiny’s impending visit, Chukka Caribbean Adventures deputy executive chairman and Jamaica Tourist Board member John Byles pointed to the benefit it will bring to local artisans and attractions. According to Byles, Disney passengers tend to leave the ship and spend on Jamaican tourism experiences.

He welcomed the impending Disney Destiny call, describing it as a sign of the company’s growing trust in Jamaica.

“It is always very heartening to see the confidence that a brand like Disney continues to show for the Jamaica product and Jamaica destination,” Byles told buyers and suppliers attending the first day of JAPEX, a staple on the tourism calendar.

The trade show is being held under the theme ’Jamaica Reimagined’. Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association (JHTA) President O’Brian Heron used his address to stress that Jamaica’s recovery from Hurricane Melissa must lead to a stronger and more adaptable tourism industry.

“Resilience is not simply about recovering, It is truly about what comes next,” he said.

He noted that changing travellers, technology and artificial intelligence were reshaping how people discover and experience destinations, requiring Jamaica to embrace innovation without sacrificing its authenticity.

The JHTA head said Jamaica’s strongest differentiator remains its people, pointing to the warmth of the welcome, culture, creativity, music, spirit, and food.

Officially declaring the trade show open during an address delivered virtually, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett stressed the importance of adapting to shifts in the global tourism marketplace, strengthening competitiveness and building resilience while safeguarding the characteristics that make Jamaica distinctive.

“An event like JAPEX is never just a trade show. Last year, JAPEX facilitated an estimated US$100 million in contracts and business negotiations. Behind that figure are real hotels, real workers, real families, and real communities. That is precisely why, in fact, we do this,” Bartlett said.

World.title: King Charles: Pace of AI is ‘deeply concerning’
World.content:
He will say that “those in our world who value our humanity and its vital moral component are anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny.”

And he will warn that the “decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations,” calling on attendees “not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world.”

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar are set to attend. Scale AI CEO Francis deSouza and senior figures from Anthropic and Cohere are on the invite list.

U.K. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the Vatican, are also expected to attend, alongside other “thought leaders.”

The Palace said Charles will invite guests to consider “how can we harness the benefits of AI, with safety at its heart,” and “build international cooperation and consensus to achieve this, so no nation is left behind — and the future of mankind protected.”

The event has been organized by the King’s Trust, the King's Foundation and the Sustainable Markets Initiative, and will also explore whether a “shared set of principles” can be developed to help guide the future application of AI “not merely as a driver of capability and efficiency, but as a tool that upholds human dignity and contributes to the flourishing of both people and the planet.”

World.title: Von der Leyen makes it awkward with Canada
World.content:
Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney takes the stage in Strasbourg after Commission President Ursula von der Leyen surprised EU capitals by floating “associate membership” for Canada — a status that doesn’t actually exist, and that Ottawa itself seems reluctant to define.

Zoya Sheftalovich and Sarah Wheaton ask whether von der Leyen got ahead of both member countries and the Canadians, and what Carney’s speech could tell us about how close the two sides really want to get.

Then, Germany’s Friedrich Merz faces a potentially decisive weekend as pressure grows on his leadership.

And finally, why is the EU still allowing plastic waste exports to Turkey despite its own assessment warning of serious environmental problems?

World.title: Kann die Tanksäule den Kanzler aus Krise retten?
World.content:
Rekordpreise an den Zapfsäulen und der Kanzler versucht sein Standing zu retten, auch indem er Entlastung verspricht. Doch die Koalition streitet über das richtige Rezept zur Entlastung.

Während SPD-Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil auf eine saubere Gegenfinanzierung pocht, will Friedrich Merz direkte Auszahlungen an die Bevölkerung. Für ihn steht nach bitteren Wahlniederlagen in Sachsen-Anhalt viel auf dem Spiel: Er braucht dringend einen politischen Befreiungsschlag, um seine Handlungsfähigkeit zu beweisen.

Im 200-Sekunden-Interview spricht Rasmus Buchsteiner mit dem CSU-Fraktionschef im bayerischen Landtag, Klaus Holetschek über die Lage, wer wie zum Kanzler hält und warum Markus Söder den Unterstützerbrief der Ministerpräsidenten nicht unterschrieben hat.

Das Heidelberger Start-up Aleph Alpha und das kanadische Unternehmen Cohere fusionieren nun und wollen zu einem globalen KI-Champion werden. World.title: In Ceuta, it’s up to Europe to clean up the Spanish government’s mess
World.content:
A border is not just a line on a map. It is the expression of a political community that decides which values to protect and which responsibilities to share. When a European border is breached, Europe as a whole becomes weaker. When a border is not properly defended, Europe as a whole is left unprotected. That is what is happening.

The response of the current Spanish government, incapable of acknowledging the true nature of the problem and implementing the correct solution, obliges me to reiterate, first and foremost, the obvious, as the President of Ceuta did last week during his visit to Brussels. We are not witnessing a conventional migration crisis, but rather the consequences of an invasion originating from Morocco, which must therefore be held responsible for having condoned or instigated it.

Normality has disappeared from Ceuta for more than six weeks, and the scenes of chaos, overcrowding and insecurity should both shame us and compel us to act. To think that the prolongation of this situation will have no consequences is a mistake we cannot afford to make: it affects our sovereignty, our collective capacity to defend the rule of law, the safety of our citizens, and the credibility of the European project in ensuring its own stability.

Undoubtedly, the national authorities are the first to bear the responsibility for resolving this crisis, in accordance with a non-negotiable principle shared by all EU member states under the Pact on Migration and Asylum: those who have entered irregularly must be returned. All of them. The Spanish government’s obligation is not to find accommodation for them, but to expedite their departure.

That said, given the time that has elapsed and the escalation of violent incidents in Ceuta, Europe as a whole must recognize the failure of the Spanish government and exert the necessary pressure to prevent this crisis from becoming entrenched, spreading, or happening again. Just as Europe has responded when faced with other hybrid threats — on energy, trade or disinformation — the attack on our southern border now demands the same determination.

Firstly, the European Union must ensure that Spain implements, with due rigor and efficiency, all the European instruments available to facilitate returns. Secondly, it must clarify why the Kingdom of Morocco itself has reiterated in an official statement its willingness to take back all those who entered on July 30, while Spanish ministers maintain that no such cooperation exists.

World.title: Reform aide caught in donor sting attended Egypt retreat with JL Partners
World.content:
During the trip, Jukes was asked what a Reform government would want from a polling company and replied: “Showing that we’re winning,” according to the same person.

JL Partners director James Johnson shared several pictures of the Egypt excursion on social media, but Jukes did not appear in any of them. A spokesperson for JL Partners said that Jukes had been invited in a personal capacity and, like other guest speakers, had expenses covered, adding: “Anyone familiar with these sorts of events will know that no inference can reasonably be drawn from the participation of any individual speaker.”

A Reform UK spokesman acknowledged that Jukes, who resigned from his official role earlier this month, was at the gathering but also said it was not on behalf of the party, saying: “Mr Jukes attended the event in question in his capacity as a political consultant and not as part of any political activities in connection with his membership of Reform UK. Reform UK had no involvement and no breach of electoral law has taken place.”

A representative for Jukes said: “There is an active police investigation which has just been announced and as such our client is not commenting further until that is concluded. For the record, he denies any allegations of wrongdoing.”

Caught on camera

Jukes served as Farage’s closest aide and communications director until earlier this month, when he stepped down in the wake of an undercover sting. He was filmed making arrangements for a fictitious wealthy American benefactor and his son to pay for a set of polls by JL Partners on behalf of Reform that were published in British national newspapers.

The polls were released without disclosing the ties to Reform, prompting an inquiry by the British Polling Council, the industry watchdog, which specifies that all research carried out by pollsters which enters the public domain “must include reference to the … client commissioning the survey” as well as dates, methodology and sample size.

World.title: Don’t get ‘locked in’ by EU rules, top nuclear adviser warns Burnham
World.content:
“When the reality is that member states within the European Union have a lot of freedom to be flexible within the EU framework. And I don’t think the U.K. should, in its discussions with the European Union, accept less flexibility than a member state has in terms of our ability to comply with that.”

The Labour government has promised to bring forward a “golden age of nuclear,” signing off on both Sizewell C and Rolls-Royce’s small modular reactors since entering office in July 2024.

But it still faces four of the U.K.’s five existing power stations closing down by 2030. Hinkley Point C will be the first new nuclear power station in the U.K. since Sizewell B opened in 1995.

Fingleton’s 2025 review urged ministers to bring forward a “radical reset” of the U.K.’s nuclear regulations, including scrapping duplication across existing environmental laws.

The U.K. is currently negotiating a post-Brexit “reset” in relations with the European Union. As part of those talks, both parties are seeking so-called “dynamic alignment” across electricity markets. This would mean the U.K. potentially following EU rules on electricity, while making it easier to trade electricity in and out of the trading bloc.

So far, discussions have not extended to nuclear policy and environmental protections, but the U.K. brought its existing EU-compliant habitat regulations into domestic law during the Brexit process.

World.title: Friedrich Merz’s endgame: All the scenarios, rated
World.content:
That same poll shows the far-right Alternative for Germany leading with 29%. The AfD also finished first in a recent state election in Saxony-Anhalt, coming close to winning an absolute majority, while Merz’s CDU lost more than half of its voter support.

European and international allies are watching with bewilderment as Germany — once a bastion of stability during the 16 years of Angela Merkel’s leadership — faces its second quick-fire change of leadership (Merz’s predecessor Olaf Scholz saw his ruling coalition collapse in November 2024).

Merz canceling his trip to the U.N. General Assembly next week threw the scale of his domestic crisis into sharp focus. “His presence is required in Berlin,” said a senior German official, as the chancellor fights for his political survival.

POLITICO analyzed five scenarios for how the German leadership tumult could unfold — and rated their likelihood.

1. Merz resigns lacking party support

The chancellor has convened a high-stakes meeting of his party’s leadership on Sunday at 5 p.m., which will coincide with the state election exit polls at 6 p.m. At that meeting, Merz reportedly wants to ask his party allies whether they still back him and his reform plans. If not, he wants to urge them to put forward the name of a potential successor.

By seeking the confrontation, Merz will try to exploit a weakness of his critics: There is no clear consensus on who should take over.

World.title: In Germany’s east, a rare center-left star looks to stem the far right’s rise
World.content:
It’s emblematic of just how far mainstream parties have fallen across large swaths of Germany that Schwesig is considered a rare and remarkable success for simply managing to keep her SPD — a sinking party that has suffered a string of historic defeats — within range of beating the far right on Sunday in what would amount to a major upset. “Manuela Schwesig could be Germany’s savior,” ran the headline of one column in Der Spiegel magazine.

Schwesig, a former tax inspector who has risen to become one of Germany’s most well-liked politicians, has thrived by casting herself as a bulwark against the far right — employing the slogan “Frau gegen Blau” — “Woman against Blue,” a reference to the AfD’s party color.

To help her cause, she has also frequently attacked the deeply unpopular Merz as out of touch with ordinary people and their financial struggles — exhibiting a populist streak that both distances her from a historically unpopular federal coalition while blunting the AfD’s ability to capitalize on the widespread anti-Merz sentiment that propelled its regional election victory in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month.

Schwesig’s approach has effectively turned the election in her state into a two-party race that has greatly weakened Merz’s conservatives. Her strategy was clear during a “citizen dialogue” with a few hundred supporters held in a tent on the waterside in the port city of Rostock one evening this week.

When someone from the crowd asked what she would do to halt rising gasoline prices, Schwesig, dressed in the bright red of her SPD, called it “fully unacceptable” that Merz had failed to implement a price cap to lower costs for consumers in her rural state, where people often need to drive long distances to get to work.

“I’m pretty angry at Chancellor Merz,” she said.

World.title: Climate change was key factor in deadly Nepal-China flood, scientists say
World.content:
Climate change played a significant role in last month's deadly Himalayan disaster in Nepal, thinning glaciers and thawing mountain permafrost in ways that likely destabilised the slope before it collapsed, a report released Thursday by the World Weather Attribution group said.

 

The collapse, near Nepal's border with China on 26 August, triggered a torrent of water, ice, boulders and sediment that swept through communities along the Trishuli River corridor, killing more than 1,300 people and leaving over 5,000 missing.

"This disaster was not an extreme weather event, but the fingerprints of climate change are still clear to see in long-term changes," said Ben Clarke, a climate researcher at Imperial College London who contributed to the report.

Climate scientists said that across the Himalayas rising temperatures are causing glaciers to retreat and permanently thawing ground that helps bind fractured mountain rock together. That means climate change can alter not only weather hazards such as heat and heavy rain but also the stability of the mountains themselves — threatening communities concentrated in narrow river valleys below.

The analysis did not determine whether the collapse would have happened without climate change, caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases when fuels like oil, gas and coal are burnt. However, researchers concluded that warming intensified several processes that made the slope less stable over decades.

Global warming weakens high mountain slopes

The report found that one of the clearest changes directly linked to climate change was the rising elevation of the freezing threshold.

Warming had pushed the altitude at which ground remains consistently frozen upward by roughly 100 metres per decade, according to the report.

This exposes rock at increasingly high elevations to longer periods above freezing, thawing permafrost and causing cracks within the ice, ultimately weakening the rock face under the ice.

The aftermath of the Birch Glacier collapse is visible in Blatten, Switzerland, on June 11, 2025. (AP Photo/Matthias Schrader) AP Photo

Jakob Steiner, a geoscientist at the University of Graz who has worked in the Himalayan region since 2006 but is not an author of Thursday’s report, said monitoring instruments around 5,000 metres now show that some rock and ground no longer remain frozen throughout the year.

“This means that the ground that was sitting below ice for hundreds and thousands of years is now becoming exposed,” said Steiner.

The report also found that glacial retreat was another destabilising force.

Glaciers in the region have been losing mass for decades at a rate equivalent to more than half a metre of thinning each year, the report found. The Langtang Lirung glacier, located in the region where the disaster occurred last month, has retreated about half a kilometre since the 1990s, exposing rock once covered by ice.

The Himalayan region contains the largest volume of snow and ice outside the polar regions. More than 63,000 glaciers in the area feed at least 10 major Asian river systems and support the food, water, energy and livelihood security of billions of people. However, various studies have found that around 78% of the glacier area, located between 14,763 and 19,685 feet above sea level, is highly exposed to warming.

United Nations reports have found that between 2000 and 2019, glaciers lost 267 billion tonnes of ice per year, roughly equivalent to the mass of 46,500 Great Pyramids of Giza.

As glaciers shrink, they can remove pressure that helped support adjoining rock walls while producing additional meltwater.

According to the analysis, the weeks before the 26 August collapse were also unusually warm. July and August 2026 were the warmest such months recorded locally.

“Other than the potential geological factors like earthquakes that are weakening the bedrock, all these other factors are made worse by human-induced climate change,” said Friederike Otto, climate scientist at Imperial College London and one of the report’s authors.

World.title: Rheinmetall boss Papperger: "Robots will come"
World.content:
Germany wants to significantly strengthen its defence capabilities. But it is no longer just about more ammunition and missiles. Air defence, drones and new technologies such as humanoid robots and space systems are also playing an increasingly important role.

 

Rheinmetall chief executive Armin Papperger talks about rearmament, current bottlenecks – and which weapons systems could prove decisive in future.

At the keel-laying ceremony for the third class 424 fleet service vessel in Wolgast, we spoke to Papperger about Germany's arms production, the role of the Skyranger and the weapons of the future.

Euronews: Mr Papperger, in March you said missile stockpiles were worryingly low. What is the situation now?

Papperger: I believe that is still the case. You simply cannot produce missiles that quickly, and that is why we at Rheinmetall are launching a major investment programme – and not just us, many manufacturers are doing the same.

And there are huge bottlenecks when it comes to rocket motors, but also warheads, and we need to get much faster here to bring Germany, but also Europe and NATO, back up to target levels that are sufficient if we come under threat.

Euronews: Where do we stand with the Skyranger? The systems have been ordered, but will they arrive in time? How fast is it moving now?

Papperger: Yes, with the Skyranger – and this is really a narrative that keeps coming up. Under the contract, we have to start series deliveries of the Skyranger in 2027. That will happen; at the moment we are only facing minor delays.

There are several technologies we need to update: the chassis, the radar technology and the missiles that have to be integrated.

But I am firmly convinced that, together with BAAINBw (the Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support) and the ministry, we will find a good solution in this area.

Our people are working on it day and night and, as you know, we are massively ramping up Skyranger capacity. From the end of next year we will build, or be able to build, up to 400 a year. So I have no concerns at all in that respect.

Papperger and Pistorius at the keel-laying of the third class 424 vessel in Wolgast Stamm, Bundeswehr

Euronews: There is a joint venture for deep strike capabilities. Where do we stand on that?

Papperger: The joint venture we have is, on the one hand, with Destinus and, on the other, with Lockheed Martin. With Lockheed Martin we are working on artillery rockets; the cruise missiles we are developing with Destinus. Both joint ventures are in the final stages before signing, and we expect to receive the first order for cruise missiles by the end of this year or the beginning of next year.

Euronews: Shouldn't we be building simpler systems, but more of them? Isn't that what Ukraine is showing?

Papperger: We are doing that as well, but in some areas it doesn't help. If you look at what the Skyranger can do today – it can shoot down a missile flying at Mach 3. You cannot do that with an interceptor and you cannot do it with a simple system.

And if you speak today to the Inspector of the German Army, he will tell you: "In two years the threat will look completely different." The Skyranger really offers multiple capabilities; we cannot achieve that with our interceptor solution or with our simpler systems.

For example, we also have ".50 guns" that can shoot down light drones, category 1 drones. That becomes very, very difficult once you are dealing with, say, jet drones – they are hardly manageable with such systems. That is why we believe a sustainable solution is the better one.

Euronews: How big a driver of employment are the defence industry and Rheinmetall in reality?

Papperger: I think we are an important engine of job creation. At the moment, excluding the civilian business, around 34,000 people work at Rheinmetall. We are growing by roughly 10,000 net per year, and our aim is to reach 70,000 by 2030, with a supply chain employing another 210,000 people. So if you add that up, it's almost 300,000 people. That is a jobs engine.

Euronews: How quickly can arms and ammunition production be ramped up – for companies like Rheinmetall?

Papperger: Yes, we are already doing it. We have shown it, for example with ammunition. In medium calibres we have gone from under one million to four million rounds. In artillery we have increased output from 70,000 to 1.5 million rounds. Tank ammunition is now at 240,000 rounds, up from 40,000, 50,000 or 60,000, depending on the year. So we are doing this. And what we are doing now is doubling our trucks.

So our logistical and tactical vehicles are now being more than doubled. So we are doing this. At the moment we simply don't have the orders to do even more. Rheinmetall has a six-year investment programme worth 30 billion euros, and the scale of our current investment is enormous. That is why it is so important that the signal we have sent again today – that the minister is here, that he is committed – shows that we are not just building up capacity, but that it will be used sustainably and that people will have work.

For me that has been an excellent signal, a very, very good sign, and it reassures me somewhat that the federal government is really shouldering its responsibility here.

Euronews: What comes next? Drones have been a major issue recently. What is the next step – space, which is already playing a role, or combat robots, humanoid robots?

Papperger: Robots will come, that is absolutely clear. We have a research centre in Bremen focusing on humanoid robots. We are working on them. We do not yet have products ready for series production, which is why we have not gone public with it. But we are investing a lot of money there. Space is another area in which we are investing heavily, both in satellite construction and in processing communications.

In other words, all the information we receive from satellites should be properly processed. And drones will remain, and so will everything else – because it's all needed. For combined-arms combat you need artillery, armoured weapons, conventional ammunition, drones and missiles.

The only question now is how much of each you need. It has to be a mix. And that will change: the quantities in the individual areas will shift.

World.title: Most waste ends up in landfill. This scientist finds unexpected ways to give it a second life
World.content:
Ten years ago, academic Lynne Loo was a scientist researching how waste could be repurposed in Australia.

 

She began looking at waste from the abalone industry and now she's using her expertise to enable startup businesses with new ideas on how to repurpose waste.

What started as a research project soon led to a much bigger idea, finding value in the things we throw away.

According to the Australian government's Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, the country produces 76 million tonnes of waste each year.

That’s 2.9 million tonnes per person. And a significant portion of it heads straight to landfill.

But there are innovative and sometimes unexpected ways to give waste a second life.

Transforming cellulose from food waste into paper and leather

Matt Barber is using his home made laboratory to get cellulose from food waste.

“So, what I get is pure cellulose that comes out and then from there, I process that into other paper, leather or wood products. But it could be turned into a bioplastic. It can be turned into any uses. So you can, instead of growing a tree, which takes 75 years, you can grow this in a week,” explains Barber.

For Barber, the project fits around his day job, and having Loo assist as a reliable waste broker is key to making the system work.

“You have a start up and you don't know what to do with it and she [Loo] helps you find a market for it,” says Barber.

Turning rubbish into vinegar and biochar

At a waste facility in Collie, Western Australia, Renergi is taking that idea even further.

Using thermal conversion technology, the company is turning rubbish into products including vinegar, biochar and oil.

“We can process just under about 30,000 tonnes of biomass waste per year and 4,000 tonnes per annum of the town’s municipal solar waste,” says Deejay Parker of Renergi.

More than 70 per cent of the material is recovered and transformed into something new.

The biochar is already being put to work on fruit farms and at a winery across Southern Western Australia.

The project has received funding from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency, as part of efforts to expand renewable technologies into regional areas.

And when it reaches full production, it's expected to become one of the country's largest producers.

“I think it's important for people to see that it's possible because there are so many naysayers,” says Loo.

A waste warrior on a mission to recycle, reuse and reimagine what we throw away.

World.title: Macron to host King Abdullah II and Lebanon's Aoun to discuss support for Lebanese Armed Forces
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron is set to host Jordan’s King Abdullah II and Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in Paris on Thursday, ahead of an international summit, aimed at mobilising support for the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF).

 

According to an Elysée source, the talks — which are part of the Aqaba Process launched by Jordan in 2015 — will bring together senior officials and military experts from France, Britain, Jordan, Lebanon and the US to discuss plans for deploying the LAF, as well as wider efforts to stabilise the region.

At present, Lebanon is seeking international support for its armed forces and working to avoid a security vacuum in the south, following the UN Security Council's decision to end the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL’s) on 31 December 2026, followed by a year-long drawdown and withdrawal — a move supported by the United States. At present, it has around 7,500 peacekeepers from nearly 50 countries.

Thursday’s meeting will focus on “direct operational matters” as France and its partners seek to assess how to assist the Lebanese Army with financial aid, equipment, intelligence and, if needed, operational guidance, according to an Elysée source.

UNIFIL was established in 1978 to oversee the withdrawal of Israeli troops from southern Lebanon and assist the government in restoring its control of the area. At the time, Israel's three-month long occupation was sparked by the March 1978 "Coastal Road Massacre" — a deadly hijacking carried out by militants from the Palestinian Fatah group, which killed more than 30 Israelis.

In 2006, following the war between Israel and Hezbollah, UNIFIL's mandate was expanded to help prevent Hezbollah and other armed groups from maintaining a military presence in southern Lebanon.

European efforts to establish a post-UNIFIL

In June, France and Italy announced they would lead efforts to establish a post-UNIFIL international coalition in support of Lebanon during the autumn of 2026, at a Franco-Italian summit.

Meanwhile, EU Foreign Policy Chief Kaja Kallas said on 1 September that more than 10 EU member states were willing to provide personnel and resources for a new civilian and military mission to support Lebanese forces, stressing that the EU was not seeking to “replace” UNIFIL, but instead to invest in “Lebanon's capacity to provide security for itself."

Ahead of his France trip, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun told Agence France-Presse (AFP), Aoun stressed the importance of a new force for Lebanon — whether it be European or not.

“Whatever the nature of this force, that poses no problem for me: European, non-European, American, another United Nations force, Asian, or even a mix of European, Arab and Asian forces,” he stated, adding that “the best and most optimal option remains extending UNIFIL's mandate”.

Aoun said that any new force in southern Lebanon, part of which is occupied by Israel, would be “temporary until the (Lebanese) army can deploy”.

Although he stressed that the goal was to strike a security agreement with Israel “primarily to end the state of hostility and the deployment of the army on the border”, he cautioned “we cannot jump directly to a peace agreement”.

The ongoing conflict

Lebanon was drawn into the wider regional Middle Eastern conflict after Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Shiite militia, launched rockets at Israel in early March in retaliation for US-Israeli strikes on Iran — prompting an Israeli military response across the country.

More than six months after the conflict erupted, and despite a ceasefire agreed in June, Israeli airstrikes, military operations and demolitions have continued in southern Lebanon, leaving villages abandoned and residents displaced.

Meanwhile, Hezbollah has continued to attack communities in the north of Israel, causing civilian and military casualties, as well as leading to the displacement of residents from communities along the Lebanese border.

Multiple rounds of US-mediated talks between Israel and Lebanon have yet to resolve the conflict. Hezbollah has rejected calls for its disarmament, while Israel has linked its full withdrawal from southern Lebanon to the group’s disarmament and the removal of its military infrastructure.

Meanwhile, hardline right-wing politicians, such as Israel's Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, have called for Israel to annex southern Lebanon up to the Litani River. Israel and Lebanon have experienced repeated periods of armed conflict and renewed hostilities since the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.

Speaking to AFP ahead of his Paris trip, Aoun said that Lebanon remained determined to disarm Hezbollah, describing the issue as “neither negotiable nor open to discussion."

Despite this, Lebanon’s armed forces have struggled to enforce the government’s decision to establish a state monopoly on weapons, amid Hezbollah’s refusal to disarm.

Hezbollah has long maintained a substantial arsenal, which it has used to fight repeated wars with Israel, while also playing a major role in Lebanese politics. It operates both as an armed group and as a political party, with members in parliament and ministers serving in the government cabinet.

France's role in the process

Karim Émile Bitar, associate research fellow at the Institute for International and Strategic Affairs (IRIS) said that in his view, Hezbollah's disarmament campaign was an "impossible" task.

“The army is a cross-community institution in Lebanon and it faces an impossible mission. It is being asked to disarm, within a few weeks, a militia that has been more powerful than the state for decades. This army lacks everything, from logistical resources and financial means. Politically, it is also not easy to confront Hezbollah, which continues to enjoy significant support from the Lebanese Shia community", he told Euronews.

Bitar said Thursday's meeting serves as an example of France’s longstanding role in Lebanese affairs (from 1920 to 1943, Lebanon was governed under a French mandate).

"Today, France views itself and has often been viewed, as the guarantor of unity, of sovereignty, of territorial integrity for Lebanon. These three things are now threatened: territorial integrity is absent as Israel occupies 6% of Lebanon's territory, sovereignty is because Hezbollah is refusing to hand over its military arsenal to the army and unity is being challenged in light of rising extremism, polarisation and fragmentation", Bitar told Euronews.

The US and Israel's decision to exclude France from ceasefire negotiations between Israel and Lebanon earlier this year left Beirut in a difficult situation, stressed Bitar.

"For Lebanon, this posed a problem because the United States is not perceived as an 'honest broker.' The Lebanese would have liked countries such as France, Italy and Saudi Arabia to have been involved in these negotiations, so that they would not have found themselves confronted with Israeli intransigence, supported by the United States", he said.
