World.title: Anthropic priced above $2 trillion as markets eagerly await IPO filing
World.content:
Crypto traders are assigning Anthropic an implied valuation more than $1 trillion (€866bn) above its last funding-round price, before public investors have even seen its accounts.

 

The company behind Claude has filed its IPO paperwork confidentially and chosen Nasdaq for its initial public offering.

What remains is the public release of its S-1 filing, the official registration package that a US company submits to the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Until it arrives, the only live price on Anthropic comes from a corner of the crypto market where pre-IPO speculation runs rampant, and it currently sits far above anything the company has ever agreed with an investor.

The last agreed valuation was $965 billion (€836bn), set when a $65 billion (€56bn) Series H round closed at the end of May, led by Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks and Sequoia.

That was already an extraordinary figure for a company founded in 2021 by Dario and Daniela Amodei, and it followed a valuation of $61.5 billion (€53.3bn) barely a year earlier, representing a nearly sixteenfold increase in roughly 12 months.

Revenue has moved almost as fast.

Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate passed $65 billion (€56bn) by the end of July, driven by enterprise adoption of Claude.

The losses are also enormous, reportedly reaching close to $42 billion (€36.4bn) in 2025, reflecting the cost of training frontier models. Amazon has committed to investing as much as $33 billion (€28.6bn) in the company, while Anthropic has committed to spending more than $100 billion (€86.6bn) on AWS technologies over the coming decade.

Given these figures, investors are already aiming considerably higher than the valuation in the last round.

Reports have put the target IPO valuation at $2 trillion (€1.73tn), with Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley leading an offering expected to raise more than $60 billion (€52bn).

The market that is already trading

Perpetual futures contracts tracking Anthropic's pre-IPO valuation are currently trading on Hyperliquid, the largest decentralised derivatives venue, where the implied market capitalisation reached an all-time high of roughly $2.36 trillion (€2.05tn) and sits near $2.15 trillion (€1.86tn) at the time of writing.

That is about 2.2 times the Series H valuation.

Heng Yu Lee, partner at market maker DWF Labs, which is active in these instruments, rejects the suggestion that leverage rather than conviction is driving the premium.

"Whether it's leveraged or not, everyone trading the pre-IPO market is genuine demand at the price that's reflected," he told Euronews, adding that "the premium is pricing in public information that's available, such as expected revenue numbers and expected market demand for the stock."

These contracts will also be the first instruments to react when the filing lands, trading around the clock while equity markets are shut.

"At a moment like the S-1 dropping, you typically see volume spike and prices fluctuate heavily as the market digests the information," Lee explained.

However, the market remains small relative to what it is valuing.

"Currently, the market isn't super deep, with just $6M in 24-hour volume and $31M in open interest on Hyperliquid," Lee said, adding that liquidity should improve as the listing approaches, given that more investors are likely to pile in.

Lee is also candid about how much weight the number deserves.

"As of now, I wouldn't rely too heavily on the absolute pricing as we have yet to have a public S-1," he stated while clarifying that "the direction of how the prices move typically still accurately reflects the shifting sentiment towards the company as things develop."

A crowded year for AI listings

Once Anthropic files publicly, it will cement 2026 as the year of AI IPOs.

It started with chipmaker Cerebras Systems, which designs wafer-scale processors pitched as an alternative to Nvidia's. The firm listed on Nasdaq in May after two false starts, raising $5.55 billion (€4.76bn) at $185 a share, above its revised price range.

The stock opened 89% higher and closed its first day near $311, valuing the company at roughly $67 billion (€58bn) compared with the $23 billion (€20bn) it had been worth three months earlier.

Investor appetite for a credible Nvidia challenger proved fierce, though the enthusiasm cooled quickly after a disappointing first earnings report. Cerebras is currently trading at a valuation of around $43.7 billion (€37.8bn).

Then came SpaceX, which listed in June, raising more than $85 billion (€73.6bn) at a valuation that briefly touched $2.8 trillion (€2.4tn) before falling back to around $1.95 trillion (€1.69tn).

OpenAI was also slated to hold an IPO this year and had already filed confidentially, but has now stepped back entirely. The company has a private valuation of $852 billion (€738bn), set during a $122 billion (€105bn) round in March.

CEO Sam Altman told Fortune on Saturday that listing this year would be "ill-advised", ruling out 2026 and declining to commit to 2027. He said the company had "a lot of stuff to do" on safety and alignment and that being private made that easier.

FILE. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaks in Abu Dhabi, UAE, June 2023 AP Photo/Jon Gambrell

Altman's comments arrived the same day that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier", arguing that AI companies should deliberately slow the rate at which they improve their most capable models.

Amodei proposed three steps: independent evaluators with employee-level access to frontier systems, coordination on safety standards among labs in democratic countries, and international agreements on the most dangerous categories of use.

Anthropic has already committed unilaterally to the first, and the endorsements came quickly, with Sam Altman saying he agreed on the need to pace the frontier and Elon Musk replying simply: "Dario is right".

However, US President Donald Trump did not.

In his first public response to the three CEOs, Trump, speaking in Ireland on Sunday, dismissed the argument.

"We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins," Trump said, describing some warnings as things "that won't happen".

Trump has since reiterated that argument in several social media posts.

Likewise, China's foreign ministry called the warnings "fearmongering".

Markets registered the exchange, with shares in SoftBank, Kioxia and SK Hynix falling sharply on Monday. Shares in the Japanese and South Korean companies fell more than 6% and 4.3%, respectively.

This leaves Anthropic in an awkward position as it approaches what could be the largest listing ever attempted in public markets.

The company is asking public investors to fund frontier AI development while its founder argues publicly that such development should proceed more slowly.

That is not necessarily a contradiction, since pacing is not stopping, and Anthropic has always argued that safety-focused labs should be at the frontier rather than ceding it.

However, it is a story the S-1 filing will have to tell convincingly, and the risk factors section will be read unusually closely.

World.title: Inside von der Leyen's pitch for a new EU security architecture
World.content:
A new European Security Council, an emergency protocol and a new strategic enabler initiative: in her State of the Union speech on Wednesday, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen laid out a new security architecture for Europe. But several question marks still hang over it.

 

With the war in Ukraine increasingly spilling over into Europe's eastern flank and Russia intensifying its campaign of sabotage attacks and drone incursions, security and defence took centre stage in von der Leyen's annual address.

"We already have many tools. And we are strengthening our work with NATO. But our doctrine, our institutions and our decision-making have not kept pace with the new reality," she said.

The speech previewed several of the main elements expected in the EU's new security strategy, due next month, which is meant to redefine Europe's security architecture.

European Security Council

Among the most significant proposals von der Leyen teased is a new security-focused political format dubbed the European Security Council, a special configuration of the EU leaders' summit that will include partners such as Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway and Canada.

In practice, leaders like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are already frequently invited to European Council meetings. The new format would institutionalise this relationship, giving it a dedicated framework to discuss security matters.

"For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent," von der Leyen said. "This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."

The idea itself is not new. French President Emmanuel Macron floated it during his 2017 presidential campaign, and it received formal backing the following year in the Franco-German Meseberg Declaration.

"We cannot allow ourselves to stay with the status quo. Doctrines and institutions, which were created during peacetime, are not fit any more for the purpose," said European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius.

Still, how this moves from proposal to reality remains unclear: von der Leyen set no start date and offered no tangible deliverables beyond future-proofing Europe's security. How far the new initiative will overlap with NATO and the so-called Coalition of the Willing is also an open question.

"A European Security Council is no panacea. Consensus would presumably still be necessary, but compared to the European Council, a shared threat perception would presumably instil a greater sense of trust and shared destiny amongst its members," wrote Nathalie Tocci, director of Rome's Istituto Affari Internazionali, in a policy brief.

Emergency security protocol

Hybrid warfare was another major flashpoint, after weeks marked by a flurry of Russia-suspected sabotage acts, attempted attacks and drone incursions intended to destabilise EU countries.

"Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook," von der Leyen said on Wednesday. "We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents: those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security. In other words, a mechanism to flank NATO's Article 4."

Article 4 allows NATO members to formally request emergency consultations when they believe their security, territorial integrity or political independence is under threat.

For von der Leyen, the bloc needs its own version of Article 4, dubbed an Emergency Security Protocol, built on the EU treaty's mutual defence clause, which states that "when an EU member state is the target of armed aggression on its territory, the other member states must assist it by all the means in their power".

The mutual defence clause resurfaced earlier this year when an Iranian-made drone, suspected of being launched by the Lebanese militia Hezbollah, targeted a British airbase in Cyprus – a member of the EU, but not of NATO.

Discussions around the clause prompted a "war gaming" exercise conducted by EU ambassadors to map out what triggering it would mean in practice, and von der Leyen's security protocol appears to take the preparation one step farther.

"When triggered by one member state, all member states would convene to coordinate a European response [and] to deter further escalation and mitigate the impact," she said.

At the same time, EU officials have previously warned that invoking the mutual defence clause could further incentivise the US to disengage from NATO – even though "assistance" doesn't automatically mean joining an armed conflict, and could instead take the form of financial support or civilian protection.

As hybrid threats across Europe grow increasingly kinetic, the advantage of a European defence clause is that it can be activated even for lower-intensity activity, without necessarily requiring a military response, Euronews understands.

Oana Lungescu, NATO's former spokesperson, said that while it's welcome that the Commission President wants closer EU-NATO cooperation, it's hard to see how this would actually deter Russia.

"Protocols and playbooks already exist in both organisations," she said.

Strategic enablers

With the US signalling its intention to reduce its military presence in Europe, subject to a posture review due later this year, the EU is now scrambling to fill key defence capability gaps known as strategic enablers.

Strategic enablers are the logistical backbone of modern warfare: satellites, airlift, refuelling and intelligence capabilities that allow military forces to operate effectively.

"The war in Ukraine has shown us the importance of strategic enablers," von der Leyen said. "These systems are essential, and we need more of them. Only together does Europe have the scale to deliver them."

To that end, she announced a new European Instrument for Strategic Enablers, meant to channel the long-term investment needed to build up these capabilities in alignment with NATO.

In June, Commissioner Kubilius warned that replacing US military assets in Europe would require an eye-watering €500bn investment.

How exactly the new instrument will close this gap remains unclear, as Brussels tries to work out how to incentivise national investment in the area.

"We welcome our European allies and partners stepping up to do more in support of our shared security," a NATO official told Euronews. "NATO is the bedrock of our collective defence, and we will continue to work closely with the EU in pursuit of our shared agenda."

World.title: ADHD is linked to almost 50% increase in gut problems
World.content:
A new review suggests that ADHD is associated with a substantial burden of functional gastrointestinal symptoms — problems affecting how the digestive system works without necessarily reflecting an identifiable structural disease.

 

Researchers screened over 9,000 records and included 23 studies, and found that ADHD was associated with higher odds of every gastrointestinal symptom examined — including irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, indigestion and encopresis.

"Almost every gut symptom we looked at … appeared to be associated with ADHD,” said co-lead author Sarah Blake, a Medical Student at Warwick Medical School. “These symptoms can have a real impact on daily life, but they could easily be overlooked if the focus is on ADHD itself.”

The researchers found a 48% increase in the odds of experiencing gastrointestinal symptoms overall among people with ADHD. The association was particularly strong for constipation, where the odds were almost twice as high, and encopresis — loss of bowel control — where they were more than four times as high.

Why the link?

The researchers say there are several possible explanations, but the study does not establish that ADHD itself causes gastrointestinal problems.

One possibility is behaviour. Emotional dysregulation and increased sensitivity to stress, both associated with ADHD, may affect gut sensitivity and contribute to functional abdominal pain. Irregular eating patterns, skipped meals and binge eating may also influence symptoms such as indigestion, bloating, constipation and abdominal pain.

Food-related sensory sensitivities could play a role, too. People with ADHD may experience differences in sensitivity to food textures and smells, potentially contributing to selective diets that are lower in fibre and could affect bowel habits.

The researchers also point to differences in interoception — the ability to recognise internal bodily signals — as a possible factor. Reduced awareness of the need to have a bowel movement could potentially contribute to constipation or encopresis.

Medication may be another contributor. Stimulants such as methylphenidate are known to cause side effects including appetite suppression, abdominal pain, nausea and constipation. Sleep disturbances, which are common among people with ADHD, may also affect gastrointestinal motility and sensitivity.

The gut-brain connection

The researchers also highlight the gut microbiome as a possible biological pathway.

Previous research has identified differences in gut microbial composition between adults with ADHD and neurotypical controls. Other studies have linked changes in the gut microbiome with gastrointestinal symptoms.

One hypothesis is that these differences could influence inflammation and communication between the gut and brain. Genetic factors may also contribute.

"We can't yet say ADHD causes these gut problems, or exactly what is driving the link, but the pattern is striking enough to warrant attention,” Saran Shantikumar, associate clinical professor at Warwick Medical School, said. “Clinicians caring for people with ADHD may want to consider asking about gastrointestinal symptoms, particularly if they may be affecting quality of life."

World.title: Ukraine: Russian strikes injure several in Kyiv, Odesa
World.content:
Russian airstrikes on Ukrainian cities of Kyiv and Odesa injured at least 13 people early on Thursday, Ukrainian officials said, as the war heads toward its fifth winter.

"An air raid alert has been declared in Kyiv due to the threat of missile strikes. We urge residents to proceed to the nearest shelters," the Kyiv City Military Administration wrote on Telegram.

At least 10 people were wounded in the Ukrainian capital, officials said on the messaging app. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said apartment buildings and warehouses had been damaged in the latest strikes, and that debris also fell near a petrol station.

News agencies such as Reuters and AFP cited witnesses hearing "strong" explosions in Kyiv.

In the Black Sea port City of Odesa, at least three people were injured when a Russian strike hit a 19-story apartment building, authorities said. A child was among those injured.

Both Russia and Ukraine have increased their use of long-range missiles in recent months, along with the continued use of drones, to strike inside each other's territories.

Mediated talks ahead?

The strikes continue even as Russia and Ukraine recently signalled their readiness to resume talks under US mediation. Earlier this week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office said officials were preparing for talks in October. Similar signals came from Moscow, which said it did not rule out such a possibility.

The last round of trilateral talks took place in January and February 2026 in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, without producing a breakthrough, as the issue of territory control in eastern Ukraine remained unresolved.

World.title: Trump threatens EU with further sanctions over Canada
World.content:
The EU had signaled that Canada is poised to become the bloc's first associate member. Trump called the idea both "laughable" and a "hostile act."

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday responded to the European Union's plans to add Canada as an associate member with threats and ridicule.

During her annual speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was opening the door for ‌Canada ⁠to ⁠become its first associate member.

Such a relationship to the bloc does not currently exist and would have to be created from scratch.

How did Trump respond to Canada's EU associate membership idea?

In comments to reporters on Wednesday, Trump said the idea could become a "hostile act." He threatened to impose sanctions on the EU in response.

"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina.

The US president also described the prospect of Canada joining the EU as "laughable."

Why is Canada turning to the EU?

The potential Canadian EU associate membership comes as Trump, during his second term in office, has shaken Washington's relationship with its northern neighbor to the core.

Canada was among the first victims of Trump's tariff policy.

Tensions escalated between Ottawa and Washington after trade talks broke down last month, with Trump imposing further sanctions on Canada and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowing to respond in kind.

As Trump menaces, some think Canada should join the EU To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Washington's transatlantic ties have also suffered under Trump, most notably after the US president's push to take control of the Arctic island of Greenland, which is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.

The EU was also hit by Trump's wide tariffs, as were most countries worldwide, but the two sides reached a trade agreement to bring them down.

World.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
World.content:
A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.

Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing.

The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26.

"This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone."

With no time to prepare, families in Devighat returned to mud-filled homes days later to salvage whatever survived Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

How the disaster unfolded

The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years.

The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow.

Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours.

Relatives are going through photographs of missing people, trying to find loved ones Image: Safal Prakash Shrestha/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

How did this happen?

It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events.

Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades.

Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it.

Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable.

In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean.

An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater.

Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure.

A disaster beyond adaptation

Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one.

Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation.

The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in.

"When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said.

"Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come."

World.title: US Congress passes Russia sanctions bill
World.content:
The sanctions package is considered the most substantial US legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to the White House. Measures in the bill could lead to secondary sanctions on India, China and Iran.

The US Republican-led US House of Representatives passed on Wednesday a package of broad new sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine.

The bill passed 262-159, after breezing through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.

The bill, considered the toughest legislative effort against Russia during US President Donald Trump's second term, awaits the president's signature to come into law. Trump has said he will sign it.

Russia's economy is growing, despite sanctions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What does the sanctions package against Russia entail?

The package targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, old tankers it uses to circumvent sanctions.

More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries that rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. China and India are expected to be the main targets of such measures.

The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran.

It was drafted in April 2025 by late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July.

But Trump had delayed the bill's passage, as his foreign policy favors retaining control over tariffs and sanctions rather than leaving such decisions to Congress.

How much leverage does the US have over its adversaries? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Who opposed the bill and why?

Democrats who voted for the bill broke ranks with the party leadership, which argues the legislation expands Trump's tariff powers and that the president already has the power to sanction Russia should he choose to.

"What this legislation will do ​is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash ⁠tariffs on the American people," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a speech on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, some Republicans opposed to the bill were wary of compounded tariffs further increasing consumer prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.

The bill's supporters say it is integral to keeping up the pressure on Russia.

It has been celebrated by Ukrainian activists. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with lawmakers to urge its passage and even watched an early procedural vote from the chamber.

World.title: Sweden's center-left bloc set to win election, STV reports
World.content:
The center-left opposition won the Swedish elections by a very slim margin, the public broadcaster reported after 99% of the votes were counted. Thorny negotiations await the bloc even if the result is confirmed.

Sweden's center-left opposition bloc looks set to win the most votes in the country's parliamentary election, albeit by the slimmest of margins, public broadcaster SVT said on Wednesday with 99% of the votes counted.

As of 1647 GMT, with fewer than 1% of votes left to count, the center-left bloc was ahead by just 26,169 votes.

The bloc is led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats, the party that ruled Sweden for most of the 20th century.

If the results are confirmed, it would usher in a change in government from the right-wing bloc led by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.

The election authority was now counting late incoming ballots, such as those from voters abroad Image: Christine Olsson/TT News Agency/REUTERS

What do we know about the Swedish election results so far?

Data from Sweden's election authority shows Kristersson's bloc was on track to win 174 seats, against 175 seats for the center-left. Both Kristersson and Andersson have said they would be open to exploring coalition options.

"The likelihood of a turnaround at this stage is so low that we ​can confidently state that the opposition will secure the most seats in this election," ⁠SVT ​said.

The election authority was counting late incoming ballots from home and overseas, a process expected to continue until Thursday.

Sweden awaits final outcome of razor's-edge election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Even with Andersson's slim lead, her bloc is bracing for tough negotiations before forming any government, especially amid deep divisions between the liberal Center Party and the socialist Left Party.

After the 2022 elections, it took 37 days to form a government, which was considerably shorter than in 2018, when the process took 134 days.

Parliament cannot vote in a new prime minister before September 29.

World.title: US Fed raises key rate for first time in 3 years
World.content:
In an attempt to address the persistently high inflation in the world's largest economy, the US Federal Reserve increased interest rates by 25 basis points. The president, on the other hand, said they should be cut.

The US Federal Reserve (Fed) on Wednesday raised interest rates by 25 basis points in an attempt to tackle stubbornly high inflation in the world's largest economy.

This move is sure to anger President Donald Trump, who has called for lower rates and who recently nominated Kevin Warsh to the post of Federal Reserve Chair.

"Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long," Warsh told a press conference.

Warsh has served as Fed Chair since May and during his confirmation process, he had assured Congress that central bank policymakers would "have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation."

"Today's policy action will support a ​timelier return to the committee's 2% goal," Warsh added.

The increase boosts the Fed's target rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%.

Trump had promised to lower prices in his 2024 election campaign, but things turned out differently after his inauguration. The US now faces the combined impact of Trump's global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom.

After the announcement of the rate increase, Trump said US interest rates should ‌be 1% or lower and that the rates ⁠should be cut fast.

"I ... talked to Kevin," Trump said. "And I said you might as well vote with the board because ​it's not going to matter. The board is very hostile. They're very political. They're doing the wrong thing."

Fed plans to 'stay in our lane'

Since his appointment to the job, speculation circulated around which direction Warsh would take the Fed, as Trump has pressured the institution to follow his lead.

But on Wednesday, Warsh joined the unanimous decision to raise interest rates, saying it had been made independent of what the market may be doing.

"We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation," he said. "I'll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision."

"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane," Warsh said. "We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too. That's how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them."

Why 9.5 million US Americans are defaulting on student loans To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Borrowers will feel some impact

The raise in interest rates will affect those who borrow money to make large purchases, such as a home, car or large appliance.

The new rate will also raise monthly payments and costs for those who are already paying interest on credit card debt.

Currently, household debt payments are relatively low overall as a percentage of after-tax income. So many households will not feel the burden on borrowing in the short term.

But the move could be good for those who are saving, as interest rates on savings accounts and certificates of deposit will rise.

World.title: Germany: Oktoberfest beer prices rise, outpacing inflation
World.content:
Oktoberfest's traditional beer mug, the Mass, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) at this year's festival in Munich.

The price of a liter of beer at Munich's Oktoberfest has risen fivefold since 1985, far outpacing overall inflation in Germany, according to an analysis by UniCredit's chief economist in Germany.

A Mass, the traditional 1-liter (2.1-pint) serving at Oktoberfest, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) this year. In 1985, it cost about 6.25 Deutschmarks, equivalent to €3.20 after conversion at the fixed euro exchange rate.

The figures were analyzed by UniCredit economist Andreas Rees ahead of the opening of the world's largest beer festival on Saturday.

Beer prices at Oktoberfest have increased by around 400% since 1985, according to Rees, using data from Munich's statistical office.

Consumer prices across Germany, by comparison, have risen by around 120% over the same period.

Women conquering Oktoberfest's toughest jobs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What determines the Mass' price?

This year's increase is considerably more modest. The average price of a Mass is up 2.4% from last year, below Germany's expected overall inflation rate of close to 3%.

"Beer prices at the Oktoberfest depend on a peculiar cocktail of harvests, energy prices, wages, tent costs, security and the willingness of millions of visitors to spend generously," Rees said.

Although the trend has been one of sharply rising prices, this year's Mass saw a price of 2.4% compared to 2025, the smallest increase in two decades.

Rees explained that ingredient prices could be playing a role, as hops have become cheaper while malting-barley prices have stabilized.

Festival draws millions

Oktoberfest is the largest folk festival in the world. Locals and tourists alike wear the traditional Bavarian lederhosen and dirndl dresses on the festival grounds.

The festival dates back to 1810, and it takes place at the Wiesn, a the local dialect abbreviation for Theresienwiese, the fairgrounds in Munich named in honor of Crown Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen.

This Saturday, Munich will celebrate the 191st Oktoberfest, expecting somewhere between 6 and 7 million visitors.

The party begins when the city's mayor opens the first barrel in a ceremony officially marking the opening of the festival.

World.title: UK: Village votes to 'secede' in asylum center plan protest
World.content:
Residents of Piddington, a tiny, remote village in Oxfordshire in England, have staged a "referendum" on leaving the UK. They are objecting to plans to open an asylum reception center at a disused military base nearby.

An English village of about 350 people has voted to "secede" from the United Kingdom, in a symbolic protest against government plans to set up an asylum reception center nearby.

Residents of Piddington, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Oxford, celebrated with a placard reading "Principality of Piddington" near the village road sign on Wednesday.

They oppose plans, still under review, to house asylum seekers in a disused military base, MoD Bicester (Site A).

Piddington is home to about 350 people and has few amenities or facilities to speak of Image: Joe Giddens/PA Images/picture alliance

What happened in the tongue-in-cheek breakaway vote?

The village's parish council said that 312 people cast ballots in the vote, a turnout of almost 92%.

Participants in the vote, which had no legal basis, were asked to agree or disagree with the statement: "I support Piddington seeking to secede from the United Kingdom and pursuing self-determination."

Of them, 285 voted to secede, 26 voted against, and one spoiled their ballot.

Parish council chair Tim McNally said that, going forward, the village would identify as the "Principality of Piddington."

"For us, it's about proportiality," McNally told Sky News. "How does a small village of 350 odd people assimilate with 1,250 males?"

He accused the government of "trying to rush this whole plan through."

An Oxfordshire County Council official told the BBC the plan risked making the village and the facility a "lightning rod" for potentially violent far-right protests.

The vote attracted the attention of self-styled anti-migration "influencers" online.

MoD Bicester (Site A) exists, is disused, and has inbuilt security facilities — but it is also a remote rural facility that is not in easy reach of major built-up areas [FILE: September 8, 2026] Image: Hannah McKay/REUTERS

How did the government react?

The Labour government has been trying to move asylum seekers housed in hotels, an unpopular legacy they inherited from previous British governments, into disused military facilities by 2029.

This follows repeated protests at or near hotels and rented accommodation used for the purpose.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who only recently took over the rapidly rotating top job in British politics, promised to "look at the issues raised by the community and in the referendum."

But he also said that the "vast majority" of British people backed a government plan to stop housing asylum seekers in hotels and argued that it was "fair" to locate holding centers around the country.

Speaking to the BBC, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said a former military base was "a better option for housing asylum seekers" than hotels or rented accommodation.

One drawback with disused military bases, however, is that they are often intentionally placed in remote and rural areas. This can be ideal for military training and activity, but is less obviously suited to housing migrants with limited mobility and resources.

Migration and asylum have been contentious political issues in the UK for decades. But successive governments have faced particular pressure in recent years, with the populist right-wing Reform UK and Restore Britain parties gaining ground against the established political giants the Conservatives and Labour.

The most recent manifestation of this was anti-migrant protests in the coastal city of Portsmouth earlier this month.

Burnham promises a new political and economic model To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What does the government say about its plans for MoD Bicester?

In a Q+A published in July about its plans for Ministry of Defense (MoD) Bicester (Site A), the British government said the site "would provide basic, safe accommodation and would be designed to be largely self‑sufficient to minimize any impact on the local community."

It stressed the plan was still subject to feasibility studies, planning permission requirements and other red tape.

It didn't state how many people would be housed there, except to say: "The Home Office would take a phased approach to full occupancy, starting with smaller numbers at first."

It did specify that the facility would hold males aged 18-65.

The government said that if used, the site would be in operation for a minimum of 10 years. Relocating to military bases was "just the first step in the government’s work to exit hotels and source more appropriate accommodation to meet our statutory obligations," it said.

Safety for the local community, staff, and those accommodated on site would be "of the utmost importance," it said. The facility would be monitored round the clock by a security provider and via surveillance footage.

It would also be "designed to be as self-sufficient as possible including laundry facilities and communal spaces," the British government said.

World.title: Los documentos que prueban que Madrid manipuló la lista de espera del Ramón y Cajal: “Evitad anotarlos como preferentes”
World.content:
Fachada del hospital Ramón y Cajal de Madrid superpuesta a los documentos con las pruebas del cambio en la lista de espera quirúrgica.

La consejera de Sanidad ha acusado al cirujano Luis Alberto Martos de alterar la prioridad de los pacientes en lista de espera, pero las pruebas que mostró a EL PAÍS apuntan a dos superiores

La Comunidad de Madrid ha reconocido este miércoles que las listas de espera del Hospital Ramón y Cajal fueron manipuladas, pero sorprendentemente ha eximido de culpa a los dos jefes señalados y ha dirigido su acusación contra uno de los cuatro médicos que denunció los hechos, el único que dio la cara, Luis Alberto Martos. La Consejera de Sanidad, Fátima Matute, ha hecho esta condena pública a pesar de que reconoce que no ha concluido la investigación. Además, Martos no ha sido entrevistado, según asegura él, y las pruebas que aportó el cirujano a EL PAÍS, dejan claro que él no es el autor.

“Este caso es muy sencillo”, ha dicho Matute, solo un día después de que EL PAÍS destapara el caso. “El mismo denunciante es quien manipuló las listas de espera. Es un trabajador del Hospital Ramón y Cajal que ha manipulado de manera irregular la gravedad de 57 pacientes de traumatología para su beneficio, para trabajar menos y operar casos menos complejos”, ha añadido, en la rueda de prensa posterior al Consejo de Gobierno de los miércoles. Poco después, la presidenta Isabel Díaz Ayuso ha difundido en X un vídeo de la consejera pronunciando esas palabras y el mensaje: “El bulo del día contra el Gobierno de la Comunidad de Madrid”.

La acusación sin pruebas contra el cirujano Martos es desmentida por los correos y documentos del servicio de admisión del hospital que Martos compartió con EL PAÍS, según los cuales los responsables de los cambios son el jefe del servicio de Cirugía Ortopédica y Traumatología, Basilio de la Torre, y el director médico, Rafael Martínez. El cambio se produjo entre el 28 de febrero y el 14 de marzo de 2025 y supuso que 57 pacientes con dolencias que aconsejaban una operación prioritaria (que debe hacerse en menos de 90 días) fueron rebajados a la categoría de normal (menos de 180 días), doblando el tiempo de espera. El sentido de esta alteración pudo ser económico porque los jefes de servicio son premiados si cumplen metas de productividad, según se deduce de uno de los correos.

Martos aportó capturas de pantalla del sistema informático en el que se reflejan comunicaciones externas (con el paciente) e internas (entre departamentos) sobre los pacientes en lista de espera quirúrgica. En esos documentos, el personal de administración anotó que se había cambiado la prioridad de los pacientes con mensajes como “cambio prioridad p.i. (por indicación) Dr. De la Torre” o “cambio prioridad p.o. (por orden) de trah (traumatología) y direcc. médica”.

Además, Martos también facilitó varios correos enviados a responsables del hospital por él mismo y por otra cirujana del mismo servicio, Susana Alonso, que es su pareja. En las respuestas de esos superiores nadie acusa a Martos. Al contrario, no desmienten que los cambios habían sido obra de los dos señalados.

Más información Uno de los mayores hospitales de Madrid altera la gravedad de los pacientes para maquillar su lista de espera quirúrgica

La doctora Alonso escribió el 14 de marzo de 2025 al jefe del servicio para quejarse, acusándole directamente del cambio. Adjuntó una captura en la que se veía la modificación a uno de sus pacientes con una anotación que indicaba que había sido orden de los dos superiores: “Podría explicarme las razones que lo justifican, sin contar el criterio del cirujano?”

Hilo de correo entre una cirujana y el jefe del servicio de cirugías ortopédicas y traumatología, Basilio José de la Torre, del Hospital Ramón y Cajal por los cambios de prioridad.

El jefe, de la Torre, admitió esas alteraciones y le dio a la doctora una respuesta que esta no entendió: “Gracias por su contestación, pero no he entendido nada de lo que me acaba de decir”, le dijo ella.

Hilo de correo entre una cirujana y el jefe del servicio de cirugías ortopédicas y traumatología, Basilio José de la Torre, del Hospital Ramón y Cajal por los cambios de prioridad. Hilo de correo entre una cirujana y el jefe del servicio de cirugías ortopédicas y traumatología, Basilio José de la Torre, del Hospital Ramón y Cajal por los cambios de prioridad.

Tres días después, el jefe volvió a escribirle con un mensaje más claro. De nuevo, admitió esos cambios y dio a entender que el motivo era la meta de eficiencia pactada con la Consejería de Sanidad: “Tened en cuenta que el compromiso que adquiere el hospital con ellos es ser operados en el plazo de 90 días”, le respondió por escrito. “Si no son operados en ese plazo, la dirección recibe notificación por parte de la Consejería para que sean operados lo antes posible”.

Agregó que se había reunido con “la dirección y el servicio de admisión” para resolver cómo deben ser tratados los pacientes preferentes y le indicó a la doctora Alonso: “Evitad en la medida de lo posible anotarlos como preferentes, y sí quedáis con el paciente en una fecha aproximada para ser operado y el estudio preoperatorio se pide como preferente”. Esto equivalía a decirle que podían operarlos cuando quisieran, pero engañando al sistema sobre el tipo de prioridad.

Hilo de correo entre una cirujana y el jefe del servicio de cirugías ortopédicas y traumatología, Basilio José de la Torre, del Hospital Ramón y Cajal por los cambios de prioridad.

Martos también proporcionó a este diario sus propios correos quejándose de lo sucedido al director médico, el 21 de marzo de 2025; y al gerente, Carlos Mingo, el 7 y el 28 de abril de ese año. Asimismo, la doctora Alonso envió una queja al gerente el 12 de mayo. Este nunca acusó a Martos de los hechos. En sus respuestas a ambos cirujanos, trató de quitar hierro al asunto y les sugirió que en adelante se pusieran en contacto con sus responsables en el servicio de Cirugía Ortopédica y Traumatología.

El cirujano Martos también facilitó pruebas de que los dos jefes señalados, de la Torre y Martínez, solicitaron al gerente el 29 de abril de 2025 y el 7 de mayo de 2025 la apertura de un protocolo de prevención y actuación ante las situaciones de conflictos internos y acoso. El gerente dio trámite al procedimiento que ha seguido su curso y aún no ha concluido. De hecho, este miércoles a las 11.00 compareció de la Torre en la Dirección General de Recursos Humanos de la Consejería de Sanidad. Martos asistió como testigo.

El coche del jefe

Para ganar la batalla de la opinión pública, la Comunidad de Madrid ha tratado de manchar la imagen de Martos. “Es llamativo que la peor ministra de la historia y su corifeo tomen en consideración a un denunciado con expedientes disciplinarios que además ha sido acusado por rajar las ruedas del coche y rallar el coche de su jefe de servicio”, ha dicho Matute. OkDiario publicó horas después un artículo en el que se asegura que Martos está “encausado” por esos hechos, y que fue compartido en X por Ayuso.

Martos había avisado a este diario sobre este conflicto previo con su jefe, de la Torre. Ahora responde que es falso que esté encausado y que ha sido absuelto de esa acusación, lanzada por su jefe en 2023. Para probarlo ha compartido con este diario dos sentencias absolutorias. Es consciente de que intentan desacreditarlo con ataques a su persona, pero responde que están tratando de desviar la atención: “Lo importante no es si soy un cafre o un memo, lo importante es lo que han hecho”.

Su pareja, Susana Alonso, quiso guardar anonimato en la primera noticia. Pero ha cambiado de opinión, después de que Matute señalara este miércoles que uno de los médicos anónimos que respaldaban su versión tenía una relación de parentesco con Martos. “Sí, soy su mujer desde 2022. Pero eso no implica nada. Soy cirujana del Ramón y Cajal desde 2003″.
