World.title: Seoul momentum - how Japarov is advancing Kyrgyzstan in new format with Korea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 17. President of Kyrgyzstan Sadyr Japarov participated in the first Central Asia–Republic of Korea Summit in Seoul, which elevated cooperation between the five Central Asian countries and South Korea to the level of heads of state and laid the groundwork for a new multilateral format of cooperation.

The summit, chaired by President of the Republic of Korea Lee Jae Myung, brought together the leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. The discussions focused on economic and technological cooperation, energy, transport and logistics, critical minerals, digitalization, artificial intelligence, human capital development and the strengthening of regional ties.

For Sadyr Japarov, participation in the summit provided an opportunity to position Kyrgyzstan not only as an individual partner of Seoul, but also as part of an emerging regional economic and technological platform. In his address, the Kyrgyz leader emphasized the importance of translating political agreements into practical outcomes, including investment, production, technology transfer, and the creation of new jobs.

"Investment in the knowledge, professional skills and talents of our citizens must become a solid foundation for technological modernization, sustainable economic growth and the long-term competitiveness of our countries. Political will must be transformed into practical achievements," Sadyr Japarov emphasized.

Sadyr Japarov proposed reinforcing this approach through specific mechanisms. In particular, he called for the establishment of a Council of State Investment Institutions, the creation of a unified portfolio of priority projects, the establishment of a joint investment fund, as well as the development of a network of pilot technology platforms in artificial intelligence and digitalization. Energy, green mobility, and human capital development were also among the key areas highlighted in his proposals.

"The key task at the current stage is to translate the high level of political trust into long-term economic and technological partnership," the Kyrgyz president emphasized.

In practical terms, Kyrgyzstan is proposing to use the new format not only to attract South Korean investment, but also to integrate the country into broader production, technological and transport chains. For Seoul, Central Asia is of interest, among other things, in terms of diversifying supply chains, energy and critical minerals. The South Korean side also views the region as a promising area for expanding economic cooperation.

He emphasized that by the next meeting, the Central Asia-Republic of Korea format should demonstrate tangible results - launched production facilities, attracted investment, implemented technologies, and new opportunities for citizens.

In this context, Sadyr Japarov’s proposals have a broader dimension. Kyrgyzstan has opportunities to participate in energy and transport projects, including the Kambarata-1 hydropower project and the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway route. At the business session held as part of the summit, Sadyr Japarov specifically invited South Korean companies to participate in the development of industrial parks and logistics centers along the railway, as well as in the country’s energy projects.

Another area that Sadyr Japarov links to expanding Kyrgyzstan’s presence within the new format is tourism and the agro-industrial sector. In particular, he invited South Korean investors to participate in the Ala-Too Resort year-round mountain resort project. At the same time, the Kyrgyz side is emphasizing joint professional training, educational programs, technology startups and digital solutions.

The significance of the summit also lies in the fact that it is not a one-off meeting of leaders. Following the talks, the Seoul Declaration was adopted, providing for the regular holding of summits every two years and the development of cooperation at the ministerial and senior-official levels. The second summit is planned to be held in Kazakhstan in 2028. Thus, interaction between Central Asia and South Korea is gaining a permanent institutional foundation.

Against this backdrop, Sadyr Japarov’s bilateral meeting with Lee Jae Myung complemented the broader summit agenda. The leaders discussed expanding economic cooperation, investment projects and infrastructure. Sadyr Japarov proposed establishing a joint medical center in Kyrgyzstan, considering mechanisms to facilitate the visa regime and increasing Kyrgyz exports to the South Korean market. Lee Jae Myung, in turn, noted the development of relations between the two countries since 1992 and the importance of further strengthening cooperation between investment agencies.

The economic component already demonstrates potential for further growth. According to the Kyrgyz Ministry of Economy and Commerce, trade turnover with South Korea reached $508.7 million in 2025, increasing by 17% year-on-year, while it grew 9.2 times in 2021-2025. At the same time, the structure of trade leaves room for an increase in Kyrgyz exports to the South Korean market.

Going forward, several avenues could emerge for developing the initiatives outlined by Sadyr Japarov at the summit. One option is a transition from signed agreements to the implementation of specific investment projects in energy, industry, transport and tourism. Another could involve the gradual expansion of Kyrgyz exports to South Korea and the integration of local producers into broader regional supply chains.

A separate trajectory could develop around technology and human capital. The establishment of joint educational and technology platforms could provide a foundation for training specialists in AI, digital technologies, and engineering, while creating conditions for the emergence of new joint ventures.

Another option involves strengthening the multilateral dimension itself. In this case, Kyrgyzstan could use the regular summit format to promote joint regional projects related to transport connectivity, energy, digitalization, climate resilience and investment.

Thus, the first Central Asia-Republic of Korea Summit creates several levels of interaction, ranging from political dialogue among heads of state to concrete business projects. For Sadyr Japarov, this provides an opportunity to advance Kyrgyzstan’s bilateral agenda while also strengthening the country’s position within a new regional format, whose further substance will depend on the implementation of the agreements reached in Seoul.

World.title: Czech Republic signals interest in new Kazakhstan flight routes (Exclusive)
World.content:
Photo: Embassy of the Republic of Kazakhstan in the Czech Republic

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 17. The Czech Republic is open to further discussions on additional passenger and cargo air connections with Kazakhstan, including possible routes involving Shymkent and, on the Czech side, Karlovy Vary, the Czech Ministry of Transport told Trend.

The ministry welcomed the recent progress in air connectivity between the Czech Republic and Kazakhstan, including direct flights between Astana and Prague and the newly launched Almaty-Prague route operated by VietJet.

"The Czech side is open to further discussions on additional passenger and cargo connections, including possible routes involving Shymkent and, on the Czech side, Karlovy Vary. Czech aviation stakeholders, including training institutions and companies active in air navigation and aviation technologies, are also ready to explore cooperation with Kazakh partners," the ministry said.

The ministry noted that, building on the launch of the Czech Smart Mobility Ecosystem (Smart Mobility and Transportation Technology | Centrum dopravního výzkumu, v. v. i.), which brings together intelligent transport systems, transport research, Czech companies, academia and research institutions, the Czech Republic can offer comprehensive smart mobility solutions.

These include intelligent transport systems, autonomous driving, transport digitalisation, safety and traffic management systems, logistics tools, and advanced solutions for road, rail and air navigation.

The ministry said that Czech Minister of Transport Ivan Bednárik is scheduled to visit Kazakhstan as part of a broader business and scientific mission to Central Asia planned for October 11-16, 2026.

"The mission aims to explore potential cooperation in this area with relevant stakeholders, including the city governments of Astana and Almaty and local integrators. We are also following the development of the National Digital Transport Platform for the real-time management of transport and logistics chains, which could create opportunities for experienced Czech companies to participate in this emerging ecosystem," the ministry said.

World.title: EDB reveals Central Asia’s industrial export share in Eurasian region
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 17. Central Asian economies sell a share of their processed industrial goods within the wider Eurasian region that, on average, closely matches the region-wide norm — although the share varies across individual countries and reflects different trade structures.

This is according to a report by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB), titled "Architecture of Industrial Transformation of Developing Economies."

According to the report, the Eurasian region as a whole absorbs around 59% of member countries' exports of second-stage processed goods. Within Central Asia, the figure is highest for Kyrgyzstan, at more than 85%, followed by Kazakhstan at 57%, Uzbekistan at 53%, and Tajikistan at 39%, the EDB said.

Trend's calculations show that the simple average across these four Central Asian economies is approximately 58.5% — almost identical to the 59% regional average cited by the EDB across all member countries, including Russia and Belarus. Trend's calculations also reveal that the share recorded for Kyrgyzstan, at over 85%, is more than double the 39% recorded for Tajikistan, representing the largest difference among the four Central Asian economies covered.

For reference, the EDB report identifies chemicals, metallurgy and machine-building as the sectors with the greatest potential for deeper regional cooperation, alongside emerging opportunities in electrical equipment, agricultural machinery, packaging and pharmaceuticals.

World.title: Materials account for two-thirds of Turkish construction costs
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 17. Materials represent approximately two-thirds of Türkiye's construction cost index.

This is according to data released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK).

"Material index increased by 1.28% and labour index increased by 0.92% compared with the previous month," TÜİK said in its July 2026 report, adding that the two sub-indices increased by 27.13% and 30.51%, respectively, over the past year.

As TÜİK does not publish the exact weighting of materials and labor in the overall construction cost index, Trend's calculations use the relationship between the growth rates of the sub-indices and the overall index to estimate their implied shares. The calculations indicate that materials account for approximately 64% of the overall construction cost index, while labor represents the remaining 36%.

The estimated weighting remains broadly consistent when calculated using both monthly and annual changes, providing an additional cross-check of the result.

Trend's calculations also show that materials account for an estimated 63% of the building construction index and approximately 67-68% of the civil engineering index. The difference indicates that the composition of construction costs varies between building construction and civil engineering projects.

For reference, this estimate is independently calculated by Trend based on the relationship between each sub-index's growth rate and the overall index's growth rate. It represents an approximation and does not reflect TÜİK's official weighting methodology.

World.title: Teen's murder case delayed after NT's forensic pathologist takes leave
World.content:
A teenager charged with murdering a 21-year-old man in Tennant Creek in June will have to wait another three months for a key piece of evidence in the case against him, a court has heard.

Northern Territory Police charged the 17-year-old boy with murder on June 14 after he allegedly stabbed the man to death two days earlier in the outback town five hours north of Alice Springs.

The case was mentioned in the Youth Justice Court today where the boy, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was excused from appearing.

Prosecutor David Dalrymple said investigators were still waiting on crucial evidence including forensic testing results, and both police and civilian witness statements.

Mr Dalrymple said crime scene evidence was also still being reviewed and was unlikely to be ready before mid-November.

NT Police allege the teenager stabbed the man to death "following an altercation" in the early hours of the morning. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

He singled out the post-mortem examination report as a particularly "difficult item" as the NT's permanent forensic pathologist was on leave and it was unclear who else might take over.

Mr Dalrymple asked Judge Carly Ingles for a three-month adjournment but said he could not guarantee the post-mortem report would be complete by then.

Defence lawyer Kieran Bonser said the delay was a concern for their client but given the nature of the charge, it was appropriate that the Crown had a chance to obtain the material.

In granting the adjournment, Judge Ingles said as the case was proceeding under the Youth Justice Act, it should be resolved "as quickly as possible", however she said she understood prosecutors' hands were tied.

The case will return to court on December 17.

World.title: Woman, 28, found deceased hours after alleged domestic violence assault
World.content:
Northern Territory Police are investigating the death of a 28-year-old woman in a house in suburban Darwin, hours after she allegedly suffered a domestic violence assault.

A crime scene has been declared at the property on Paqualin Road in Malak after officers found the woman unresponsive at the property yesterday morning.

Following a report from a neighbour, police said they attended the scene and began CPR, before paramedics "took over and the woman was declared deceased a short time later".

Police have cordoned off the house in Malak on Paqualin Road. (ABC News: Michael Donnelly)

In a statement, an NT Police spokesperson said "the exact circumstances surrounding the death remain under investigation, and the cause of death is unknown".

Police declined to provide any further detail, citing an autopsy scheduled for today.

The woman's 26-year-old partner was arrested at the scene over an alleged assault on her in the hours before she was found deceased and for breaching a domestic violence order.

The spokesperson said the man was in custody and yet to be charged with any offence.

"Major Crime detectives are currently investigating the death," they said.

"A report will be prepared for the coroner."

Neighbours told the ABC that at least three children also lived at the Malak property.

History of reported domestic violence

One neighbour who spoke to the ABC on the condition of anonymity said they had reported alleged incidences of domestic violence at the property dozens of times over multiple years.

"It's been ongoing for years, and I've been constantly calling the police and putting in reports to the Children and Families Department," they said.

"Over the years it would've been dozens of times.

" It gets to the point where you say 'Do I bother about reporting it again as it doesn't go anywhere'. "

The NT has the highest rates of family and domestic violence in Australia, with a rate of intimate partner homicide seven times the national average.

NT Police and the Department of Children and Families have been contacted for comment in relation to the neighbour's allegations.

Brian O'Gallagher says his condolences go out to the woman's family and friends. (ABC News: Erin Parke)

Local member for the Malak and Karama area, Brian O'Gallagher, described the death of his constituent as "an absolute tragedy".

"Our hearts and condolences go out to all the family and friends of the [alleged] victim," he said.

Mr O'Gallagher said while he could not speak further about the incident while it was under police investigation, he said the Malak area had recently seen a surge in violent crime.

"There seems to be a spate of increasing crime, particularly around Malak, a lot of that is violent crime," he said.

"There has been a hotspot around Malak at the moment."

Mr O'Gallagher is calling for a targeted police operation in the area "as soon as possible".

World.title: Remote waterhole live stream a window into secrets of NT desert
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

In the red heart of Central Australia, a dingo wanders to the edge of a waterhole.

A wedge-tailed eagle dips its beak for a drink, wallabies move through the rocks and, after dark, frogs announce themselves from the shadows.





The live stream has been running for about a month. (Supplied: Jenny Davis) Until now, witnessing these moments in Watarrka National Park would have been a challenge, but now anyone with an internet connection can watch them unfold.

A camera been installed at a pool on a temporary stream on the Watarrka escarpment near Kings Canyon, about 350 kilometres south-west of Alice Springs.

The live streaming project is a collaboration between Charles Darwin University's Research Institute for the Environment and Livelihoods and NT Parks and Wildlife.

Bringing the bush online

Freshwater ecology professor Jenny Davis has studied Central Australian waterholes on and off since 1986 and has used motion-sensitive cameras at sites in Watarrka for about a decade.





Jenny Davis says anyone who walks to the site could make a cameo on the stream. (Supplied: Jenny Davis) But now it is possible to see what is happening there continuously.

"In the last year or two technology has reached the point where we realised we could actually live stream from one of the waterholes," Dr Davis said.





A four-person team installed the equipment. (Supplied: Jenny Davis) The camera, solar panels and communications equipment were carried to the remote site and installed by a four-person team.

With no mains power or internet connection available, the system relies on solar energy, a Starlink Mini and an onsite computer.

Dr Davis said the installation took about a week, during which the team repeatedly hiked 2 kilometres from the Kings Canyon car park to the site.

"We had to put everything there at the waterhole," she said.

"We were going up and down that 2 kilometres every day and I can tell you by the end of that week I was starting to feel it."

Dingoes, wallabies and life after dark

The result is a window into a part of Watarrka that relatively few people will ever spend significant time observing.

Dingoes have already emerged as some of the live stream's regular stars.





A euro is captured by the camera at the waterhole after dark. (YouTube: Watarrka Waterhole Wildlife) Dr Davis said dingoes with golden, black, and white-and-tan coats had been recorded.

"Sometimes it's a lone dingo, sometimes they're in a mob," she said.

"They're coming in to drink, but they're also quite curious."

Euros, also known as hill wallabies, frequent the area, while birds, insects and the occasional feral cat have also appeared.

At night, viewers may spot frogs by the reflection from their eyes or hear their calls following rain.

Dr Davis said viewers could also hear rain falling, frogs calling and birds, including the grey shrike-thrush.

"There's a lot to take in," she said.

Watching a changing climate

For researchers, what appears on the screen is more than a wildlife spectacle.

The camera overlooks a temporary stream that can shrink or dry completely, making changes in rainfall and water availability particularly important.

Dr Davis said the site had held water more consistently during several wetter years in Central Australia.

"As a freshwater ecologist, I'm really keen to see when there's water present, when it's raining, because this is a very arid environment," she said.

"We're looking for what's happening with global warming because, at this site, the only real impact on the amount of water present is going to be climate change."

Dingoes have been a fixture of the live stream. (YouTube: Watarrka Waterhole Wildlife)

Researchers will also be able to observe which animals use the waterhole and how their behaviour changes over time.

"The live stream allows us to see what's coming in, what's drinking, what the behaviours are and how they might also change as the planet warms," Dr Davis said.

Previous motion-triggered cameras could capture individual moments, but the live stream provides a more continuous picture of what animals are doing.

Dr Davis said the technology could also allow the camera to track and zoom in on wildlife.

"In many ways it's surveillance, but it's providing wonderful information," she said.

The George Gill Range in the Watarrka National Park. (Facebook: Professional Helicopter Services)

A window into Watarrka

Dr Davis said she hoped watching the waterhole would encourage people to value biodiversity and natural environments.

"The more you understand these systems, the more you do value them," she said.

"That's at the very basis of nature conservation."

A perentie ambling along at Watarrka waterhole. (Supplied: Jenny Davis)

NT Parks and Wildlife senior district ranger Di Bowman said Watarrka was home to distinctive landscapes and wildlife.

"This live stream allows people to experience some of our wildlife and gain an appreciation of life in the outback, all from the comfort of home," she said.



Watarrka National Park holds deep cultural significance for the Matutjara people and is internationally known for the sandstone walls and gorges surrounding Kings Canyon.

The waterhole itself is along the Giles Track, away from the park's busiest visitor areas.

World.title: Labor unveils migration cuts targeting students, backpackers and overstayers
World.content:
Australia will crack down on visa overstayers, stop international students from bringing family and limit the stay of backpackers under a series of changes to drive down migration.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has outlined a raft of changes he said would restore the "integrity" of the migration program and give the federal government more "control" over the demand-driven components of the system.

In a speech at the National Press Club (NPC) in Canberra on Thursday Mr Burke described the overhaul as the "next stage" of policies designed to deliver the net overseas migration (NOM) figures in the budget of 245,000 this year and 225,000 next financial year.

He confirmed the government now considered these forecasts a target to meet due to the "challenges" Australia was having with housing.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke at the National Press Club. (ABC News: Matt Roberts )

Net overseas migration fell to 292,100 people in the year to March, according to new figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics released today.

Mr Burke declared claims that Australia was a country of mass migration were "absurd" and warned deeper cuts to the NOM — as flagged by opposition parties — would destroy the economy.

He said Labor's changes amounted to a "relatively simple proposition".

"If you want to come on a temporary basis to Australia, apply for a temporary visa," he said.

"If you want to come to Australia permanently, apply for a permanent visa.

" And if you no longer have a valid visa, you should leave Australia. "

Labor's announcement comes as One Nation unveiled plans to push the country into negative NOM for three years and then 130,000 after that, while the Coalition is finalising plans for a policy expected to target between 150,000 to 170,000 people.

750k visas cut under One Nation plan One Nation unveils its plan to slash immigration by 750,000 places over three years, with major cuts targeting international students and the families of skilled migrants.

Asked how he would win the case with the public that the government's higher target was the right thing to do, Mr Burke said because the "lower levels will trash Australian services and trash the Australian economy".

In addition to immediate visa rule changes, Mr Burke flagged further areas Labor would like to legislate but could not do without the support of the parliament, including limiting unrealistic applications for asylum.

But he said he would not blame this limitation for any failure to achieve the government's NOM target because overshooting the number "won't happen".

Mr Burke also criticised One Nation's policy of preventing skilled migrants from bringing their spouses and children to Australia, arguing about half of all doctors and construction workers and two thirds of nurses came to the country with family.

"Imagine half of the construction workers who we have to build the houses that we need, not coming," he said.

" Imagine two-thirds of the people who we rely on in aged care or nursing not coming. "

Housing and lack of control among problems with current system

Mr Burke said a key problem with Australia's current migration program was that too much of it was demand driven.

He said Australians wanted the government to be able to take a "higher level of control" over different parts of the system.

Mr Burke also identified "visa hopping" as an issue related to individuals who would "never" meet the qualifications to become a permanent resident.

"(They) effectively jump from visa to visa, use the appeals process to be able to stay here as long as possible until it eventually becomes absurd to not just let them stay," he said.

Mr Burke said migration needed to slow enough for housing supply to "catch up", but blamed falling household sizes and other issues for the shortage of homes in Australia.

"The housing shortage we have is not caused by immigration," he said.

" But immigration needs to be part of the solution for the housing crisis. "

Mr Burke says migration needed to slow to allow housing construction to catch up. (ABC News: Matt Roberts )

Changes to skilled work visas

Among the changes flagged in Mr Burke's speech was a redesign of the points test to increase the economic value of skilled permanent migration, with housing construction trades to receive the same recognition as a university qualification.

Mr Burke also announced Ministerial Direction 119 would be changed to give processing priority to construction, healthcare, agriculture, fisheries and teaching after business backlash to an earlier decision.

In July, he had issued a sweeping directive pushing skilled visa applications, lodged offshore, to the back of the queue.

The change meant visa processing times for visas blew out from a few days to more than a year in some cases.

Backpacker ballot for second and third year stays

Mr Burke unveiled a dramatic overhaul of the Working Holiday Maker program, also known as backpackers.

After a months-long go slow on applications, processing will return to the previous faster pace for countries whose schemes require regional work to qualify for a second or third year of stay.

Alarm at backpacker visa slowdown Farmers are concerned they will lose an essential workforce as the brakes are put on working holiday visa applications.

However, a ballot system would be introduced to limit the number of backpackers who are able to stay in Australia beyond one year.

Eligibility for a second year stay will be capped at 45,000 places and applicants would still need to complete 88 days of regional work before entering the ballot.

For the third year, the ballot would be restricted to just 5,000 places with a six-month regional work requirement to qualify.

Last year about 57,000 backpackers stayed in Australia for a second year and about 31,000 did a third year.

Mr Burke said not everybody would get to stay in Australia beyond the first-year because the government needed to have "some control and certainty of what those numbers are".

UK applications would be excluded from the faster processing because the scheme does not have a regional work requirement and is part of the UK, Australia free trade agreement.

Premier warns against 'race to bottom' on immigration The federal government is in discussions with the opposition over immigration as SA Premier Peter Malinauskas warns major parties against a "political race to the bottom".

The number of UK backpackers in Australia has risen sharply since the FTA took effect during the pandemic when there were about 17,000 people to now just under 80,000.

"It's a level of growth that means we are just, at the moment, going to continue to be processing that one slowly," Mr Burke said.

Labor to tackle international student 'visa hopping'

Another major change impacts international students, who would largely no longer be able to attach family members to their visas.

Existing families already in Australia would not be separated, and exceptions would continue for Pacific and ASEAN nationals and certain courses, such as PhDs.

Australia suspends new private college bids to enrol international students Australia suspends private colleges from applying to offer new courses to international students as part of a crackdown on abuse in the student visa system.

To tackle "visa hopping" students who wanted to transfer courses would have to apply for a new visa.

Meanwhile international students who complete from a course would only be able to move into a new course of a higher qualification level.

For example, Mr Burke said a bachelor's degree graduate could apply for a master's course.

"To hop around, up and down, to different institutions, and claim that what is actually just seeking a migration outcome as part of Australia's export of international education will come to an end as a model," he said.

Mr Burke also flagged changes to visitor visas so they would all generally carry a "no further stay" condition.

He said this would prevent people from arriving as visitors and then applying onshore for another visa and moving onto a bridging visa.

Huge crowds fill Pitt Street Mall and the CBD shopping district. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

Crackdown on visa overstayers

In a section of his speech about who would be required to leave Australia, Mr Burke announced a crackdown on migration agents encouraging baseless claims.

The code governing this sector would be changed so agents could be sanctioned or deregistered for encouraging clients to lodge "non-meritorious" claims.

"We cannot have people with some sort of official, formal status, using that official formal status to encourage people to make something which, by any definition, is an unacceptable abuse of the system," Mr Burke said.

He also announced the government would increase its capacity to detain and remove people who remain in Australia after their visas expired.

The extra resources included 100 additional compliance officers and 250 new detention beds.

The government is also examining if the former quarantine facility in Melbourne could also be repurposed.

Mr Burke said he wanted to restore a pre-2015 deterrent where detention was used to influence behaviour and encourage visa overstayers to leave.

"When people had overstayed a visa, we would bring people into detention centres, give them a bridging visa, tell them to leave," he said.

"If they hadn't left, you'd bring them into the detention centre, and within a few weeks they'd organise their own flight and leave."

Mr Burke said the "behavioural change" was "actually the biggest outcome".

Burke flags legislation wish list

Mr Burke outlined two gaps in the migration package he said would require legislation to implement, noting Labor at this stage did not have a likely pathway through the parliament for new laws.

The first would be the creation of an expression of interest mechanism that would allow government to control student arrivals rather than simply processing demand.

Mr Burke said this would directly address the broader "demand driven" problem but could not happen without legislation.

The second area to tackle would be disingenuous protection visa claims.

Mr Burke said he wanted changes aimed at people who lodge weak asylum claims after exhausting other visa pathways in order to remain in Australia during lengthy review and court processes.

"That's not a legitimate reason for the protection system," he said.

"It actually holds up the processing of the legitimate claims."

He revealed applicants from countries where more than 85 per cent of protection applications fail accounted for about 80 per cent of the processing caseload.

Mr Burke said the reason Labor would not simply introduce its preferred migration legislation and try to negotiate Coalition or crossbench support was because it would immediately cause people to exploit migration pathways before the laws passed.

"If people see something you're doing that you're closing down a visa-hopping process, and the legislation is then before, you'll get a behavioural change completely against the national interest that would happen immediately," he said.

Burke hits out at 'absurd' migration arguments

Mr Burke made the case against what he said were a series of "absurd" claims, including that Australia was a country of "mass migration".

He said the country was instead on track to have 700,000 fewer people in 2030-31 than had been forecast prior to the pandemic.

Mr Burke described Australia's migration peak post-COVID as "too high" but argued the country was now 47 per cent lower.

Mr Burke said migration was "critical" to the economies of the regions and cities, defending foreign students as an important job creator.

"For all the talk about student visas, it is also the case that there are people who work and have jobs in Australia as a result of international education being an incredibly important export," he said.

"Drastic cuts, wherever you make them, hurt the economy in every part, in every area."

On Australia's need for extra housing, Mr Burke said in both Sydney and Melbourne almost two-thirds of plasterers were born overseas.

"It's pretty hard to get a house built without having a plasterer involved," he said.

" We need immigration. "

Mr Burke said the "silliest of all" the arguments made about migration was the "endless refrain" that Australia was "bringing in yoga teachers and not construction workers".

He said under Labor there had been 15,000 construction workers enter Australia and "zero" yoga teachers.

Mr Burke said yoga teaching had been added on the migration skills list under the former Coalition government in a deal with India.

World.title: Disgraced MP who fraudulently claimed public money avoids jail
World.content:
Former South Australian MP Fraser Ellis has avoided jail for deliberately rorting a parliamentary allowance, but maintains his actions showed a "casualness" or "recklessness" and "certainly not criminality".

The former member for Narungga on the Yorke Peninsula appeared in the Adelaide Magistrates Court today, where he was convicted for seven counts of deception and handed a 10-month jail term that was suspended on condition he sign a 12-month good-behaviour bond.

In sentencing, Magistrate Simon Smart said Ellis had misused the Country Members Allowance — an accommodation fund used by regional MPs who are required to travel for parliamentary duties.

"Your claims … were not mistakes but deliberate falsehoods," he said.

Former Narungga MP Fraser Ellis was convicted of charges relating to the misuse of the Country Members Allowance. (ABC News)

Mr Smart said the father-of-two "fraudulently received" $4,676 in dishonest claims relating to 20 nights between December 5, 2018, and May 1, 2020, and noted the money had been repaid.

He said Ellis's offending "involved gross breaches of trust".

"You were a public official. These were public monies, if you like, money of the people of South Australia," he said.

"There is a general public expectation public officials will act with probity and honesty, particularly as [it] concerns public monies, and will be held accountable should they not do so."

At the time of the offending Ellis was a Liberal MP, but after the allegations became public in 2021 he quit the party to become an independent.

He was one of two MPs, alongside Troy Bell, who were charged over their use of the allowance after a series of exclusive ABC News stories.

Fraser Ellis was elected to the seat of Narungga at the 2018 SA election. (Facebook)

Ellis was found guilty of four counts of deception in 2024 following a trial but was acquitted of a further 19 counts.

The Director of Public Prosecutions appealed against those acquittals and three were replaced with convictions by the Court of Appeal in July this year.

During sentencing submissions earlier this month, Ellis's lawyer, Scott Henchliffe KC, said his client's actions were of a "haphazard nature" and not part of an orchestrated plan.

Reading from his handwritten remarks, Mr Smart said that since Ellis lost his seat at the March state election, the former MP — who studied journalism and law at university — had applied for other jobs without success and now worked for his father in a casual role.

As he imposed the good behaviour bond, Mr Smart noted Ellis was still a young man, had no prior convictions, had not offended since his arrest and had family responsibilities.

Ellis still disagrees with the court

After signing his good-behaviour bond, Ellis exited the court and said he was "grateful" the "incredibly draining" six-and-a-half-year legal proceedings were over, but said he continued to "disagree with the court".

"I don't believe that my actions arose to a level of criminality," he said.

"I believe it was a casualness with my paperwork that I could plead guilty with in a heartbeat, but I do not believe that I acted in a criminal manner.

"Evidence of that, which has not been talked about much in court, was the fact that while I was found guilty of 20 nights, there were a further 19 where the phone data showed I was in Adelaide and did not lay a claim.

"That, to me, shows a casualness — a recklessness perhaps — but certainly not criminality."

Fraser Ellis said after sentencing that he did not believe his actions rose to a level of criminality. (ABC News: Bethanie Alderson)

Ellis said he took responsibility for that casualness and accepted the punishment he had been given.

"I am looking forward to moving on with my life, however that may be, and whenever that may come around," he said.

World.title: Smart glasses in sights of Fringe venue, Adelaide City Council
World.content:
An Adelaide councillor wants an investigation into banning or restricting smart glasses in parts of the city, amid concerns about people being recorded without their consent.

The call comes amid growing national debate, with a prominent Adelaide Fringe venue also signalling potential support for a ban, and the SA Greens pushing for the technology to be outlawed in settings including schools and playgrounds.

Government not planning import ban for smart glasses The federal government is not currently considering an import ban on smart glasses as it unveils a draft of sweeping new privacy laws including the "right to erasure".

Adelaide city councillor Phillip Martin will put forward a motion next week for an investigation into restrictions on glasses with built-in cameras in places like the parklands, libraries and meeting halls.

"With smart glasses you have no idea somebody could be simply looking at you but recording your every action," Cr Martin told ABC News.

He is particularly concerned about women and children being subjected to covert recording.

"I am aware from reports to the eSafety Commissioner of men approaching women, asking them for a date, recording the response, and then using that response on social media as a dating tip," he said.

"Children have a right to play within playgrounds, parklands and other areas without the threat of being recorded without their knowledge or without their parents' or guardians' consent."

Adelaide City Councillor Phillip Martin wants the council to consider a smart glasses ban. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

The councillor's calls come a week after Yarra City Council banned smart glasses in their playgrounds, childcare centres and gyms.

In August, Brisbane City Council announced a blanket ban on the non-consensual use of all camera-enabled devices, including wearable technology, phones, and action cameras.

Those steps have in turn followed a drop in the cost of the devices, which have risen in popularity after cheaper options hit the shelves.

Push for import ban on 'pervert' smart glasses Support is growing for a ban on the import of so-called “smart glasses”.

Smart glasses have been around for several years, with Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses costing as much as $700.

But some Meta smart glasses retail for significantly less than that, and Kmart Australia has been selling its own alternative for $89.

The ABC has contacted Meta and Wesfarmers — which owns Kmart — for comment, but they did not respond.

Fringe venue Gluttony has flagged a potential ban.

"If someone's got their toddler running around Gluttony while they're having something to eat, they don't exactly want some guy filming them clandestinely," co-director Daniel Michael told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"A burlesque show, for example, might have rules around filming in the show for good reason.

"You can't allow people to bring guns and knives … so it's just about adding to that list to say, 'Look this is something that is not allowed here'."

Adelaide Fringe venue Gluttony is considering steps against smart glasses. (ABC News: Sarah Maunder)

AI smart glasses are not without reported social benefits, and have proved transformative for blind or low-vision users in helping them identify objects and read labels.

"What I would ask people to do before they make these decisions is to consult ... around the positive aspects of these glasses," chair of the See Differently Client Advisory Committee, Michael Hutchinson, said.

"I really worry about the fact that people are calling these 'pervert glasses'.

"To have an individual cafe or a group say we're just going to ban the glasses - I would be very sad if that happens."

SA Greens MP Robert Simms will introduce a bill to state parliament next month to ban smart glasses at "schools, childcare centres, playgrounds, swimming pools and gyms" but said it was important to include exemptions for disability aides.

'Stop the supply'

Last month, the federal government said it was not currently considering an import ban on smart glasses but said the devices could be restricted by local councils.

Caught on candid camera glasses A new pair of camera glasses purchased online has been found to contain video footage of factory workers who appear to have been unknowingly filmed.

SA's Local Government Association (LGA) said while the devices had some legitimate uses, they raised privacy concerns.

"Development and adoption of the technology is outpacing existing regulations," an LGA spokesperson said.

"It's a complex conversation and we welcome engagement with state and federal governments about establishing one set of clear, consistent rules that get the balance right."

Cr Martin said conducting an investigation before implementing a ban would guide the best approach.

"There must be a way of determining what are legitimate glasses or spectacles, what are smart glasses, and when it is appropriate for smart glasses to be used," he said.

A push to investigate the use of smart glasses across Adelaide's CBD will be put to the city council. (ABC News)

Cr Martin's proposed investigation has the support of several other councillors, including Eleanor Freeman, who said the council should examine the outcomes of the moves "to restrict AI glasses in Melbourne and Brisbane".

Adelaide University cyber governance expert Mohiuddin Ahmed said smart glasses had legitimate applications, but said using them around others without their consent amounted to a significant "violation of privacy".

He said there was a need to ensure the technology did not fall into the hands of paedophiles and those "with a history of violence against women and children".

"If it's used for the wrong reasons, for malicious purposes, obviously banning these glasses would deter this type of criminal activity," Dr Ahmed said.

"If there is a general recall Australia-wide, it could work."

Mohiuddin Ahmed says policing a ban would be difficult for council. (Supplied)

He said bans would not be without enforcement challenges.

"If you really want to stop this, stop the supply. Cut it from the neck," he said.

World.title: Concern over federal Labor's quiet extension of mandatory income management
World.content:
The federal Labor government has extended a scheme which sees part of the Centrelink payments of 30,000 Territorians compulsorily quarantined for essential items, despite many experts claiming the practice is discriminatory.

Social services, Aboriginal organisations, politicians and human rights groups have raised the alarm over a federal government extension to compulsory income management via the BasicsCard, despite a 2022 election promise to abolish the system, which also blocks the purchase of items like tobacco and alcohol.

The BasicsCard has been described as discriminatory. (ABC News: Emilia Terzon)

In 2022, while in opposition, the Australian Labor Party said they would "scrap the discriminatory Cashless Debit Card and make the BasicsCard voluntary for those individuals or communities who wish to keep a form of income management".

Labor pledges to scrap compulsory income management More than 24,000 Northern Territorians are on the BasicsCard, but just over 2,000 have volunteered for the income management plan.

But four years on from the promise, in June 2026, the federal government quietly extended income management legislation until 2033 — repealing a clause that would have ended it in July this year.

Last week, the Greens' Penny Allman-Payne introduced a motion to stop the extension, which Labor and the Coalition voted against.

A number of stakeholder organisations have made submissions against the legislative extension, including the Central Land Council (CLC).

Josie Douglas says the Central Land Council is concerned the election promise has been delayed by federal Labor. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

CLC general manager Josie Douglas said the organisation had been "long opposed" to compulsory income management.

In their submission the organisation says their position is "based on lived experience and awareness of the lack of evidence supporting its effectiveness as a social benefit instrument".

"The recent decision to remove the self-repeal dates from the legislation means that residents in the Northern Territory will remain under income management for the next 10 years," Dr Douglas said.

What is compulsory income management?

Compulsory income management was introduced as part of the Howard government's NT Emergency Response in 2007, also known as the Intervention, and is described by advocates as discriminatory since it disproportionately affects First Nations people.

The system quarantines a portion of a person's Centrelink payments for essential items and blocks the purchase of items like tobacco and alcohol.

A BasicsCard is a form of compulsory income management — it is a restricted debit card holding a portion of a person's welfare that is issued by the Australian government through Services Australia.

The federal government has quietly extended compulsory income management. (ABC News: Elsie Lange)

Whether a person is placed on compulsory income management largely comes down to where a person lives.

People are placed on the scheme automatically if they live in a declared area and receive particular kinds of welfare payments, or if they are flagged by social services.

The Cashless Debit Card (CDC), also known as the Indue card, however, was introduced nine years after the BasicsCard, and applied to a broader, more diverse group of jobseekers.

The CDC compulsory income management scheme became optional in 2022 and was abolished the following year.

The scheme has been highlighted by the government as a delivery of their election promises about welfare payments, but is separate to the BasicsCard, which remains in place and continues to disproportionately impact Indigenous Territorians.

In 2023, the old CDC system was turned into an 'enhanced income management' smartcard — those who were still on compulsory income management could switch to the new card, or stay on the BasicsCard.

According to the Northern Territory Council of Social Services, more than 30,000 people in the NT are still on compulsory income management, most of whom are Indigenous.

Research shows scheme 'causes harm'

Australian National University social policy researcher Elise Klein who has been researching compulsory income management for a decade, said governments had not been able to provide evidence that the scheme helped meet social policy goals.

"There is really strong peer-reviewed research that shows that [compulsory income management] causes so much harm," she said.

"Researchers have shown a link between the BasicsCard and the reduced rate of weight of babies and school attendance, that research has been out for years now."

Elise Klein has been researching the compulsory income management scheme for more than 10 years. (Supplied)

She also said it raised human rights concerns, noting while it had been broadened out to include non-Indigenous people, at least 82 per cent of people on compulsory income management were Indigenous.

"You see that disproportionate impact, this racialised impact, still being lived today by people," Dr Klein said.

" It is significant because compulsory income management removes people's rights and it has been under quite a lot of scrutiny, thinking through the human rights lens in terms of removing people's rights to social security and a whole host of financial rights. "

Dr Klein said Labor had laid the groundwork to break its 2022 election promise well ahead of the recent extension of the scheme.

"We've also seen in the federal government's budget an over $200 million commitment to income management arrangements over five years, and then after that, about $50 million thereafter," she said.

"So to me, that suggests a government forward planning to continue compulsory income management."

The CLC's Dr Douglas called for a "well-managed transition plan away from compulsory income management to a voluntary system".

"The transition plan must involve Aboriginal leadership and financial capability experts working in with the Commonwealth government to ensure that the right protections are in place for a voluntary system that will work," she said.

Federal government says promise fulfilled

Federal Labor politicians say they stuck to their election promise by abolishing the cashless debit card in 2023.

"What we agreed to abolish was actually the cashless debit card, and that's what we took to the election, and that's the card we actually abolished," Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy said.

"There has always been the BasicsCard in place, we know that some forms of income management has to be there, usually through the courts, usually it's part of conditions for people either in family and domestic violence situations or in regards to legal circles."

Malarndirri McCarthy says Labor stuck to its election promise by abolishing the cashless debit card. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

Senator McCarthy said First Nations people had indicated at various points that they wanted to keep the BasicsCard.

In a statement, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said the government had consulted with 81 communities and thousands of people on income management.

"These discussions told us that people want the government to work with them to create solutions, rather than make decisions for them," she said.

" We will take the time to get any future changes right, and ensure any reforms continue to support and empower communities rather than harm them. "

Ms Plibersek did not directly respond to questions from the ABC about why compulsory income management was extended indefinitely, why no announcement or justification was made, whether the government was committed to ending mandatory income management and its timeline to do so.

Speaking with ABC Radio Alice Springs on Wednesday, member for Lingiari Marion Scrymgour defended the use of income management in the NT, however she said she thought it should eventually be made voluntary.

Marion Scrymgour says compulsory income management ensures children have access to food and clothing. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"We've got to use income management when we've got families that have been struggling and doing it, and kids are suffering because they're not getting access to food and clothing and those things," she said.

"I think that income management should be part of the tool that is used with families."

The Community Affairs References Committee will examine the legislative changes on Friday, September 18.

World.title: WA police officer pleads guilty to assaulting his five-week-old baby
World.content:
A Western Australian police officer has pleaded guilty in a Perth court to assaulting his five-week-old baby.

Nickolas Wayne Peake, 30, appeared at the Midland Magistrates court today charged with aggravated common assault.

In a statement, WA police said detectives from the Child Abuse Squad laid the charges on Sunday after the assault, and the baby was taken to Perth Children's Hospital as a precaution.

Police said Peake, a serving officer, had been stood down.

Peake is due to face court again next month. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

He was released on bail after pleading guilty to the charge.

Peake declined to answer any questions from the media outside court.

He is due back in court next month.

World.title: Burke says the quiet part out loud: immigration and housing are linked
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalImmigration Burke says the quiet part out loud: immigration and housing are linked Paul Sakkal September 17, 2026 — 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The sands have shifted rapidly in Australia’s migration debate and Labor has belatedly sniffed the wind. Last year the vanquished Liberal leader Peter Dutton was being assailed by party moderates for saying loudly that the high migration was contributing to elevated rents and property prices. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke at his National Press Club address. Alex Ellinghausen Liberal senator Andrew Bragg said, in the wash-up, that Dutton’s message had hurt the Coalition badly in its election thrashing. “We love multicultural Australia,” Bragg said, and “we’re not wanting to make people feel unwelcome.” An example of Dutton’s rhetoric came in a budget-in-reply speech in which he said Labor’s “poor management of migration” had helped cause “congestion on our roads and pressure on services”.



The notion that the housing crisis was driven solely by a lack of housing supply had become a shibboleth in the left. Until Home Affairs Tony Burke stood up at the National Press Club. Related Article Immigration Labor migration plan revealed: Burke to ramp up deportations and bring in backpacker ballot “Immigration will need to be part of the solution to help provide some space for housing supply to catch up,” he said on Thursday, as Labor aims to neutralise the political issue driving voters to Pauline Hanson. “We’re both improving supply and reducing demand.” “The housing shortage we have is not caused by immigration, but immigration needs to be part of the solution.” It wasn’t the only striking admission from Burke, who left Labor flailing for six weeks after the last-minute delay of his speech.



The minister blew the whistle on a bipartisan, two-decade miscalculation since John Howard liberalised Australia’s migration rules in the early 2000s. “Effectively, the decision that Australia took when we had a demand-driven program was to say that if employers can get the workers that they need and our educational institutions can get the students who are willing to pay, and we get the business, then infrastructure and housing will take

care of themselves,” he said. “That is no longer the experience of Australians. That is no longer the view of Australia.” The failure to maintain public confidence in the program, displayed in a litany of opinion polls, has created a void that’s been filled by an opportunistic populist who feels so unrestrained as to outrageously suggest that none of Australia’s 800,000 Muslims are good people. A 2024 study in the Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance found that every one per cent rise in immigration led to between 1.8 to 3 per cent rise in support for far-right parties across 4500 electoral results in Europe.



Former Labor adviser and migration expert Henry Sherrell last month called for a ceiling of one per cent population growth from immigration. Australia exceeded that figure in half of the last 20 years, much more than peer democracies, but just once in the 50 years before that. Related Article Immigration What are Labor’s new migration rules for Australia? Burke called out the use of the term “mass migration”, which some bad-faith conservatives on the right have co-opted but it has increasingly been used by mainstream figures like Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Labor hopes its intervention in the migration debate will finally cauterise the political problem and show it’s alive to voters’ concerns. Labor knows it cannot win back Hanson’s hardcore supporters, but Albanese’s primary vote has taken a hit and Labor thinks it can recover about 5 per centage points on its primary vote through sustained work to persuade voters they’ve listened. Its opponents will cast Burke’s measures as half-arsed and focused too heavily on backpackers, a cohort One Nation and the Coalition do not view as a problem.



With one and maybe two interest rate rises on the way, don’t expect Hanson to take her foot off the pedal. And prepare for more ugly politics on who comes and goes from Australia. Burke’s warning: Is Australia becoming a guest worker economy?

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination of complainant ‘M’ resumes as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the alleged physical acts occurred.

Alan Jones and his legal team arrive at court on Thursday. Dominic Lorrimer

On Monday, the third of the six complainants, a former athlete dubbed “M”, started giving evidence.

His cross-examination started on Tuesday, and he returns to the witness box today for further questioning by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, after a break in the trial on Wednesday. “M” has told the court:

Jones kissed him on the corner of his mouth at an event in Sydney about a decade ago. “I think I froze at that time,” “M” said.

He rejected suggestions by Bashir on Tuesday that the alleged kiss didn’t happen.

The court has heard Jones texted “M” after the function: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after, had to go back to work. You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

“M” replied: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now; thanks mate xoxo.” The conversation ended in “M” saying “let me know when we can catch up. Lots of love” and Jones replying: “I will darling. Big kisses forever.”

“M” agreed during cross-examination that he did not tell police in his statements that Jones kissed him on the lips at the event. But he said that “I believe I pointed to where it was”.

The complainant said he had “a close relationship with Jones over a period of time” and that “in certain areas” he could go to the broadcaster if he needed help.

The court has previously heard that Jones texted “M” on another occasion, after receiving a photo: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up darling [name] xxx”. “M” said he did not respond immediately. Hours later, Jones wrote: “I hope my message did not upset you. I love you.” The man said he responded the next day, writing: “Not at all mate. It’s nice to be loved.”

The complainant said he had used the word “mate” for many reasons. “I know I’d made it very clear that ... it wasn’t moving into a relationship, so ‘mate’ was my way of pushing back, I guess.”

Reflecting on the messages, “M” told the court that he believed “it’s a person that is in love with me”, adding that he did not return those feelings.

“M” said that on the last occasion he visited Jones at his harbourside apartment, the broadcaster kissed him on the cheek towards his lips and said words to the effect of, “I love you so much, you don’t know how much I love you.” The complainant said he could feel Jones’ genitals on his leg .

The complainant said he pushed the broadcaster away and said, “OK, mate”, in a tone intended to convey “get away from me”, and “got out of there as quickly as possible”.

The court heard Jones had sent the complainant gifts including weekly flowers for years and a dinner set. The complainant agreed he also sent Jones flowers at least once.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Why AI hasn’t taken your job yet
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAI Opinion Why AI hasn’t taken your job yet Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer September 17, 2026 — 3:56pm

September 17, 2026 — 3:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

OpenAI and Anthropic, the dominant frontier labs, have thrown plenty of elbows in their race toward stratospheric, trillion-dollar stockmarket listings. But this week, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, their respective leaders, reached a rare unity ticket along with fellow AI kingpin Elon Musk, calling for a slowdown on artificial intelligence development in the name of saving humanity. This latest bout of fear coming from inside the house began after Anthropic researcher Jacob Poxon resigned last week, accusing the companies of “gambling with our lives”. That announcement prompted his former colleague, Evan Hurbinger, to claim that there was a greater than 10 per cent chance that AI would “kill all humans” within the next decade. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has warned of the risks of unfettered AI growth. Bloomberg How very reassuring. Fortunately, all this has been rejected by US President Donald Trump, who has insisted that attempts to slow down AI are a “sick conspiracy” to let China get ahead, creating the absurd situation where highly valuable companies are begging a recalcitrant government to regulate them.



Related Article AI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates Most people’s concerns about AI are more prosaic. They are less worried about geopolitical rivalry or the prospect of rogue agents creating a devastating virus than whether the machines will take their jobs. In May 2025, the Anthropic boss Amodei predicted that half of all entry-level white-collar jobs would be obliterated in the next five years, sending unemployment rates into the double digits. If there is perhaps one micro-dose of optimism among all the bleak AI news, it is that the tsunami hasn’t yet hit. Instead, employment data from around the world paints a messy, paradox-filled picture. The United States added 162,000 jobs in September, exceeding expectations and strengthening the case for the country’s Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, which it did for the first time since 2023 on Wednesday, much to Trump’s chagrin.



Here in Australia, unemployment crept up unexpectedly to 4.5 per cent in July, its highest rate in the post-COVID era in trend terms. While it’s too soon to tell whether this is the start of a longer-term trend, a 0.1 per cent increase does not seem like the start of a job apocalypse. The rose-tinted view of the AI boom suggests that, like every past industrial revolution, the latest technological rupture will destroy many jobs but create different new ones. Some recent number-crunching in The Economist magazine found that AI had created around 1 million new jobs in the United States, with many attributable to the data centre construction boom. The problem is that while data centres are delivering reliable, well-paid blue-collar work, those jobs are temporary. These AI “factories” don’t resemble the real thing when it comes to employment. Then there’s the fact that they have become a widely despised symbol of everything people resent about AI, with opposition to their development cutting across political lines and threatening to stall that job explosion. Whether that infrastructure delivers in Australia is also contested. The local sector’s lobbyists insist it will “support” 935,000 jobs. But as this masthead recently reported, that figure comes from a line in a 2024 report by consulting firm Mandala (which has partnered with OpenAI in the past) and conflates data centre work with all tech sector jobs. More importantly, the report was commissioned by five of the country’s biggest data centre operators.



Separately, economic think tank the e61 Institute claims there are only around 11,500 data centres workers in Australia nationally. Even if data centres are the future, it’s quite a stretch to imagine soft-handed software engineers (let alone journalists) to retrain as construction workers. Related Article Opinion

AI Will AI kill us all? I doubt it, but let’s reduce the risk ... now Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Beyond blue-collar work, AI is still causing ruptures in the labour market. Research from Princeton University’s Sania Edlich and Apollo Global Management chief economist Tortsen Slok found that rather than destroying jobs, AI was stifling wage growth. Those “different” jobs created by the AI boom could well be repetitive, boring and lower paid. Witness the poor workers recording themselves doing tasks as dull as screwing lids onto milk bottles to train future generations of robots how to hold things. The next few years could see Australia struggle with the “K-shaped” economy which has characterised the United States post-COVID in which the asset-rich few thrive thanks to a surging stock market and corporate profits, even as wages stagnate for the many. The problem is that AI is moving at such a fast clip that there are many people with opinions, but few are truly informed. Now, it is the frontier lab bosses, the people who have seen what the technology can do, who are sounding the loudest alarms.



At least the unemployment rate probably doesn’t matter too much if humanity is wiped out. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: KPMG consultant admits to ‘gaps’ in its whistleblower report
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWhistleblowers KPMG consultant admits to ‘gaps’ in its whistleblower report Colin Kruger September 17, 2026 — 3:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The authors of a report designed to document KPMG’s whistleblower failings qualified their findings on the basis that they were unable to interview key staff – including the whistleblower – and found gaps in the accounting firm’s records of crucial meetings. Boutique advisory Andrews Group, which penned the report published on Thursday, said it conducted interviews and relied on public and internal documents from KPMG, but admitted this exercise, “despite providing rich information, still left gaps”. KPMG chief executive John Sams (right) said the firm recognises “the challenges created by our own failings” from the whistleblower scandal. Alex Ellinghausen “Some individuals who were associated with and played a pivotal role in the disclosures were, for a variety of reasons, unable to be interviewed. This included the whistleblower,” they said. The report found that KPMG adopted an overly legalistic approach to the complaints levelled against the firm and failed to uphold its core values, which led to the poor treatment of the whistleblower.



KPMG has been under siege after admitting that some of its staff accessed confidential information from corporate clients to win business – a serious breach of the trust in the world of auditing that is essential to the integrity of financial markets. The consultancy confirmed that former employees associated with the whistleblower scandal were unable to be interviewed. The firm has yet to respond to this masthead’s question of whether current employees declined to talk to the report’s authors. The report, which had been commissioned and paid for by the embattled accounting firm, noted there were multiple discussions, meetings and decisions within KPMG Australia relating to the handling of the whistleblower and their disclosures “for which records have not been kept”. “Given these gaps, rather than document findings which would need to be unequivocal, hypotheses were developed,” the report’s authors said. These hypotheses were strongly supported by the weight of evidence and “therefore, despite not being proven or true, are difficult to refute”. Andrews Group said the report didn’t have to determine accountability, but was meant to identify lessons to be learnt from KPMG’s failure to deal with the whistleblower allegations for almost two years.



The scandal cost it some of its most lucrative contracts, with Lendlease and Macquarie Group both dumping KPMG as their external auditor. Related Article Consulting ASIC launches review of whistleblower complaints at accounting giants And it won’t be the end of the matter for the firm. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission told a parliamentary hearing last month that it is conducting its investigations in relation to the whistleblower scandal. This includes looking into documents that KPMG had lodged with the regulator last year to determine if they contained any false or misleading statements. “Initial inquiries are focused on the basis for statements made in that report, including the statement that there were no whistleblower complaints related to audit quality,” ASIC said in a submission to the parliamentary hearing last month.



The scandal first came to light in March – almost two years after the whistleblower made their initial complaint to KPMG – when Labor senator Deborah O’Neill read out the whistleblower’s allegations in parliament. It led to an exodus of KPMG’s most senior executives, including CEO Andrew Yates and chairman Martin Sheppard, and also prompted the sacking of former chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett, who has lodged action to sue the firm. Former KPMG board member Kim Lawry resigned, but is still negotiating her exit after an investigation found screenshots on her phone of confidential Lendlease board documents. She was due to retire last month. KPMG reiterated its apologies to the whistleblower in the report, saying “senior people in our organisation behaved in a manner that was unacceptable and not in line with our values, and when someone had the courage to raise their concerns, we did not respond as we should have.” The report made recommendations to help remedy KPMG’s whistleblower failings by establishing an independent integrity office at the firm, and appointing a dedicated whistleblower protection officer. World.title: Coroner finds shark control measures ‘appropriate’ after teen killed
World.content:
NationalQueenslandInquest Coroner finds shark control measures ‘appropriate’ after teen killed Cloe Read September 17, 2026 — 3:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An inquest will not be held into the shark attack that killed Queensland teenager Charlize Zmuda, with a coroner finding the Queensland government’s management of drum lines and nets to be appropriate. Charlize Zmuda, 17, a dedicated lifesaver, died in February 2024 after she was bitten by a shark at Woorim Beach, north of Brisbane, just before 5pm. In findings released on Thursday, coroner Carol Lee found that Zmuda died from injuries to her right upper limbs due to a bull shark attack. Charlize Zmuda (left) loved the beach and had been a member of the lifesaving club since she was a young girl. Zmuda had been at the unpatrolled beach with a friend when she decided to swim alone. A short time later, her friend, who was waiting on the beach, saw a commotion in the water, heard a scream and saw blood.



Zmuda was found floating on her back, and the alarm was raised. Emergency services, and a lifeguard who rushed from a patrolled beach, were unable to revive the teenager. In the findings, Lee reviewed Queensland’s current shark control measures, which include drum lines and drone patrols. Hundreds gathered on Woorim Beach in February last year to pay tribute to Charlize Zmuda. Darren England At the time of the attack at Woorim, the drone trial was in its first phase and conducted over the summer school holiday periods until further evaluation of its success, Lee said. “Given the availability of funding remaining in the budget from days lost due to bad weather, Surf Life Saving Queensland were additionally flying drones on weekends up to and including February 2, 2025, the day before the incident,” Lee said.



“Shark nets are not suitable at the Woorim Beach location due to the high tidal currents experienced in this area which tend to twist the nets or drag it off station, which would render it ineffective.” She said while nets and drum lines reduce the risk, they were not an impenetrable barrier. Charlize Zmuda. TikTok As of March 2025, there were 18 shark control drum lines located off Woorim, about 300 to 350 metres from the beach. Between January 2024 and March 2025, there were four sharks found at the Woorim Beach drum lines – a bull whaler shark, a blacktip whaler shark, a bull shark and a tiger shark.



Lee said substantial reviews were now under way through shark management plans, in addition to a significant funding investment. Related Article Sharks SharkSmart drone program expanded at south-east beaches amid criticism of nets “This demonstrates an evolution of Queensland’s shark-mitigation approach, from the operational status at the time of Charlize’s death to an enhanced, technology-enabled, research-driven program designed to reduce risk across the state’s coastlines,” she said. Lee said having considered the information from the department and the government’s response to shark control measures, she was satisfied there was an appropriate risk mitigation framework in place to reduce shark attacks, with the aim of protecting human life whilst maintaining environmental protection. “Against that background, I am not satisfied that it is in the public interest to hold an inquest,” she said, adding that publishing the findings online would raise awareness to prevent future deaths.



“There is also no uncertainty or conflict of evidence to justify the use of the judicial forensic process and no suspicious circumstances that have not been resolved or resulted in criminal charges.” After her death, Zmuda’s mother, Renee, said her daughter was a shining light who touched the lives of everyone she met. “She loved the beach, and it truly was her happiest place on earth,” she said at the time.
