World.title: One of Brisbane’s best restaurants gets a cookbook
World.content:
Eating outFood One of Brisbane’s best restaurants gets a cookbook Now you can cook zucchini chips at home, along with more than 100 other recipes that span Hellenika’s 16-year history. Matt Shea September 17, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Books are hard, Simon Gloftis says. And he doesn’t mean cookbooks. Just, any book. “I couldn’t even fathom the idea of how I would do a book. I struggle even now to read and write properly,” the restaurateur says disarmingly. “For me, it was a big deal. It wasn’t a matter of jotting down some ideas. It was like asking me to jump off a building.” Simon Gloftis with the Hellenika cookbook. Courtesy of Hellenika That’s one of the reasons it’s taken this long to produce the new Hellenika cookbook, which will be released October 1. The others? A pandemic and a couple of restaurant openings (Sushi Room and Sunshine, both in 2022). “It’s been a process,” he says. “I almost gave up and then I was at a dinner and [co-writer] Marie[-Christine] Sourris’ husband was there and said, ‘Mate, finish this book. You need to do it.’ … And I thought, ‘OK, I’d better put my money where my mouth is’.”



Related Article Exclusive Melbourne game-changers announce ambitious first Brisbane restaurant The result is a 272-page cookbook that presents 110 recipes spanning the entire history of the popular James Street restaurant, split into 12 sections, from breakfast to mezedes, mains, desserts and even cocktails. Besides Sourris, the book features photography by Annika Kafcaloudis and styling by Stephanie Stamatis, both from Melbourne. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Gloftis said it was the book’s publishing consultant, Julie Gibbs, who convinced him to make it so extensive. Yes, you can now cook the restaurant’s zucchini chips at home. Courtesy of Hellenika “They said, ‘Simon, just own it. They’re yours. Go out there and give them everything. Don’t hide one thing’,” Gloftis says. “So that’s what we’ve done. We have the entire menu on there … all the tricks are in there.”



So yes, you can cook the restaurant’s iconic zucchini chips, slow-cooked lamb shoulder, and spanner crab kritharaki. The emphasis throughout, Gloftis says, is on how simple Mediterranean cooking can be. “My motto from when we first opened Hellenika was, ‘If it doesn’t need that one extra ingredient, it doesn’t go in’,” Gloftis says. Hellenika restaurant at The Calile Hotel. Markus Ravik But this is also about telling the narrative of Hellenika, from its beginnings at Nobby Beach perched above the Gold Coast Highway, to Theo Kampolis coming onboard as partner in 2017, to the restaurant’s expansion to Brisbane in 2018, where it made its home at The Calile Hotel. The cookbook also forms one part of Hellenika’s 15-year celebrations (it actually opened 16 years ago on the Gold Coast, in March 2010) with the restaurant also hosting a pop-up at Miami Marketta in late October. That event sold out in a matter of days.



The cookbook is available October 1. Courtesy of Hellenika. Hellenika wasn’t Gloftis’ only venue in those early Gold Coast years – there was The Fish House, which closed in 2020 after he sold the restaurant in 2016, and Nineteen at the Star, which he exited from in 2019. So, what made Hellenika stick, both for him and diners? “There was very little shared dining when we opened,” he says. “There was no one doing lamb shoulder falling off the bone with that kind of quality … we were flying King George whiting up from Melbourne every day. And the Greek community [got right behind the restaurant]. You can’t fool them. That’s why it’s stood the test of time. “I wanted to call the book The First 15 Years because I truly believe Hellenika is going nowhere. Hellenika’s story has a long way to play out.”

World.title: Clover Moore lashes NSW government’s ‘extraordinary’ intervention in Town Hall square
World.content:
NationalNSWPlanning Clover Moore lashes NSW government’s ‘extraordinary’ intervention in Town Hall square Megan Gorrey September 17, 2026 — 3:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

City of Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore has accused the NSW government of attempting to block a controversial $150 million plan to raze seven buildings for a new civic square, after Planning Minister Paul Scully sought independent advice on whether he should seize control of the project. Citing the cost and prominent location of the council’s long-vaunted Town Hall square, Scully on Wednesday intervened by referring the project to the NSW Independent Planning Commission for advice on whether it should be declared “state significant” development decided by the government. Lord Mayor Clover Moore says more public space was “not a nice to have″⁣, it is essential infrastructure that we are committed to delivering”. City of Sydney “The proposal, as it stands, would have significant impact on the commercial heart of Sydney’s CBD, requiring the demolition of seven buildings and an expenditure of at least $150 million in ratepayer funds,” Scully said. The move prompted a fiery response from Moore, who said she was “shocked and disappointed” by the Minns government’s “extraordinary and highly unusual intervention in established planning processes”, which she was concerned “could delay or even block the Town Hall Square project”.



Their remarks set the stage for a showdown between Moore’s council and the Minns government over the square – which was first proposed in the 1980s – in the run-up to the March state election. Related Article Exclusive

Planning Sydney might get a new civic square. One building stands in the way For the past three decades, the council has been gradually acquiring a parcel of properties between George and Pitt streets opposite Town Hall, which it has hoped would eventually constitute a rare public domain in the centre of the city. The council in February voted to accelerate demolition of the buildings, including Woolworths supermarket, stating its ambition to complete demolition and construction within about six years. Moore said Scully had not raised any concerns when the council briefed him on the project in 2025, and the government had approved its acquisition of the final property needed to deliver the square.



“Against that history, the timing and nature of [this] intervention inevitably raises questions, particularly as political attention begins to turn towards the next state election,” Moore said. “If the government ultimately uses its powers to stop this project rather than simply scrutinise it, that would be a deeply concerning and regressive intervention in the delivery of important public infrastructure.” The City of Sydney’s Lord Mayor Clover Moore, NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully and Transport Minister John Graham in The Rocks on Wednesday. Sitthixay Ditthavong Scully has powers under the NSW Environmental Planning and Assessment Act to declare a project as state significant if he has received and made public advice from the IPC about the state or regional planning significance of the proposal. He said the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure would prepare an assessment report on the square for the commission. Moore said the council was still reviewing directions issued to the council, which would prevent it from determining demolition orders or development applications for the project, and what they would mean for the square’s delivery timeframe. The project was estimated for completion in 2031.



Moore said the project would be assessed by an independent planner and determined by the Central Sydney Planning Committee, most members of which have been appointed by the state government. “Any suggestion that council had a conflict of interest or isn’t managing approval appropriately is incorrect. We remain confident in the merits of the proposal and see no planning reason why it should not ultimately be supported,” Moore said. The council says the space could be used as a sporting event live site. City of Sydney In August, the council revealed designs for the 4200-square-metre plaza, prepared by Sydney design practice JPW and landscape architects ASPECT Studios, featuring eucalypts, moving water, seating and circular paving patterns to provide an outdoor venue for large events and celebrations including markets, festivals, concerts and sports event live-sites. The square would have an Aboriginal name. The proposal to demolish the buildings for the square has triggered a wave of opposition from the Business NSW lobby group, Woolworths and The Daily Telegraph.



Business NSW executive director Paul Nicolaou said the government had “made the right call in putting the brakes on the City of Sydney’s plan to demolish seven buildings in the commercial heart of the CBD in favour of a controversial Town all square that would cost a minimum $150 million”. Related Article City life Cars out, diners in: Final section of George Street set for $25m revamp Nicolaou said the plaza concept “might have been a nice-to-have when it was first mooted more than 30 years ago”, but it was “not the right project amid the economic realities of 2026”. “The $150 million could be directed to more important needs including crisis accommodation for the hundreds of people sleeping rough in our city every night or living in encampments on our streets.” The Independent Planning Commission was formed in 2018 to decide, and provide advice on, the state’s most complex and contentious developments. In 2019, a three-member panel killed off The Star’s $530 million plan to build a 66-storey hotel and apartment tower above its Pyrmont casino. World.title: The first Immortal? Where four-time champion’s legacy places her in history
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cast an eye to the future and consider who the first rugby league Immortal of the women’s game might be. Given her status as a trailblazer, State of Origin hero and four-time premiership winner, Ali Brigginshaw’s name must be front and centre of those discussions. “Ali Brigginshaw: when you hear that name, you know she’s something special,” Brisbane Broncos teammate Julia Robinson told this masthead. “What she’s done for the game is incredible. She’s just one of those players and people you just look up to … you want to play for, and whenever she goes out there she plays with her heart on her sleeve and is an inspiration to all. “She’s inspired so many girls, she’s going to have this legacy forever. There are so many girls who can be Immortals, but Ali is definitely up there.” Each game could be Brigginshaw’s last, with the 36-year-old stressing she would not be backflipping on her decision to retire at season’s end as she sought to eradicate the “mum guilt” she felt being on the road with two stepdaughters at home. Broncos players Julia Robinson, Ali Brigginshaw and Chelsea Lenarduzzi after winning the 2025 NRLW grand final against the Roosters. NRL Images “People have definitely questioned that response, but to me, I think I’ve done a lot in the game, and I’m happy with where I’m at,” Brigginshaw laughed.



“I want to see what else is out there; I want to spend time with my family, thinking about holidays and all that. It’s time to see what Ali can do now.” The Brisbane champion was reduced to tears after a final round triumph of the Warriors, when New Zealand players performed a Hakka in her honour – ending a shortened last regular season in which she copped a three-game suspension for a dangerous tackle which left her “heartbroken”. Celebrations of her career, according to Brigginshaw, needed to be discarded for now, as the Broncos plot another piece of silverware – beginning with Saturday’s elimination final against Newcastle. Loading “I’ve always just said I play the game that I love, and I’m lucky that I get to be a part of all these moments of games that we never even thought we’d be standing here doing and watching women’s rugby league,” Brigginshaw said. “It wasn’t really spoken about or thought about when I first started. Playing the game I love, leaving a legacy for young girls to always have rugby league available to them, it’s a crazy world I live in that I get to do that. “But it’s why I wanted to celebrate and have my family around at the last home game of the rounds because the focus isn’t me, the focus is the finals’ series. I never want to make something about me.”



While no women have been included in rugby league’s most illustrious club across the game’s 118-year history – Ron Coote named as the 14th Immortal in 2024 – the first female members of the NRL Hall of Fame who were named that same year has suggested an inaugural inductee beckons. Those Hall of Fame members – Natalie Dwyer , Katrina Fanning , Tarsha Gale , Veronica White , Karyn Murphy , and Tahnee Norris – would come into consideration, while modern-day stars such as five-time premiership victor and two-time Dally M Medal winner Tamika Upton is already arguably the code’s greatest player, despite being just 29. Upton – who served as co-captain alongside Brigginshaw last year, before the latter stepped down for this campaign – laughed when it was put to her that she could factor into that debate, before shifting attention to the role Brigginshaw has played in pioneering the women’s space. Related Article NRL 2026 The boxer, teacher and curse breaker: The coach who shone from Bennett’s shadow “Her story is definitely not closed in rugby league. I don’t know what the future holds for her, but I’m sure she’ll be in and around the fold in some capacity, so she’s still adding to that [legacy],” Upton said. “You want to go out with a win for Ali – I think she is the NRLW. It’s going to be weird, I haven’t really thought about it too much just yet because we’re still in it, and she’s still here, but there hasn’t been an NRLW game without her in it or in the fold.”



Brigginshaw has no intention of closing the book on her rugby league journey – one which began playing juniors with the boys before a Queensland and Australia debut in 2009, nine years before the NRLW launched when a professional women’s outlet seemed to be a pipe dream. Murphy remains the only woman at the helm of a senior side, with her Gold Coast Titans finishing second, and Brigginshaw hinted she harboured a desire to join her in the coaching ranks. “I’ve been around for a long time and had many coaches where I feel I can pass on the knowledge to the younger girls, but I always dreamt and still dream of coaching 15, 16-year-old boys,” Brigginshaw revealed. “I had a coach who was a female in the boys space when I first started, and something about that was something I wanted to do. You never know where it’s going to land, but I’m pretty much open to all opportunities. Ali Brigginshaw has been a staple of the Australian, Queensland and Broncos side since the NRLW began in 2018. Getty Images “I know it’s time for me to step away because the young generations are coming, and they’re ready to take on the next step.” That coaching future should not come as a shock, given Brigginshaw has already served as a mentor and player to aspire towards for the next generation.

World.title: Burke says the quiet part out loud: immigration and housing are linked
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalImmigration Burke says the quiet part out loud: immigration and housing are linked Paul Sakkal September 17, 2026 — 3:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The sands have shifted rapidly in Australia’s migration debate and Labor has belatedly sniffed the wind. Last year the vanquished Liberal leader Peter Dutton was being assailed by party moderates for saying loudly that the high migration was contributing to elevated rents and property prices. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke at his National Press Club address. Alex Ellinghausen Liberal senator Andrew Bragg said, in the wash-up, that Dutton’s message had hurt the Coalition badly in its election thrashing. “We love multicultural Australia,” Bragg said, and “we’re not wanting to make people feel unwelcome.” An example of Dutton’s rhetoric came in a budget-in-reply speech in which he said Labor’s “poor management of migration” had helped cause “congestion on our roads and pressure on services”.



The notion that the housing crisis was driven solely by a lack of housing supply had become a shibboleth in the left. Until Home Affairs Tony Burke stood up at the National Press Club. Related Article Immigration Labor migration plan revealed: Burke to ramp up deportations and bring in backpacker ballot “Immigration will need to be part of the solution to help provide some space for housing supply to catch up,” he said on Thursday, as Labor aims to neutralise the political issue driving voters to Pauline Hanson. “We’re both improving supply and reducing demand.” “The housing shortage we have is not caused by immigration, but immigration needs to be part of the solution.” It wasn’t the only striking admission from Burke, who left Labor flailing for six weeks after the last-minute delay of his speech.



The minister blew the whistle on a bipartisan, two-decade miscalculation since John Howard liberalised Australia’s migration rules in the early 2000s. “Effectively, the decision that Australia took when we had a demand-driven program was to say that if employers can get the workers that they need and our educational institutions can get the students who are willing to pay, and we get the business, then infrastructure and housing will take

care of themselves,” he said. “That is no longer the experience of Australians. That is no longer the view of Australia.” The failure to maintain public confidence in the program, displayed in a litany of opinion polls, has created a void that’s been filled by an opportunistic populist who feels so unrestrained as to outrageously suggest that none of Australia’s 800,000 Muslims are good people. A 2024 study in the Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance found that every one per cent rise in immigration led to between 1.8 to 3 per cent rise in support for far-right parties across 4500 electoral results in Europe.



Former Labor adviser and migration expert Henry Sherrell last month called for a ceiling of one per cent population growth from immigration. Australia exceeded that figure in half of the last 20 years, much more than peer democracies, but just once in the 50 years before that. Related Article Immigration What are Labor’s new migration rules for Australia? Burke called out the use of the term “mass migration”, which some bad-faith conservatives on the right have co-opted but it has increasingly been used by mainstream figures like Opposition Leader Angus Taylor. Labor hopes its intervention in the migration debate will finally cauterise the political problem and show it’s alive to voters’ concerns. Labor knows it cannot win back Hanson’s hardcore supporters, but Albanese’s primary vote has taken a hit and Labor thinks it can recover about 5 per centage points on its primary vote through sustained work to persuade voters they’ve listened. Its opponents will cast Burke’s measures as half-arsed and focused too heavily on backpackers, a cohort One Nation and the Coalition do not view as a problem.



With one and maybe two interest rate rises on the way, don’t expect Hanson to take her foot off the pedal. And prepare for more ugly politics on who comes and goes from Australia. Burke’s warning: Is Australia becoming a guest worker economy?

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination of complainant ‘M’ resumes as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the alleged physical acts occurred.

Alan Jones and his legal team arrive at court on Thursday. Dominic Lorrimer

On Monday, the third of the six complainants, a former athlete dubbed “M”, started giving evidence.

His cross-examination started on Tuesday, and he returns to the witness box today for further questioning by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, after a break in the trial on Wednesday. “M” has told the court:

Jones kissed him on the corner of his mouth at an event in Sydney about a decade ago. “I think I froze at that time,” “M” said.

He rejected suggestions by Bashir on Tuesday that the alleged kiss didn’t happen.

The court has heard Jones texted “M” after the function: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after, had to go back to work. You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

“M” replied: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now; thanks mate xoxo.” The conversation ended in “M” saying “let me know when we can catch up. Lots of love” and Jones replying: “I will darling. Big kisses forever.”

“M” agreed during cross-examination that he did not tell police in his statements that Jones kissed him on the lips at the event. But he said that “I believe I pointed to where it was”.

The complainant said he had “a close relationship with Jones over a period of time” and that “in certain areas” he could go to the broadcaster if he needed help.

The court has previously heard that Jones texted “M” on another occasion, after receiving a photo: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up darling [name] xxx”. “M” said he did not respond immediately. Hours later, Jones wrote: “I hope my message did not upset you. I love you.” The man said he responded the next day, writing: “Not at all mate. It’s nice to be loved.”

The complainant said he had used the word “mate” for many reasons. “I know I’d made it very clear that ... it wasn’t moving into a relationship, so ‘mate’ was my way of pushing back, I guess.”

Reflecting on the messages, “M” told the court that he believed “it’s a person that is in love with me”, adding that he did not return those feelings.

“M” said that on the last occasion he visited Jones at his harbourside apartment, the broadcaster kissed him on the cheek towards his lips and said words to the effect of, “I love you so much, you don’t know how much I love you.” The complainant said he could feel Jones’ genitals on his leg .

The complainant said he pushed the broadcaster away and said, “OK, mate”, in a tone intended to convey “get away from me”, and “got out of there as quickly as possible”.

The court heard Jones had sent the complainant gifts including weekly flowers for years and a dinner set. The complainant agreed he also sent Jones flowers at least once.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Why AI hasn’t taken your job yet
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAI Opinion Why AI hasn’t taken your job yet Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer September 17, 2026 — 3:56pm

September 17, 2026 — 3:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

OpenAI and Anthropic, the dominant frontier labs, have thrown plenty of elbows in their race toward stratospheric, trillion-dollar stockmarket listings. But this week, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, their respective leaders, reached a rare unity ticket along with fellow AI kingpin Elon Musk, calling for a slowdown on artificial intelligence development in the name of saving humanity. This latest bout of fear coming from inside the house began after Anthropic researcher Jacob Poxon resigned last week, accusing the companies of “gambling with our lives”. That announcement prompted his former colleague, Evan Hurbinger, to claim that there was a greater than 10 per cent chance that AI would “kill all humans” within the next decade. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has warned of the risks of unfettered AI growth. Bloomberg How very reassuring. Fortunately, all this has been rejected by US President Donald Trump, who has insisted that attempts to slow down AI are a “sick conspiracy” to let China get ahead, creating the absurd situation where highly valuable companies are begging a recalcitrant government to regulate them.



Related Article AI ‘The world should trust us’: Silicon Valley billionaire’s plea as fight escalates Most people’s concerns about AI are more prosaic. They are less worried about geopolitical rivalry or the prospect of rogue agents creating a devastating virus than whether the machines will take their jobs. In May 2025, the Anthropic boss Amodei predicted that half of all entry-level white-collar jobs would be obliterated in the next five years, sending unemployment rates into the double digits. If there is perhaps one micro-dose of optimism among all the bleak AI news, it is that the tsunami hasn’t yet hit. Instead, employment data from around the world paints a messy, paradox-filled picture. The United States added 162,000 jobs in September, exceeding expectations and strengthening the case for the country’s Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, which it did for the first time since 2023 on Wednesday, much to Trump’s chagrin.



Here in Australia, unemployment crept up unexpectedly to 4.5 per cent in July, its highest rate in the post-COVID era in trend terms. While it’s too soon to tell whether this is the start of a longer-term trend, a 0.1 per cent increase does not seem like the start of a job apocalypse. The rose-tinted view of the AI boom suggests that, like every past industrial revolution, the latest technological rupture will destroy many jobs but create different new ones. Some recent number-crunching in The Economist magazine found that AI had created around 1 million new jobs in the United States, with many attributable to the data centre construction boom. The problem is that while data centres are delivering reliable, well-paid blue-collar work, those jobs are temporary. These AI “factories” don’t resemble the real thing when it comes to employment. Then there’s the fact that they have become a widely despised symbol of everything people resent about AI, with opposition to their development cutting across political lines and threatening to stall that job explosion. Whether that infrastructure delivers in Australia is also contested. The local sector’s lobbyists insist it will “support” 935,000 jobs. But as this masthead recently reported, that figure comes from a line in a 2024 report by consulting firm Mandala (which has partnered with OpenAI in the past) and conflates data centre work with all tech sector jobs. More importantly, the report was commissioned by five of the country’s biggest data centre operators.



Separately, economic think tank the e61 Institute claims there are only around 11,500 data centres workers in Australia nationally. Even if data centres are the future, it’s quite a stretch to imagine soft-handed software engineers (let alone journalists) to retrain as construction workers. Related Article Opinion

AI Will AI kill us all? I doubt it, but let’s reduce the risk ... now Toby Walsh Chief scientist, AI Institute, UNSW Beyond blue-collar work, AI is still causing ruptures in the labour market. Research from Princeton University’s Sania Edlich and Apollo Global Management chief economist Tortsen Slok found that rather than destroying jobs, AI was stifling wage growth. Those “different” jobs created by the AI boom could well be repetitive, boring and lower paid. Witness the poor workers recording themselves doing tasks as dull as screwing lids onto milk bottles to train future generations of robots how to hold things. The next few years could see Australia struggle with the “K-shaped” economy which has characterised the United States post-COVID in which the asset-rich few thrive thanks to a surging stock market and corporate profits, even as wages stagnate for the many. The problem is that AI is moving at such a fast clip that there are many people with opinions, but few are truly informed. Now, it is the frontier lab bosses, the people who have seen what the technology can do, who are sounding the loudest alarms.



At least the unemployment rate probably doesn’t matter too much if humanity is wiped out. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: KPMG consultant admits to ‘gaps’ in its whistleblower report
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWhistleblowers KPMG consultant admits to ‘gaps’ in its whistleblower report Colin Kruger September 17, 2026 — 3:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The authors of a report designed to document KPMG’s whistleblower failings qualified their findings on the basis that they were unable to interview key staff – including the whistleblower – and found gaps in the accounting firm’s records of crucial meetings. Boutique advisory Andrews Group, which penned the report published on Thursday, said it conducted interviews and relied on public and internal documents from KPMG, but admitted this exercise, “despite providing rich information, still left gaps”. KPMG chief executive John Sams (right) said the firm recognises “the challenges created by our own failings” from the whistleblower scandal. Alex Ellinghausen “Some individuals who were associated with and played a pivotal role in the disclosures were, for a variety of reasons, unable to be interviewed. This included the whistleblower,” they said. The report found that KPMG adopted an overly legalistic approach to the complaints levelled against the firm and failed to uphold its core values, which led to the poor treatment of the whistleblower.



KPMG has been under siege after admitting that some of its staff accessed confidential information from corporate clients to win business – a serious breach of the trust in the world of auditing that is essential to the integrity of financial markets. The consultancy confirmed that former employees associated with the whistleblower scandal were unable to be interviewed. The firm has yet to respond to this masthead’s question of whether current employees declined to talk to the report’s authors. The report, which had been commissioned and paid for by the embattled accounting firm, noted there were multiple discussions, meetings and decisions within KPMG Australia relating to the handling of the whistleblower and their disclosures “for which records have not been kept”. “Given these gaps, rather than document findings which would need to be unequivocal, hypotheses were developed,” the report’s authors said. These hypotheses were strongly supported by the weight of evidence and “therefore, despite not being proven or true, are difficult to refute”. Andrews Group said the report didn’t have to determine accountability, but was meant to identify lessons to be learnt from KPMG’s failure to deal with the whistleblower allegations for almost two years.



The scandal cost it some of its most lucrative contracts, with Lendlease and Macquarie Group both dumping KPMG as their external auditor. Related Article Consulting ASIC launches review of whistleblower complaints at accounting giants And it won’t be the end of the matter for the firm. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission told a parliamentary hearing last month that it is conducting its investigations in relation to the whistleblower scandal. This includes looking into documents that KPMG had lodged with the regulator last year to determine if they contained any false or misleading statements. “Initial inquiries are focused on the basis for statements made in that report, including the statement that there were no whistleblower complaints related to audit quality,” ASIC said in a submission to the parliamentary hearing last month.



The scandal first came to light in March – almost two years after the whistleblower made their initial complaint to KPMG – when Labor senator Deborah O’Neill read out the whistleblower’s allegations in parliament. It led to an exodus of KPMG’s most senior executives, including CEO Andrew Yates and chairman Martin Sheppard, and also prompted the sacking of former chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett, who has lodged action to sue the firm. Former KPMG board member Kim Lawry resigned, but is still negotiating her exit after an investigation found screenshots on her phone of confidential Lendlease board documents. She was due to retire last month. KPMG reiterated its apologies to the whistleblower in the report, saying “senior people in our organisation behaved in a manner that was unacceptable and not in line with our values, and when someone had the courage to raise their concerns, we did not respond as we should have.” The report made recommendations to help remedy KPMG’s whistleblower failings by establishing an independent integrity office at the firm, and appointing a dedicated whistleblower protection officer. World.title: Coroner finds shark control measures ‘appropriate’ after teen killed
World.content:
NationalQueenslandInquest Coroner finds shark control measures ‘appropriate’ after teen killed Cloe Read September 17, 2026 — 3:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An inquest will not be held into the shark attack that killed Queensland teenager Charlize Zmuda, with a coroner finding the Queensland government’s management of drum lines and nets to be appropriate. Charlize Zmuda, 17, a dedicated lifesaver, died in February 2024 after she was bitten by a shark at Woorim Beach, north of Brisbane, just before 5pm. In findings released on Thursday, coroner Carol Lee found that Zmuda died from injuries to her right upper limbs due to a bull shark attack. Charlize Zmuda (left) loved the beach and had been a member of the lifesaving club since she was a young girl. Zmuda had been at the unpatrolled beach with a friend when she decided to swim alone. A short time later, her friend, who was waiting on the beach, saw a commotion in the water, heard a scream and saw blood.



Zmuda was found floating on her back, and the alarm was raised. Emergency services, and a lifeguard who rushed from a patrolled beach, were unable to revive the teenager. In the findings, Lee reviewed Queensland’s current shark control measures, which include drum lines and drone patrols. Hundreds gathered on Woorim Beach in February last year to pay tribute to Charlize Zmuda. Darren England At the time of the attack at Woorim, the drone trial was in its first phase and conducted over the summer school holiday periods until further evaluation of its success, Lee said. “Given the availability of funding remaining in the budget from days lost due to bad weather, Surf Life Saving Queensland were additionally flying drones on weekends up to and including February 2, 2025, the day before the incident,” Lee said.



“Shark nets are not suitable at the Woorim Beach location due to the high tidal currents experienced in this area which tend to twist the nets or drag it off station, which would render it ineffective.” She said while nets and drum lines reduce the risk, they were not an impenetrable barrier. Charlize Zmuda. TikTok As of March 2025, there were 18 shark control drum lines located off Woorim, about 300 to 350 metres from the beach. Between January 2024 and March 2025, there were four sharks found at the Woorim Beach drum lines – a bull whaler shark, a blacktip whaler shark, a bull shark and a tiger shark.



Lee said substantial reviews were now under way through shark management plans, in addition to a significant funding investment. Related Article Sharks SharkSmart drone program expanded at south-east beaches amid criticism of nets “This demonstrates an evolution of Queensland’s shark-mitigation approach, from the operational status at the time of Charlize’s death to an enhanced, technology-enabled, research-driven program designed to reduce risk across the state’s coastlines,” she said. Lee said having considered the information from the department and the government’s response to shark control measures, she was satisfied there was an appropriate risk mitigation framework in place to reduce shark attacks, with the aim of protecting human life whilst maintaining environmental protection. “Against that background, I am not satisfied that it is in the public interest to hold an inquest,” she said, adding that publishing the findings online would raise awareness to prevent future deaths.



“There is also no uncertainty or conflict of evidence to justify the use of the judicial forensic process and no suspicious circumstances that have not been resolved or resulted in criminal charges.” After her death, Zmuda’s mother, Renee, said her daughter was a shining light who touched the lives of everyone she met. “She loved the beach, and it truly was her happiest place on earth,” she said at the time. World.title: One of Brisbane’s best restaurants gets a cookbook
World.content:
Eating outFood One of Brisbane’s best restaurants gets a cookbook Now you can cook zucchini chips at home, along with more than 100 other recipes that span Hellenika’s 16-year history. Matt Shea September 17, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Books are hard, Simon Gloftis says. And he doesn’t mean cookbooks. Just, any book. “I couldn’t even fathom the idea of how I would do a book. I struggle even now to read and write properly,” the restaurateur says disarmingly. “For me, it was a big deal. It wasn’t a matter of jotting down some ideas. It was like asking me to jump off a building.” Simon Gloftis with the Hellenika cookbook. Courtesy of Hellenika That’s one of the reasons it’s taken this long to produce the new Hellenika cookbook, which will be released October 1. The others? A pandemic and a couple of restaurant openings (Sushi Room and Sunshine, both in 2022). “It’s been a process,” he says. “I almost gave up and then I was at a dinner and [co-writer] Marie[-Christine] Sourris’ husband was there and said, ‘Mate, finish this book. You need to do it.’ … And I thought, ‘OK, I’d better put my money where my mouth is’.”



Related Article Exclusive Melbourne game-changers announce ambitious first Brisbane restaurant The result is a 272-page cookbook that presents 110 recipes spanning the entire history of the popular James Street restaurant, split into 12 sections, from breakfast to mezedes, mains, desserts and even cocktails. Besides Sourris, the book features photography by Annika Kafcaloudis and styling by Stephanie Stamatis, both from Melbourne. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Gloftis said it was the book’s publishing consultant, Julie Gibbs, who convinced him to make it so extensive. Yes, you can now cook the restaurant’s zucchini chips at home. Courtesy of Hellenika “They said, ‘Simon, just own it. They’re yours. Go out there and give them everything. Don’t hide one thing’,” Gloftis says. “So that’s what we’ve done. We have the entire menu on there … all the tricks are in there.”



So yes, you can cook the restaurant’s iconic zucchini chips, slow-cooked lamb shoulder, and spanner crab kritharaki. The emphasis throughout, Gloftis says, is on how simple Mediterranean cooking can be. “My motto from when we first opened Hellenika was, ‘If it doesn’t need that one extra ingredient, it doesn’t go in’,” Gloftis says. Hellenika restaurant at The Calile Hotel. Markus Ravik But this is also about telling the narrative of Hellenika, from its beginnings at Nobby Beach perched above the Gold Coast Highway, to Theo Kampolis coming onboard as partner in 2017, to the restaurant’s expansion to Brisbane in 2018, where it made its home at The Calile Hotel. The cookbook also forms one part of Hellenika’s 15-year celebrations (it actually opened 16 years ago on the Gold Coast, in March 2010) with the restaurant also hosting a pop-up at Miami Marketta in late October. That event sold out in a matter of days.



The cookbook is available October 1. Courtesy of Hellenika. Hellenika wasn’t Gloftis’ only venue in those early Gold Coast years – there was The Fish House, which closed in 2020 after he sold the restaurant in 2016, and Nineteen at the Star, which he exited from in 2019. So, what made Hellenika stick, both for him and diners? “There was very little shared dining when we opened,” he says. “There was no one doing lamb shoulder falling off the bone with that kind of quality … we were flying King George whiting up from Melbourne every day. And the Greek community [got right behind the restaurant]. You can’t fool them. That’s why it’s stood the test of time. “I wanted to call the book The First 15 Years because I truly believe Hellenika is going nowhere. Hellenika’s story has a long way to play out.”

World.title: Clover Moore lashes NSW government’s ‘extraordinary’ intervention in Town Hall square
World.content:
NationalNSWPlanning Clover Moore lashes NSW government’s ‘extraordinary’ intervention in Town Hall square Megan Gorrey September 17, 2026 — 3:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

City of Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore has accused the NSW government of attempting to block a controversial $150 million plan to raze seven buildings for a new civic square, after Planning Minister Paul Scully sought independent advice on whether he should seize control of the project. Citing the cost and prominent location of the council’s long-vaunted Town Hall square, Scully on Wednesday intervened by referring the project to the NSW Independent Planning Commission for advice on whether it should be declared “state significant” development decided by the government. Lord Mayor Clover Moore says more public space was “not a nice to have″⁣, it is essential infrastructure that we are committed to delivering”. City of Sydney “The proposal, as it stands, would have significant impact on the commercial heart of Sydney’s CBD, requiring the demolition of seven buildings and an expenditure of at least $150 million in ratepayer funds,” Scully said. The move prompted a fiery response from Moore, who said she was “shocked and disappointed” by the Minns government’s “extraordinary and highly unusual intervention in established planning processes”, which she was concerned “could delay or even block the Town Hall Square project”.



Their remarks set the stage for a showdown between Moore’s council and the Minns government over the square – which was first proposed in the 1980s – in the run-up to the March state election. Related Article Exclusive

Planning Sydney might get a new civic square. One building stands in the way For the past three decades, the council has been gradually acquiring a parcel of properties between George and Pitt streets opposite Town Hall, which it has hoped would eventually constitute a rare public domain in the centre of the city. The council in February voted to accelerate demolition of the buildings, including Woolworths supermarket, stating its ambition to complete demolition and construction within about six years. Moore said Scully had not raised any concerns when the council briefed him on the project in 2025, and the government had approved its acquisition of the final property needed to deliver the square.



“Against that history, the timing and nature of [this] intervention inevitably raises questions, particularly as political attention begins to turn towards the next state election,” Moore said. “If the government ultimately uses its powers to stop this project rather than simply scrutinise it, that would be a deeply concerning and regressive intervention in the delivery of important public infrastructure.” The City of Sydney’s Lord Mayor Clover Moore, NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully and Transport Minister John Graham in The Rocks on Wednesday. Sitthixay Ditthavong Scully has powers under the NSW Environmental Planning and Assessment Act to declare a project as state significant if he has received and made public advice from the IPC about the state or regional planning significance of the proposal. He said the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure would prepare an assessment report on the square for the commission. Moore said the council was still reviewing directions issued to the council, which would prevent it from determining demolition orders or development applications for the project, and what they would mean for the square’s delivery timeframe. The project was estimated for completion in 2031.



Moore said the project would be assessed by an independent planner and determined by the Central Sydney Planning Committee, most members of which have been appointed by the state government. “Any suggestion that council had a conflict of interest or isn’t managing approval appropriately is incorrect. We remain confident in the merits of the proposal and see no planning reason why it should not ultimately be supported,” Moore said. The council says the space could be used as a sporting event live site. City of Sydney In August, the council revealed designs for the 4200-square-metre plaza, prepared by Sydney design practice JPW and landscape architects ASPECT Studios, featuring eucalypts, moving water, seating and circular paving patterns to provide an outdoor venue for large events and celebrations including markets, festivals, concerts and sports event live-sites. The square would have an Aboriginal name. The proposal to demolish the buildings for the square has triggered a wave of opposition from the Business NSW lobby group, Woolworths and The Daily Telegraph.



Business NSW executive director Paul Nicolaou said the government had “made the right call in putting the brakes on the City of Sydney’s plan to demolish seven buildings in the commercial heart of the CBD in favour of a controversial Town all square that would cost a minimum $150 million”. Related Article City life Cars out, diners in: Final section of George Street set for $25m revamp Nicolaou said the plaza concept “might have been a nice-to-have when it was first mooted more than 30 years ago”, but it was “not the right project amid the economic realities of 2026”. “The $150 million could be directed to more important needs including crisis accommodation for the hundreds of people sleeping rough in our city every night or living in encampments on our streets.” The Independent Planning Commission was formed in 2018 to decide, and provide advice on, the state’s most complex and contentious developments. In 2019, a three-member panel killed off The Star’s $530 million plan to build a 66-storey hotel and apartment tower above its Pyrmont casino. World.title: The first Immortal? Where four-time champion’s legacy places her in history
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cast an eye to the future and consider who the first rugby league Immortal of the women’s game might be. Given her status as a trailblazer, State of Origin hero and four-time premiership winner, Ali Brigginshaw’s name must be front and centre of those discussions. “Ali Brigginshaw: when you hear that name, you know she’s something special,” Brisbane Broncos teammate Julia Robinson told this masthead. “What she’s done for the game is incredible. She’s just one of those players and people you just look up to … you want to play for, and whenever she goes out there she plays with her heart on her sleeve and is an inspiration to all. “She’s inspired so many girls, she’s going to have this legacy forever. There are so many girls who can be Immortals, but Ali is definitely up there.” Each game could be Brigginshaw’s last, with the 36-year-old stressing she would not be backflipping on her decision to retire at season’s end as she sought to eradicate the “mum guilt” she felt being on the road with two stepdaughters at home. Broncos players Julia Robinson, Ali Brigginshaw and Chelsea Lenarduzzi after winning the 2025 NRLW grand final against the Roosters. NRL Images “People have definitely questioned that response, but to me, I think I’ve done a lot in the game, and I’m happy with where I’m at,” Brigginshaw laughed.



“I want to see what else is out there; I want to spend time with my family, thinking about holidays and all that. It’s time to see what Ali can do now.” The Brisbane champion was reduced to tears after a final round triumph of the Warriors, when New Zealand players performed a Hakka in her honour – ending a shortened last regular season in which she copped a three-game suspension for a dangerous tackle which left her “heartbroken”. Celebrations of her career, according to Brigginshaw, needed to be discarded for now, as the Broncos plot another piece of silverware – beginning with Saturday’s elimination final against Newcastle. Loading “I’ve always just said I play the game that I love, and I’m lucky that I get to be a part of all these moments of games that we never even thought we’d be standing here doing and watching women’s rugby league,” Brigginshaw said. “It wasn’t really spoken about or thought about when I first started. Playing the game I love, leaving a legacy for young girls to always have rugby league available to them, it’s a crazy world I live in that I get to do that. “But it’s why I wanted to celebrate and have my family around at the last home game of the rounds because the focus isn’t me, the focus is the finals’ series. I never want to make something about me.”



While no women have been included in rugby league’s most illustrious club across the game’s 118-year history – Ron Coote named as the 14th Immortal in 2024 – the first female members of the NRL Hall of Fame who were named that same year has suggested an inaugural inductee beckons. Those Hall of Fame members – Natalie Dwyer , Katrina Fanning , Tarsha Gale , Veronica White , Karyn Murphy , and Tahnee Norris – would come into consideration, while modern-day stars such as five-time premiership victor and two-time Dally M Medal winner Tamika Upton is already arguably the code’s greatest player, despite being just 29. Upton – who served as co-captain alongside Brigginshaw last year, before the latter stepped down for this campaign – laughed when it was put to her that she could factor into that debate, before shifting attention to the role Brigginshaw has played in pioneering the women’s space. Related Article NRL 2026 The boxer, teacher and curse breaker: The coach who shone from Bennett’s shadow “Her story is definitely not closed in rugby league. I don’t know what the future holds for her, but I’m sure she’ll be in and around the fold in some capacity, so she’s still adding to that [legacy],” Upton said. “You want to go out with a win for Ali – I think she is the NRLW. It’s going to be weird, I haven’t really thought about it too much just yet because we’re still in it, and she’s still here, but there hasn’t been an NRLW game without her in it or in the fold.”



Brigginshaw has no intention of closing the book on her rugby league journey – one which began playing juniors with the boys before a Queensland and Australia debut in 2009, nine years before the NRLW launched when a professional women’s outlet seemed to be a pipe dream. Murphy remains the only woman at the helm of a senior side, with her Gold Coast Titans finishing second, and Brigginshaw hinted she harboured a desire to join her in the coaching ranks. “I’ve been around for a long time and had many coaches where I feel I can pass on the knowledge to the younger girls, but I always dreamt and still dream of coaching 15, 16-year-old boys,” Brigginshaw revealed. “I had a coach who was a female in the boys space when I first started, and something about that was something I wanted to do. You never know where it’s going to land, but I’m pretty much open to all opportunities. Ali Brigginshaw has been a staple of the Australian, Queensland and Broncos side since the NRLW began in 2018. Getty Images “I know it’s time for me to step away because the young generations are coming, and they’re ready to take on the next step.” That coaching future should not come as a shock, given Brigginshaw has already served as a mentor and player to aspire towards for the next generation.

World.title: Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer ejected from Parliament for using c-word
World.content:
Te Pāti Māori's co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer has been ejected from Parliament after using the c-word, allegedly to refer to the Assistant Speaker.

Politicians have been debating the Move-On orders legislation under urgency.

Ngarewa-Packer admitted she used the word which had been used three times in Parliament and was asked to leave.

Labour's Willie Jackson was then assisted from the chamber after raising an objection.

Te Pāti Māori's MP Oriini Kaipara had been making a speech and used the word "bullcrap", which prompted Assistant Speaker Maureen Pugh to remind her to "keep the language Parliamentary".

Green MP Julie Anne Genter then began her speech but NZ First's Casey Costello raised a point of order, saying Ngarewa-Packer had "used a word which I will not use that begins with C ... the fact that it has been used once in this house does not make it common use, I find it particularly offensive and disrespectful to you madam Speaker."

She said "it was directed at you, Madam Speaker".

Ngarewa-Packer then raised her own point, saying "three times the word c--- has been used in this House, by the government ... so either that word is offensive or bull-crap is."

Pugh said she personally found that offensive and asked Ngarewa-Packer to leave.

"Are you now going to challenge my ruling? I'm not going to entertain a conversation on this, the member will leave the Chamber," Pugh said.

NZ First MP Casey Costello. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Jackson then stood to say he did not wish to challenge the ruling, prompting Pugh to say "that's good, it's a good time to sit down then," but he continued, saying the word had been used in front of the Parliament.

Pugh told him to "sit down, sit down now," but Jackson continued to argue the point, until Pugh ordered him to leave as well.

When he did not, and Jackson continued shouting across Parliament, Pugh calmly directed the Sergeant at Arms to "assist Mr Jackson".

She then sought clarification from Kaipara, who said she had not used the C-word, and Pugh apologised to her.

Ngarewa-Packer's original use of the word was not picked up by the microphones.

Speaking to reporters afterwards, she explained she had been objecting to Kaipara being "growled" for saying "bullcrap" and she had been complaining in an aside "oh crike's sake, they've used the word c--- in the House before".

"Casey then stood up and narked on me ... and told the speaker, who then stood up, and I think she thought - because Casey didn't name me - I think she thought Oriini said it."

She said she had not been using the word to refer to Pugh.

Jackson, speaking to reporters alongside Ngarewa-Packer, said Pugh had seemed to think she was.

"No, of course not. No," Ngarewa-Packer said. "I was talking to Oriini, and I said to Oriini ... 'whatever, they've used c--- in the House before and so ... if you want to look at the threshold, bullcrap's not up there."

Jackson said it was hypocrisy for Ngarewa-Packer to be ejected when ACT's Brooke van Velden had previously said the word and not been cautioned.

World.title: Volunteer aviation investigators spot possible wreckage of plane missing since 1978
World.content:
Volunteer aviation investigators believe they may have spotted the submerged wreckage of a charter plane that disappeared almost 50 years ago with seven people on board in South Westland.

Police announced on Wednesday that a renewed search would be launched in Lake Moeraki near Haast for the single-engine Piper Cherokee 6.

ZK-EBU took off from Dunedin's Taieri airfield for a scenic flight through the Southern Fiords on 29 December 1978.

As poor weather rolled in from the Tasman Sea, it vanished without a trace, with 28-year-old pilot Edward "Ned" Morrison, five members of the Dunedin-based Stuart family and 20-year-old David Hogg on board.

Volunteers from the group Lost Aircraft New Zealand have spent decades on their own investigation work and searches for the plane.

Air ambulance pilot Nathan Mauchline said the group had a breakthrough a few months ago when team leader Gavin Grimmer took their search off dry land and onto water.

"We've been doing sonar searches of the lake and we came across an object that measures about the size of the plane," he said.

"If it is there, I'm pretty confident that they will find it. We believe that it's in about five metres of water."

Lodge theory

Mauchline said the group had earlier decided to probe a whitebaiter's report of a low-flying plane heading inland up the Moeraki River at dusk.

They discovered that the plane's pilot had visited a lodge at the end of Lake Moeraki two weeks before the flight, spawning a theory, he said.

"It's getting to the end of the day, there's no radio communications and he thinks to himself, well that lodge I stayed at a few weeks ago, I remember seeing a big field, a big kilometre-long field off the end that I could land the plane in and I know this lodge and they'll put us up for the night," Mauchline said.

If the Piper Cherokee crashed into the lake, the passengers would have been trapped in the cabin, he said.

"What happens with a Cherokee is if the wing impacts or there's any twist in the fuselage at all, all the doors would be locked. They would be stuck."

The group handed their sonar evidence to police, who agreed to work with Defence Force and Coastguard crews to try to find the object.

Acting Inspector Mark Kirkwood said the search was an evidence-gathering exercise.

"There's no confirmation that there's plane wreckage there but the image does warrant further investigation," he said.

Volunteers, relatives of passengers thrilled

Navy specialists would start by using an advanced side-scan sonar to try to find the object, Kirkwood said.

"If we do locate something of a large size and metal, or similar, we will deploy the police divers," he said.

Grimmer said while the plane "ain't found until it's found", he and his volunteers and relatives of the ZK-EBU passengers were thrilled.

"We are all completely blown away after all these years [by] the effort the police, military and Coastguard are prepared to put in to hopefully bring about finality to the families and put an end to this long overdue mystery," he said.

Former Te Anau police officer Lloyd Matheson said early searches for the plane focused on land.

The search area was vast and rugged, he said.

"The last known point of interest was Milford, heading towards Puysegur. There are massive fjords, sea coastal areas, mountains-a huge area to search. It was like looking for a needle in the haystack, really," he said.

'One of New Zealand's biggest aviation mysteries'

Fiorland's John von Tunzelman was a crew member on one of the search helicopters and spent almost 30 hours peering into dense bush and remote beaches.

"[It was] most disappointing not to find them. It's one of those things that you remember because you put so much effort into it," he said.

"If they can recover the wreckage, they may be able to establish what caused a forced landing into Lake Moeraki. There's all these questions to answer, hopefully that will be achieved."

Volunteer investigator Jonathan Mauchline said the renewed search had the potential to provide long-awaited answers to loved ones.

"The families of these people are still alive and just haven't had closure for 50 years," he said.

"To find this airplane puts to bed one of New Zealand's biggest aviation mysteries and it'll bring closure to all the people involved."

The three-day operation begins at the Lake Moeraki boat ramp on Monday 21 September.

Police have asked the public to stay clear of the search area.

World.title: FENZ Minister Brooke van Velden questions CEO over withheld information
World.content:
FENZ Minister Brooke van Velden says she no longer has confidence in the organisation's chief executive, following a "serious breach" of the 'no-surprises' clause.

"It is of a nature that is so significant that I no longer have confidence in the chief executive of Fire and Emergency or have confidence that the information I'm receiving is correct," said van Velden.

She said chief executive Kerry Gregory withheld information from her for a "full year" on a matter of a "seriously significant incident". The matter had now been referred to the Serious Fraud Office.

Van Velden said information had also potentially been withheld from the board.

She couldn't provide detail on the issue, but said she became aware in the last fortnight that significant information had been withheld by the chief executive, "even after he received external advice telling him that he needed to let me know".

"I immediately contacted the board chair, as well as the chief executive, to let him know that I have no longer any confidence in the chief executive.

"Having information of a significant nature withheld from me is not something I would expect of a senior official within the public service."

She added it was a "serious breach of trust".

Van Velden asked the board to meet "immediately to maintain or restore my confidence". The board will meet in the next few days.

A scathing select committee report into FENZ recommended the government look at changing the organisation's board and whether it should be allowed to buy its own firetrucks.

Van Velden said the report was disappointing reading, but also noted some of the recommendations were "things that I can't actually do as a minister".

"I'm surprised that those recommendations are in there, because they're of such an operational matter that it would actually be a breach of the Crown Entities Act for me to be that involved."

Van Velden emphasised the breach of confidence was a separate issue to the report.

A FENZ spokesperson clarified to RNZ that the original incident, not Gregory, had been referred to the Serious Fraud Office.

"The matter referred to is historical, from prior to 2021, and relates to Fire and Emergency's administration of the levy scheme.

World.title: School curriculum rewrite 'ideological', Crown breached multiple treaty principles - Waitangi Tribunal
World.content:
The Waitangi Tribunal says the government's rewrite of the school curriculum was ideological, aided by people hostile to Māori knowledge, and breached multiple Treaty principles.

This report follows the Tribunal's stage one interim report concerning proposed changes to treaty provisions in the Education and Training Act and precedes another report into the removal of school boards' treaty obligations.

In her letter to ministers, presiding officer Rachel Mullins said the adoption of a 'knowledge-rich' curriculum - which stresses the importance of all students acquiring the same knowledge, in sequence and structure, and progressing together - as government policy was a predetermined course to return to a one-size-fits-all style of education.

"For its part, 'restoring balance' to the teaching of Aotearoa New Zealand's histories has effectively meant lessening the emphasis on local and Māori experiences (including the focus on the treaty itself) and recentring international events and 'the histories and traditions of all New Zealand's people'."

Mullins said the government made changes to the curriculum in spite of the opposition of both Māori and the education sector and despite the lack of solid evidence that a knowledge-rich approach will reduce inequities.

"The Minister of Education's approach has been essentially ideological, and she surrounded herself with supporters of that position in, for example, her Curriculum Ministerial Advisory Group - which has included members either unenthusiastic about or outwardly hostile to mātauranga Māori."

The Tribunal found the Crown, through its actions related to developing a 'knowledge-rich curriculum' informed by the 'science of learning', breached a number of treaty principles.

Including that the Crown breached the principle of partnership through its lack of meaningful engagement and consensus-building with Māori about the new draft national curriculum.

And that it breached the principle of active protection by moving ahead with a knowledge-rich approach in the absence of evidence that it will reduce Māori inequities.

The Tribunal recommended the Crown recommit to working in partnership with Māori in education, and return to working with Māori on designing a truly indigenous Māori-medium and kaupapa Māori curriculum through Te Marautanga o Aotearoa.

"We believe that partnership is the key to reducing inequity, not the imposition of an overseas model untested in Aotearoa New Zealand and so strongly opposed by Māori educators," Mullins wrote.

Minister of Education Erica Stanford said she would take the Tribunal's report into consideration.

"I always make sure that article three of the Treaty and ensuring that Māori outcomes when it comes to education there is equity there, that's very important to me and that's why you are starting to see a turnaround in results for the first time in twenty years."

The government did consult with almost a hundred Māori academics and experts when creating the curriculum, she said.

"Of course I will take [the Tribunal's] considerations with care and I will consider them, but it is my intention that we get those curriculum areas out by the end of the year."

Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan said the Tribunal report showed the government had been captured by overseas organisations with a clear ideological agenda.

"[The government] has prioritsed such lobbyists over the interests of Māori, over the interests of experts here domestically."

In response Stanford said the reality is overseas experts are needed to make sure the curriculum is internationally benchmarked.

The Educational Institute said the government should pause and work with Māori and educators.

"If the minister ignores these latest recommendations, it will not only deepen the prejudice faced by ākonga Māori but also contradict her stated goal of achieving equitable outcomes," the union's president Ripeka Lessels said.

World.title: Top Kiwi cyclist questions Cycling NZ's Road World Championships funding policy
World.content:
Cycling New Zealand's long-held policy of not funding elite riders for the Road World Championships has come under fire from professional rider Finn Fisher-Black who has described the situation as creating "a strange dynamic".

Fisher-Black will pay his own way to compete at his third elite Road World Championships alongside Ben Oliver, Corbin Strong, George Bennett, Joshua Kench and Laurence Pithie in Canada next week.

In line with Cycling New Zealand's (CNZ) selection criteria of the last four annual Road World Championships a women's team of Bronwyn MacGregor, Ella Wyllie, Henrietta Christie and Niamh Fisher-Black will also compete without funding from the national body.

Finn Fisher-Black highlighted the potential for self-funding to cause a division amongst the riders who could put self-interest ahead of the team on the world stage.

"It's a strange dynamic for NZ because we don't get funding from Cycling New Zealand; we all pay to be there, so it's also a strange dynamic, like we all kind of also want to do our own race," Fisher-Black told Cycling News.

"But we're all good mates from New Zealand so it'll probably be about looking out for each other during the race and try to have numbers during the final and take it from there."

The 24-year-old said CNZ "prioritise the track" and questioned why after his sister Niamh had finished second at last year's Road World Championships there was no change to the funding situation for road riders.

In a statement, Cycling New Zealand chief executive officer Simon Peterson told RNZ the national body was predominately funded by High-Performance New Zealand for track cycling, which is unchanged in the LA 2028 Olympic cycle.

"The achievements of New Zealand road cyclists have been impressive in both women and men, the current position has been clearly communicated to all riders for some years and before they make a decision to compete at the World Championships," Peterson said.

"Consistent with prior years, CNZ has committed $70,000 for the Road World Championships this year to cover UCI requirements and on the ground delivery. This is in-line with our investment agreement with High Performance Sport New Zealand."

Fisher-Black, who rides professionally with Red Bull- BORA-hansgrohe, finished on the podium at last month's Tour de Pologne and told Cycling News he was targeting a top 10 finish on the hilly Montreal course.

World.title: Cars bearing Chinese police markings stir unease in Auckland
World.content:
Police have moved to reassure Auckland's Chinese community after cars displaying what appeared to be foreign police markings have been spotted on the city's streets.

Four reports relating to two vehicles prompted officers to speak with their owners, Auckland Central area commander inspector Grae Anderson said.

The vehicles had reportedly unsettled some members of the Chinese community who had spotted the vehicles on the road.

A Chinese New Zealander spotted a vehicle that looked like a Chinese police car parked on the corner of Shortland and Princes Streets in central Auckland on 10 September.

The witness spoke on condition of anonymity due to a fear her ability to visit China might be compromised.

"There is quite an explicit logo on the side of the door saying 'Gong An', or Chinese police," she said.

"The patterns look identical [to the markings on real Chinese police cars]."

The witness said the markings would make some in the Chinese community feel uneasy.

"It's quite frightening, as over the years that we have heard rumours [about] Chinese police operating overseas," she said, noting that security forces in China carried enormous power.

"It's pretty intimidating [for] a Chinese person who understands the context behind it."

Anderson told RNZ on Thursday that police acknowledged the concerns raised by members of the public.

"The owners [of the cars bearing police markings] were made aware that the vehicles had caused some concerns and indicated that wasn't their intent," Anderson said.

"We had a discussion with the owners and suggested that the removal of the decals would prevent the reoccurrence of further concerns and both parties indicated they would remove the decals."

Anderson reassured the community that the vehicles were not New Zealand Police vehicles and did not have any official status or authority on behalf of New Zealand Police.

He encouraged people with further concerns relating to the matter to get in touch with police.

The Chinese Embassy had earlier said the vehicles had nothing to do with China.

A variety of decals used to decorate vehicles are available online, with police markings from different countries among the options.

In addition to the cars displaying Chinese police markings, other images of vehicles in New Zealand bearing Japan and US police insignias have been shared on social media.

When first approached by RNZ, police said it was an offence for an ordinary vehicle to resemble a police vehicle, craft or conveyance under the 2008 Policing Act.

"A person commits an offence who, without reasonable excuse, represents any vehicle, craft, or other conveyance as being in the service of the Police in circumstances likely to lead a person to believe the vehicle, craft, or conveyance is in the service of the Police," the relevant provision in the act states.

Police clarified the legislation only applied to New Zealand Police.

Al Gillespie, a law professor at the University of Waikato, said decorating a car as a foreign police vehicle wasn't illegal itself, but more might need to be done in the area if the problem kept arising.

"I think it's going to cause ... problems, and you might need to have some rules around it going forward in future, especially if these are used to intimidate people," he said.

"But, at the moment, the law is about New Zealand police vehicles."

Gillespie said outlawing certain markings that were currently available as decals would need to be specifically banned by legislation in the same way as gang insignias.

He said it was good for police to raise concerns about intimidation with owners directly as a soft path going forward.

"This is a grey area, and it may be that we want law in this place so that no one can do it," he said.

Gillespie stressed that foreign agencies had no jurisdiction in New Zealand.

"Foreign police have no powers in New Zealand," he said.

World.title: Labour to pause government’s school curriculum overhaul, NCEA changes if elected
World.content:
The Labour Party says it will freeze the government's school curriculum overhaul and NCEA changes if elected to power but has not committed to ditching them altogether.

The party's education spokesperson Ginny Andersen announced this afternoon it would also create an independent body, the Independent Council for Curriculum and Assessment (ICCA), to lead decisions on what was taught in schools and how it is assessed.

She said the updated English and maths curriculums would continue, but all others would be paused for a year while experts figured out what should go ahead.

It said the NCEA, due to be phased out from 2028 to 2030, would stay until 2029 while the new curriculum and assessment body considered it.

"Whether governments are left or right, curriculum and assessment decisions should be guided by evidence, educational expertise and what will improve learning," she said.

"Governments will continue to set the broad goals and expectations for our education system. That democratic accountability will remain. But detailed curriculum and assessment design should be led by expert educators and assessment specialists, not rewritten according to the preferences of individual ministers."

Last month, the Principals Federation called for the creation of an independent curriculum and assessment council.

Teacher union the Educational Institute said educators would welcome Labour's support for an independent body because it would stop curriculum instability becoming the norm.

"The rushed and sweeping curriculum changes since the coalition government assumed office in 2023 have created significant turbulence for teachers, school leaders, ākonga, and their whānau," the union's president Ripeka Lessels said.

World.title: Privileges Committee chair calls urgent meeting over leaked FENZ report
World.content:
The powerful privileges committee has been called to an unscheduled meeting on Thursday by its chair to discuss how to handle a complaint about a leaked report.

On Wednesday the Speaker, Gerry Brownlee, told MPs in the House he had received a letter from National MP Tim Costley "raising as a matter of privilege the divulging of a draft report of the Governance and Administration Committee contrary to Standing Orders".

The complaint was in regards to a story published in The Post titled, "Leaked FENZ inquiry report rips into leadership dysfunction, calls for board replacement".

Brownlee said the publishing of the leaked report was "a serious matter, not merely a technical one".

"The unauthorised release of confidential select committee proceedings has previously been considered a contempt. It is essential that the confidence of proceedings is respected to enable committee members to work together. Furthermore, the House is entitled to be the first recipient of the finding of its committees," Brownlee said.

The matter was referred to the Privileges Committee - Parliament's court equivalent - and with just three sitting days remaining of this parliamentary term it has prompted the committee's chair, Chris Bishop, to call a meeting.

"The matter's been referred to the privileges committee, and we we are having our initial meeting, because you know Parliament rises very soon, so we don't have very much time," Bishop told reporters on his way into Question Time on Thursday.

"We've got to get on with it, so I called a meeting for this afternoon. It'll just be largely a process-based meeting, we just have to consider what we do next."

One of the options being considered is carrying the issue over to the next term, "because there may not be enough time to deal with the matter".

"I just want to see the complaint and work out what the next steps are, so I don't want to get ahead of the committee, and I'm just one member, I'm just the chair, so we'll just work our way through that," Bishop said.

The Speaker noted in his comments to the House "it is unfortunate that the Parliament has just over two weeks left until dissolution, but the timing of this matter was not a choice made by me or the House."

World.title: 'Cinema' expected as rival wingers go to battle one last time
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Robert Toia will have a front-row seat to the last instalment of the battle between teammate Mark Nawaqanitawase and Ronaldo Mulitalo, and the Sydney Roosters centre is bracing himself for more box-office entertainment.

"Cinema, that's what I expect — [another chapter in] an ongoing battle and I think if we get the win that will top it off," Toia said.

Saturday's sudden-death semifinal could be Nawaqanitawase's last in the NRL, with the 26-year-old former Wallabies star switching back to the 15-man code with Japanese side Saitama Wild Knights.

Few could have imagined the impact Nawaqanitawase would have had in rugby league when he crossed codes after the Paris Olympics.

There have been highlights in just about every game — be it his grubber ahead and tip toe down the sideline against Canterbury last season that was named try of the year, or last weekend's tap-ahead intercept before climbing off the deck and racing away to score against Penrith.

"It's pretty hard to stay alert because you don't know what's going to happen," Toia said.

"I didn't expect him to do what he's been doing, I think he has shocked everyone."

Nawaqanitawase's long-running on-field feud with the sledge-happy Mulitalo — the pair of wingers openly admire each other off it — has made Roosters-Sharks games fixtures to savour.

"There's a bit of competitiveness there but I think that is what makes the game so great — it's the best of the best going at it with each other," said Roosters forward Siua Wong.

Toia's opposite number KL Iro said of Mulitalo: "He can get personal at times but after the game he always makes sure he clears it up straight away and shakes his hand.
